sources.title: How Cognition's Scott Wu bought Windsurf in a weekend and bets on RL, agents and curated data
sources.originalTitle: Cognition CEO Scott Wu on Acquiring Windsurf: The Process, The Deal, The Rationale
sources.summary: Scott Wu explains how Cognition struck the Windsurf deal between Friday night and Monday morning, why a "husk" left behind can hold real value, and why he thinks AI coding is only starting. He also covers usage-based pricing, agents vs IDEs, RL and curated data, and takes feedback on Cognition's marketing.

principles.text: In a crisis acquisition, move in days not months: verbal deal Saturday, legal Sunday, sign and announce Monday.
principles.quote: get to a verbal agreement on Saturday hash out all the details and the terms and the legal on Sunday get everything signed and done on Monday morning

principles.text: Value accrues wherever you build real differentiation, regardless of layer (chips, models, apps, infra).
principles.quote: it occurs wherever you are able to establish real differentiation in your space.

principles.text: Price AI agents far below the value of the human time they replace.
principles.quote: we try to make things so that they're about 10x cheaper than um you know than than basically the value of your time

principles.text: For a defined vertical, a small curated dataset with the right environment and feedback loop beats mass data.
principles.quote: it turns out that like a small amount of data in exactly that vertical and you you you know set up the environments correctly and you set up the feedback loop correctly is is is more what you need.

principles.text: Cheaper, better software expands demand for software (Jevons paradox); expect far more code, not less.
principles.quote: all the software can be 10x better, you know, and I think there actually is 10x more of it to write.

principles.text: Agent adoption starts with real engineering teams tagging the agent inside their existing tools, not solo consumer signups.
principles.quote: it's really like real engineering teams that bring on Devon and they they tag Devon all the time in Slack.

sources.title: How Devin's team built an autonomous AI engineer: stickiness, speed and fighting for talent
sources.originalTitle: Inside Devin: The AI engineer that's set to write 50% of its company’s code this year | Scott Wu
sources.summary: Scott Wu explains how Cognition pivoted around eight times before landing on Devin, and how its roughly 15 engineers each run up to five Devins in parallel. He covers stickiness over moats, fighting for top hires, and executing the basic startup advice relentlessly.

principles.text: Think stickiness, not moats: build compounding learning and multiplayer use so the product gets more valuable the longer a team uses it.
principles.quote: I think it's often less about moes and more about stickiness.

principles.text: Great startups often win by doing the 3-5 basic things (move fast, hire great people, build what people want) far more extremely than expected.
principles.quote: building companies well sometimes just comes down to doing those three to five things just even more than you could possibly expect.

principles.text: Push pace everywhere: Cognition went from hackathon to launch in months and had first customers a month later.
principles.quote: we had a hackathon in November, we had another hackathon in December, we started the company officially in January, we like uh got the prototypes out to initial users in February, we did a launch in March, we got our first customers in April.

principles.text: Fight relentlessly for the candidates you really want; solve their personal constraints rather than accepting a no.
principles.quote: hiring great people is one thing but truly just never never giving up and and and really giving it everything that you can to to make it work for for people who who really makes sense for to be on the team.

principles.text: Give AI agents well-defined, easy-to-verify tasks rather than open-ended problems; expect to steer more on bigger asks.
principles.quote: you want to be giving Devon tasks, not problems, right?

principles.text: Always think about where the technology is going, not where it is today, and evaluate decisions through that lens.
principles.quote: always think about where things are going, not where they are today.

sources.title: Scott Wu on building Devin: AI software engineers, agent UX and why engineering demand grows
sources.originalTitle: No Priors Ep. 62 | With Cognition CEO and Co-Founder Scott Wu
sources.outlet: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
sources.summary: Cognition CEO Scott Wu explains how competitive programming shaped his founder mindset, why Devin is designed as a steerable AI teammate, and why he expects more engineers, not fewer. He also covers hiring high-ownership generalists and where agents are strong or weak today.

principles.text: Great startups find something the world doesn't yet believe is true but actually is; question assumptions everyone takes for granted.
principles.quote: I think a lot of building a great startup is about you know finding something that uh the world doesn't believe is true yet but actually is you know

principles.text: Make agents steerable: let users watch and give quick feedback mid-task instead of one-shot autonomy, like mentoring a junior engineer.
principles.quote: if an agent is you know you give it the task and then it goes off and does it then you you know it basically only has one try to do it all and to do everything perfectly

principles.text: Build for yourselves: use your own product daily and work backwards from how you'd want to collaborate with an AI teammate.
principles.quote: I think we worked backwards from you know what made sense and and how we would want to interact with an AI coding teammate

principles.text: Cheaper software creation expands demand: multiplying each developer yields more developers, not fewer.
principles.quote: there's just so much demand for engineering out there

principles.text: Hire high-ownership people focused on outcomes over politics; early teams do everything, so favor technical generalists.
principles.quote: working with people who are um very high ownership you know very interested to drive and you know much more focused on on outcomes than they are on you know politics or anything like that

principles.text: Scope the product honestly: the agent does the precise execution while humans decide what to build.
principles.quote: you provide the the precise formulation of of what you want built or what you want done and Devon is the one that is doing the thoughtful execution of that

sources.title: How Scott Wu built Cognition (Devin): focus, enterprise-first wedge, and the AI agent future
sources.originalTitle: The Future of Software & AI | Cognition’s Scott Wu
sources.summary: Scott Wu explains why Cognition bet on an AI software engineer, launched an early demo despite backlash, and landed its first customer by deploying the whole team to Brazil. He covers choosing repetitive migration tasks first, enterprise go-to-market, staying model-neutral, and why a focused startup can beat giants.

principles.text: A startup has no right to win on resources; it wins by planting a flag on a future and running at it.
principles.quote: you have no right to win, you know, over over over what they're doing, you know. And then the reason that you're sometimes able to anyway is if you really like um you know, plant your flag in the ground

principles.text: Narrow focus is how startups beat giants: care more about one specific thing than they do.
principles.quote: the way that you build, you know, like a real kind of like um you you know a real like lasting business or lasting product is by really really focusing and narrowing on one specific thing, making a very concentrated bet

principles.text: Find the first PMF with tasks that are repetitive, scoped and on a tight feedback loop, not the hardest or the easiest.
principles.quote: it should be some of these like really repetitive tedious ones it's not so cut and dry that you can just like have an automated script that does the exact thing every time.

principles.text: For the first enterprise customer, do things that don't scale: send the entire company onsite and build for one customer.
principles.quote: No, we didn't deploy a a team. We deployed the whole company.

principles.text: Staying neutral across model labs builds customer trust and lets you route each subtask to the best, cheapest model.
principles.quote: Devon is purposefully meant to be uh you know, a compound model system.

principles.text: Reason from first principles about exponential curves, not pattern matching on the past.
principles.quote: what really matters is just thinking about things from first principles

sources.title: Scott Wu on Cognition: building Devon, the async AI software engineer, and the Windsurf deal
sources.originalTitle: A Cheeky Pint with Cognition CEO Scott Wu
sources.summary: Scott Wu explains why Devon is an async "junior engineer" agent, how coding tools complement rather than get run over by foundation labs, and why AI wins on usage-based pricing. He also covers the weekend Windsurf acquisition, a small elite engineering team, and why AI product experiences still lag capabilities.

principles.text: Split engineering into essential decisions (human, synchronous) and accidental complexity (agent, asynchronous); hand off the latter.
principles.quote: for anything that actually needs you in loop where you can go and make the decision and you're looking at the high level strategy or deciding what you want to build you're involved and you're doing that synchronously

principles.text: Agents make productivity measurable: ticket-level, end-to-end tasks give clear hours-saved data that tab completion cannot.
principles.quote: because it's doing the whole thing end to end, it's a lot more clear of like, yeah, you just you didn't have to do this migration anymore. You reviewed the PR in five minutes

principles.text: Application-layer AI companies survive the labs by solving the messy real-world context: data, tools, and defining the benchmark for success.
principles.quote: the hard question is all right now what is the benchmark right and I think defining the benchmark in all these spaces is kind of like a lot of the the practical real messiness of the world

principles.text: AI pricing should move from per-seat to usage-based, since AI agents are effectively seats and costs track GPU spend.
principles.quote: seats don't really make sense when it is like the AI themselves are arguably seats as well you know like they're doing a lot of the labor too

principles.text: When a competitor's crisis creates a window, move fast and spend the whole weekend closing it before customers and talent leave.
principles.quote: if there is something to do here at all, then it has to be ready to go by Monday morning

principles.text: Keep the core engineering team small and elite, and hire by having candidates build their own agent in hours.
principles.quote: our whole interview process for example um for for a lot of these is basically just having people build their own Devon in in 8 hours and seeing how far they get with it

sources.title: How Scott Wu grew Cognition to $500M revenue in under 3 years and absorbed Windsurf in a weekend
sources.originalTitle: Inside the Fastest-Growing Category in AI: Scott Wu, CEO of $26B Cognition
sources.summary: Scott Wu explains how Cognition (Devin) reached roughly half a billion in revenue in under three years. He covers measuring outcomes instead of tokens, closing the Windsurf acquisition over one weekend, staying model-neutral, and why enterprises want an independent partner who drives organizational change.

principles.text: Judge AI productivity by outcomes delivered, not tokens or spend.
principles.quote: what you care about is is outcomes and like what you're actually delivering.

principles.text: Forecast growth by comparing today's adoption to where it must be in 3 years, then extrapolating.
principles.quote: take those two points on the curve and you just extrapolate out what has to happen

principles.text: A product with obvious value skips the hardest part of selling: explaining why people should care.
principles.quote: the hardest part about building a product, selling a product, all that is just like explaining to people why they should care.

principles.text: Move fast on an acquisition when product and go-to-market synergies are clear; Cognition closed Windsurf in one weekend.
principles.quote: we got in touch with the Windsor team that evening. So it was Friday evening and then basically over the course of that weekend we worked out the entire acquisition together.

principles.text: Integrate acquired products gradually and let real usage pull them together instead of forcing deadlines.
principles.quote: letting the actual usage and the the new features that we're building the kind of next paradigms that we were getting to like letting those like pull the products together more gradually rather than forcing it.

principles.text: Stay model-neutral and independent; enterprises value value delivered over tokens used.
principles.quote: what they care about is is not how many tokens they're using, it's how much value they're driving

sources.title: Scott Wu: models went from frog instinct to world models, so it's time to be ambitious
sources.originalTitle: It's time to be ambitious | Scott Wu Co-founder & CEO at Cognition, Runtime 2026
sources.summary: Scott Wu uses the frog's instinct-driven brain as an analogy for early LLMs, then argues current models show world-model-like capability. He lays out four trends for builders: product form factors track model capability, agents that own outcomes, aggressive model routing, and automated rather than human-initiated sessions. His conclusion is to be far more ambitious about what you build.

principles.text: The right product form factor is a function of how good the models are, so it must keep changing.
principles.quote: the correct answer of what the form factor should be is actually very much a function of how good the models are.

principles.text: Move from assigning agents tasks to assigning outcomes, like a virtual employee who owns a result.
principles.quote: it's basically working off of outcomes instead of tasks

principles.text: Route aggressively: only a small share of workloads need frontier models; the rest can run on commoditized ones.
principles.quote: the absolute frontier models are roughly running for about 2% of workloads, call it, you know, could be 4% or 5% or whatever.

principles.text: Model swaps often go unnoticed by users, so routing is now real rather than a meme.
principles.quote: you can swap out models and most of the time no one even notices

principles.text: Automate every trigger that makes an engineer start work (tickets, metric anomalies) so agents initiate sessions, not humans.
principles.quote: we're actually already at the point where 91% of our sessions are not kicked off by a human.

principles.text: Because AI multiplies what each person can build, be more ambitious.
principles.quote: we all can build so much more and do so much more.

sources.title: Scott Wu on Devin: how each 2x jump in agent capability changed the product Cognition had to build
sources.originalTitle: Devin 2.0 and the Future of SWE - Scott Wu, Cognition
sources.summary: Scott Wu frames AI coding agent capability as a Moore's law that doubles roughly every 70 days. He walks through Devin's tiers (repetitive migrations, small bugs, broad issues, iterative planning, backlog and projects) and shows that each tier moved the bottleneck, the key capability and the right interface.

principles.text: Agent capability in code doubles about every 70 days, so plan for roughly 16-64x more work per agent each year.
principles.quote: every 70 days which is two or three months. And so, you know, if you look at various software engineering tasks that start from the simplest single functions or single lines

principles.text: The right interface and the key bottleneck change every two to three months, so product decisions must be revisited at each tier.
principles.quote: the answer to all these questions actually is it changes every two or three months. like every time you get to the next tier, the the the bottleneck that you're running into or the most important capability or the right way you should be interfacing with it, like all these actually change at at each point.

principles.text: Start with work agents can do reliably: repetitive, step-by-step migrations. They are tedious for humans and need strong instruction following.
principles.quote: these kinds of like repetitive migrations that you would be doing for, you know, 10,000 files were, you know, in many ways the the the easiest thing, which was cool actually because it was also kind of the the most annoying thing for humans to do.

principles.text: Codify repeatable work as playbooks so the agent follows clear steps exactly.
principles.quote: we built this system called playbooks where basically you could just outline a very clear set of steps, have it follow each of those step by step and then do exactly what's said.

principles.text: As tasks get harder, humans can't fully specify them up front, so the product must support an iterative exploring-then-delegating workflow.
principles.quote: you would basically have a more L2 experience where you can go explore the codebase with your agent, figure out what has to be done in the task and then set your agent off to go do that

principles.text: Autonomous backlog work depends on the agent's confidence about when to ask a human and on asynchronous self-testing before delivering a PR.
principles.quote: this is I think the era where testing and this asynchronous testing gets really really important right which is if you want something to just deliver entire PRs for you for tasks that you do especially for these larger tasks you want to know that it is can can test it itself

sources.title: Scott Wu on building Devin: RL benchmarks, 10x use cases, and the future of software engineering
sources.originalTitle: From Math Prodigy to AI Genius: How Scott Wu Built Devin
sources.summary: Cognition CEO Scott Wu explains how a group of competitive-programming friends started Devin through hacker houses, and why code is the fastest-growing AI use case. He covers picking use cases with 10x ROI, why intelligence is no longer the bottleneck, and why demand for software keeps rising as it gets cheaper.

principles.text: Skate to where the puck is going: bet on the next shift (agents) before it has a name.
principles.quote: we have always had the view of just skating where the puck is going basically

principles.text: Target enterprise use cases where AI gives 10x gains, not 10-20% ROI.
principles.quote: we want to look for the right use cases where we can do um not just like 10% or 20% gains uh or 10% 20% ROI but more like 10x.

principles.text: With RL, any task with a clean environment and clear success feedback can be solved; define the benchmark, tools and success criteria.
principles.quote: if you have a clean set of environments, if you have um a good feedback loop to decide what is correct or incorrect, you have all the the necessary context that you need to make those decisions, you can train a model that just aces that.

principles.text: Code grows fastest because it has a natural feedback loop: you can run the code to see if it worked.
principles.quote: one of the reasons that code is growing so quickly is because you have this really great feedback loop of success or failure, right?

principles.text: Anchor strategy on the future of your domain; the answer changes every couple months as capabilities improve.
principles.quote: the answer to that question basically changes every couple months in the sense that you know you hit a new tier of capabilities

principles.text: Cheaper software means more demand, not less: teams always have far more to build than bandwidth allows.
principles.quote: I've never met an engineering team that's told me, all right, you know, we have this project and then we're going to do that project and then we're done. No more software, you know, that's it, right?

sources.title: How Scott Wu uses Devin as an async junior engineer: tasks not problems, sync-then-async handoff
sources.originalTitle: How Devin replaces your junior engineers with infinite AI interns that never sleep | Scott Wu (CEO)
sources.summary: Scott Wu, CEO of Cognition, demos how his team works with Devin as a junior engineer teammate. Scope work as clear tasks, do a short synchronous research-and-prompt step, then hand off async, and make Devin the default first responder in public Slack threads. He also shares his top Devin use cases and a voice-in-meetings habit.

principles.text: Give AI agents tasks, not problems. Clear, well-specified tasks are where a junior-level agent shines.
principles.quote: where Devon really shines is one way that we say it also is is kind of like tasks not problems.

principles.text: Split work into a short sync phase (research, spec the prompt) and then an async handoff, like briefing an intern for two minutes.
principles.quote: for a lot of tasks there's often this sync component like the synchronous component and then this asynchronous component, right? And a lot of what search and wiki is for is for for doing the synchronous part of the task before you do the async

principles.text: Async agents let you run many tasks in parallel and check in later, which suits people stuck in meetings.
principles.quote: For better or for worse, I'm in meetings for a lot of the day and it's it's it's great to be able to just kind of kick these off

principles.text: Institutionalize the agent as first responder: tag it first on every issue, crash and request in shared Slack channels.
principles.quote: it's almost just like institutionalizing Devon as first line of response is how I would describe it.

principles.text: Work with the agent in multiplayer threads: knowledge compounds for the agent and teammates learn from each other.
principles.quote: Devon is a naturally multiplayer experience

principles.text: When an agent gets stuck, review its step history to find what it missed, then re-instruct it, like pair debugging with an intern.
principles.quote: it's kind of like pair pair programming or pair debugging with an intern.

sources.title: Scott Wu on agents vs copilots, the future of software engineering, and why reasoning is the moat
sources.originalTitle: Together Talks | Ep 3: Scott Wu on Agents, Cognition AI, Competitive Programming, and the Future
sources.summary: Scott Wu explains why Cognition built Devin as an autonomous agent rather than a copilot, how engineers become managers of AI interns, and why agents shift compute toward post-training and inference. He also covers reasoning as the key capability, synthetic verifiable data, and why fundamentals still matter.

principles.text: Copilots and agents are complementary: copilots speed up work you do yourself, agents handle tasks you delegate entirely.
principles.quote: co-pilot type tools make everyone a faster engineer um and agent tools make every engineer into almost an engineering manager you know you you have your own team of interns

principles.text: Code is a naturally agentic task, which is why autonomous agents fit it better than one-shot generation.
principles.quote: code is um I I think you know one of the most powerful direct applications of better reasoning and better logic right uh out there in the world

principles.text: Future engineers act like architects/product managers: describe the exact solution, then have it built.
principles.quote: the engineers of the future will be more like yeah almost like these technical architect types um or halfway between a technical architect and even like a product manager

principles.text: Agents break the human coupling of action and context: run many in parallel sharing context.
principles.quote: you can kind of just spin up 10 different agents that are all acting and all you know kind of searching and parallel to figure it out and not only that they can actually share the context with each other

principles.text: Agents consume far more inference than chatbots, so inference and post-training infrastructure grows in importance.
principles.quote: there's going to be you know way more expensive inference things in general as you go from kind of chatbot to full-fledged you know decision makers

principles.text: Safety improves by improving reasoning; AI will reach peak human ability wherever verifiable ground-truth data is abundant.
principles.quote: any field that we have a good ground truth data label for and abundant way to create more data I think AI will generally be able to to kind of get to like Peak human capabilities

sources.title: Scott Wu on building Cognition and Devin: AI company building, launches, and the future of software work
sources.originalTitle: Cognition, & Creating an AI Programmer with Scott Wu
sources.summary: Scott Wu (Cognition CEO) explains how building an AI company differs from past platform waves, why founders must be paranoid short-term and optimistic long-term, how the Devin launch was scrambled together, and how agents change software engineering. He also covers selling to enterprises, recruiting, and focusing on tedious, repeatable use cases.

principles.text: Founders should be long-term optimists but short-term paranoid, and stay honest about what is and isn't working.
principles.quote: you need to be a long-term Optimist but you also in in the day-to-day need to be very paranoid right

principles.text: In AI, you must place concrete bets on where the technology will be, and being technical helps because every decision is technical.
principles.quote: I think it's even better now than ever to be you know a very technical founder because um you know not only is the product that you're building technical but all of the decisions that you're making are obviously heavy heavily technical as well

principles.text: Invest in work that transfers across models (like datasets) so you survive the ground moving under you.
principles.quote: one of the big things for preparing for the ground to move under you is just making sure you're investing in things that are that are transferable

principles.text: Make launch assets show what is genuinely unique about your product in action, not a generic polished format.
principles.quote: the thing that we didn't like about our previous video is that it's you know you could you could imagine other products you know or other companies having a video that looked very similar

principles.text: Start AI agent sales with tedious, repetitive use cases (migrations, re-platforming) where AI is strong and no engineer wants to do the work.
principles.quote: the use cases uh that we work with our customers on today honestly in general are the more kind of tedious or repetitive use cases

principles.text: Build what people want and be willing to look dumb with unconventional effort, like flying to a candidate's parents' dinner, because the ROI math is high.
principles.quote: the ROI on spending that eight hours of time was like unimaginably high

sources.title: Scott Wu on how Cognition built Devon and why AI agents change software engineering
sources.originalTitle: How Cognition Built the World's First AI Coding Agent—Before Claude Code
sources.summary: Cognition's CEO explains the sync-to-async spectrum of AI coding tools, why form factor follows model capability, and why post-training with custom RL environments is Cognition's bet. He also covers why computer science fundamentals matter more as engineers become architects, and how he thinks about founding.

principles.text: Form factor is a tight function of model capability; the right interface shifts as models improve.
principles.quote: the correct form factor or like the correct interface is a pretty tight function of the capabilities

principles.text: Think in terms of what the tool does for you, not where it lives. The form factor is just a software engineer.
principles.quote: it's less a question of well where do you go to interact with your tool tools. It's more like a question of like what do the tools do for you

principles.text: Keep both sync (IDE) and async (agent) tools, and hand work off between them across the build cycle.
principles.quote: up until the point where the agents are capable enough to to handle everything and let you just operate 100% in that higher layer of abstraction. You want to have both

principles.text: As a startup, your edge is speed and focus. Teach models the nuances of real-world work via post-training rather than pre-training.
principles.quote: as a startup your your edge um it always has to be speed and focus

principles.text: Once RL can solve any benchmark, the hard part is defining the benchmark: tasks, tools, decisions, and success criteria.
principles.quote: the platonic ideal of RL is that you can go and solve any benchmark, right?

principles.text: Design evals with tight, verifiable reward signals so success or failure is unambiguous.
principles.quote: if you did not get the graphana dashboard running you will never be able to answer that question and if you did get it running you will always get the right answer

sources.title: The Golden Age of Software Engineering: how Cognition 10x'd output by letting Devin close the loop
sources.originalTitle: The Golden Age of Software Engineering | Scott Wu, Cognition | RAISE Summit 2026
sources.summary: Scott Wu explains how Cognition grew shipped software 10x in six months with only ~40% more engineers, by having AI agents own tasks end to end and start work on their own. He argues companies should measure real business outcomes (not tokens or lines of code) and treat AI capacity as a way to build 10x more software, not cut engineers.

principles.text: Ask what you'd do with an infinite army of software engineers; every company is now a software company with far more to build.
principles.quote: what would you do with an infinite army of software engineers?

principles.text: Real gains come when agents close the loop: plan, write, test and review end to end, not just autocomplete code.
principles.quote: rather than just writing the code, you are doing every single step, right? Autonomously.

principles.text: Make agent work event-driven and parallel: any trigger that would prompt a human engineer can spawn an agent session.
principles.quote: every kind of mental hook that would make you as a software engineer want to go and do something, you can set up that hook for Devin as well

principles.text: Cut the human middle step: route bug reports and alerts straight to an agent so a PR is ready for review.
principles.quote: you can actually skip that middle step and say, okay, look, just have that go straight to a Devin and then you can have a pull request ready for you

principles.text: Judge AI by business outcomes, not token usage; token counts are the new lines of code.
principles.quote: It's almost exactly the same as saying, okay, how many lines of code did you write?

principles.text: AI productivity doesn't reduce the need for engineers because there is roughly 10x more software worth building.
principles.quote: every human software engineer is 10 times more productive, but guess what? We have 10 times more things to go build

sources.title: Scott Wu on building Cognition: speed-running company functions, human-in-control AI, and hedging uncertainty
sources.originalTitle: Scott Wu sobre IA, investimentos e como cuida do próprio dinheiro
sources.summary: Cognition CEO Scott Wu explains how the Devin team went from demo to real enterprise deployments, why they had to speed-run design and marketing, and why humans should stay in charge of what gets built. He also covers Brazil as an organic early-adopter market and his balanced approach to investing amid AI uncertainty.

principles.text: A demo is not a product: real-world codebases and enterprise integrations are very different work, so learn what deployment actually takes.
principles.quote: working in the real world on an actual code base, I mean, it's very different work, you know, and so learning all these details about what is it actually like to deploy at a real company

principles.text: Fast-growing startups must speed-run building missing functions like design and marketing, even if embarrassingly late.
principles.quote: we didn't have any designers in-house until like eight or nine months ago.

principles.text: Raw model intelligence is only part of winning; getting it into everyday real-world use is the larger job.
principles.quote: people think so much about the raw intelligence and the capabilities but of course I mean there's just so much more than just that in terms of how do you get it out into the real world

principles.text: Design AI products so humans decide what to build and AI handles execution, with a thoughtful human-AI communication layer.
principles.quote: it's up to the humans to decide, okay, what do we want to build? What do we want to do? What are the high-level kind of decisions that we want to make?

principles.text: Product experience, education and onboarding are required to turn raw agent capability into capability at users' fingertips.
principles.quote: you still have to build really thoughtful product experiences, you have to do the right education, you have to, you know, onboard people onto using these agents

principles.text: Target markets with large unmet demand; organic community buzz comes first, then you build a local presence to match it.
principles.quote: originally a lot of that was kind of like organic and folks just like talking about it online and the the natural demand being there and obviously you know, we we said, "Okay, well we should we should do more"

sources.title: How Cognition built Devin, the AI software engineer, and why engineers still matter
sources.originalTitle: Why You Should Join - Cognition | Scott Wu, Founder & CEO
sources.summary: Scott Wu explains how Cognition launched Devin, why code is the best domain for agents (clean feedback loops), and why they build everything in-house with a tiny, founder-heavy team. He also argues software engineering becomes more valuable as abstraction layers rise.

principles.text: Let people try the product themselves; open access beats controlling the narrative.
principles.quote: the biggest kind of the the biggest access that we have control over is is just getting the product out there and and letting people try it out for themselves.

principles.text: Pick a domain with a clean, verifiable feedback loop; code is why it took off first.
principles.quote: in code it's basically I mean you run the code and it gives you the result or it doesn't give you the result right.

principles.text: Own the core differentiators in-house when you need tight control over the agent's behavior.
principles.quote: we just want to have such tight control over you know what the action space is for example or how Devon learns over time or how we pull in the right you know files into context

principles.text: Keep the team small and dense with founders and elite talent, aiming at the biggest outcome.
principles.quote: of our 25 people actually about 18 of them uh I think 18 is right 18 of us have started companies before.

principles.text: Work backwards from the future of the field to decide what to build.
principles.quote: a lot of it starts from asking the question you know the other way around of yeah what what is the future of software engineering going to be like and how will people be building software in 5 years

principles.text: Agents need bespoke, vertical-specific interfaces, unlike chatbots; product UX shapes the tech.
principles.quote: what we'll start to see actually over the the coming months is this kind of like proliferation of vertical specific agents

sources.title: How Cognition scaled Devin to ~$500M run rate and raised $1B at a $26B valuation
sources.originalTitle: AI Startup Cognition Raises $1 Billion at $26 Billion Value
sources.summary: Scott Wu explains why Cognition raised over $1B at $26B, how revenue grew from ~$37M to near $500M run rate in a year, and why staying independent and model-neutral is a strategic advantage against the big labs. He also argues AI will increase, not reduce, the number of software engineers.

principles.text: Raise capital to scale compute and team aggressively while preserving independence.
principles.quote: it allows us to stay independent and to to really continue on as an independent business, which is really really important for us.

principles.text: Model neutrality is a moat: serve the best model per use case instead of being tied to one lab.
principles.quote: being fully independent and fully neutral is actually the best way for us to be aligned with our customers.

principles.text: Build a compound system on top of many models so you are incentivized to serve whichever is best.
principles.quote: Devin is a compound system that works with all of these different models. And because of that, we're able to um uh to to to to be the Switzerland in in the equation here.

principles.text: Sell into large enterprises and regulated institutions where AI does real work, since every company is a software company.
principles.quote: every company in 2026 is a software company and so we work with, for example, all of the top five health insurers in the United States.

principles.text: Size the market by software demand: making engineers 10x more efficient unlocks far more than 10x more software.
principles.quote: We want to make all of of 10 times more efficient. And then we think there is a lot more than 10 times more software to build.

principles.text: Dogfood your own product heavily; most of Cognition's code is written by Devin.
principles.quote: even internally at Cognition, for example, more than 90% of the code that we write is written by Devin.

sources.title: How Cognition moved fast to acquire Windsurf: product fit and conviction from use
sources.originalTitle: Cognition AI Buys Windsurf After Google Licensing Deal
sources.summary: Scott Wu explains why Cognition moved within days to acquire Windsurf after its Google licensing deal. He covers the complementary IDE-plus-agent product fit, a shared enterprise focus, building conviction by using the product firsthand, and why speed mattered for the team and customers.

principles.text: Look for acquisitions where products complement each other (IDE plus agent) and enterprise focus matches.
principles.quote: there's there's such a clean fit of all of these things, you know, both in terms of kind of the products, which is Windinsurf is uh one of the leading idees. Cognition builds Devon um the first AI software engineer agent

principles.text: Build conviction fast by actually using the product yourself rather than relying on outside opinion.
principles.quote: we we've tried the product ourselves. We've used it a lot. Um and it helped us just get to conviction very quickly.

principles.text: In a turbulent situation, a quick outcome protects the team and customers.
principles.quote: it was clear that, you know, the sooner that we could get to an outcome, I think the better for for the team and and for the customers as well.

principles.text: Combine products so users can delegate a first pass to an agent, then finish by hand in the IDE.
principles.quote: You can imagine kicking off the agent to go do kind of a first pass at a project and then coming in and doing the finishing touches yourself with Windsurf.

principles.text: Focus on making software engineering AI work in the real world; enterprise customers validate that focus.
principles.quote: both of us are have always been very focused on making software engineering work in the real world

principles.text: Treat acquisitions as real deals that take care of the whole team, not talent-only acquihires that leave people behind.
principles.quote: there are a lot of great teams that have have gotten left behind.

sources.title: The Making of Devin: Scott Wu on building an autonomous AI software engineer
sources.originalTitle: The Making of Devin by Cognition AI: Scott Wu
sources.summary: Scott Wu demos Devin and explains why Cognition built a coding agent: code gives agents iterative feedback loops, and agent UX is a new product problem. He argues agents turn engineers into managers and that software demand will grow, not shrink.

principles.text: Agents are a new wave beyond text completion: they add autonomous decision-making, which raises the consistency bar.
principles.quote: I think we're entering this new wave where you know we're going beyond that and actually introducing some amount of autonomous decision-making

principles.text: Code is ideal for agents because work is iterative and every action gets concrete feedback from running code.
principles.quote: each of these things that you're doing you know you're you're making a decision and then you're running actual code to find out what happened and from that you're you're able to iterate

principles.text: Agent UX is a deep, new product problem; don't just copy existing software or human-collaboration patterns.
principles.quote: an agent is actually pretty different from both you know there's a lot of nuances and details of parallel work information gathering how it manages context

principles.text: Run agents in parallel and become the manager: each engineer delegates several tasks and reviews the output.
principles.quote: you have four devans that are all running in parallel and it's kind of turning every engineer into an engineering manager

principles.text: Dogfood the product: use your own agent to build your own product, and meet developers where they work (Slack, GitHub PRs).
principles.quote: a lot of the API Integrations that Devon has were built by Devon you know a lot of our own internal dashboards and metrics tracking within Devon are actually also built by Devon

principles.text: AI frees engineers from implementation to focus on problem solving; cheaper software means more demand and more engineers, not fewer.
principles.quote: there's actually going to be way more software Engineers than ever

sources.title: Scott Wu on Devin: applied AI labs, RL evals, and the next 12 months for coding agents
sources.originalTitle: Cognition CEO Scott Wu on Devin and the Next 12 Months for AI Agents
sources.summary: Cognition CEO Scott Wu explains how Devin started, why an applied AI lab differs from a foundation lab, and why RL needs the right evals and environments. He predicts agents will expand across the whole software lifecycle (testing, codebase understanding, PR review) and shares founder advice on honesty.

principles.text: An applied AI lab starts from the product; research serves the product, not the other way around.
principles.quote: as an applied AI lab, we are most focused on figuring out how to build something um that people will, you know, will use uh and to deliver a product of value to our customers. Um and all of the research that we do comes from there.

principles.text: Target the whole job (software engineering), not just the narrow task (writing code), and solve the hairy practical problems.
principles.quote: there are a lot of labs foundation labs that focus on code. We focus on software engineering which is a little bit different

principles.text: RL can ace any benchmark but doesn't generalize, so the key question is which environments and evals to build.
principles.quote: you can train a model that aces any benchmark. what is the benchmark that you want to ace, right?

principles.text: Code was early for RL because it has a clean, automatic feedback loop.
principles.quote: code is I think one of the first to to really get there with RL because you have this very clean feedback loop where instead of having a human have to judge it or whatever you can just go and run the code.

principles.text: Stay laser focused on your long-term view of the future, especially in hot, chaotic markets.
principles.quote: it's really important to just stay laser focused on okay well how do we think code will actually be written in 5 years or in 10 years and just making sure we get closer to that.

principles.text: Be honest with yourself: optimism is needed long term, but don't ignore evidence of what is and isn't working.
principles.quote: the most important part of founding a company is is basically like being honest with yourself.

sources.title: Introducing Devin: Scott Wu's launch of the first AI software engineer
sources.originalTitle: Introducing Devin, the first AI software engineer
sources.summary: Scott Wu announces Devin, an autonomous AI teammate that plans, codes, tests and deploys using a shell, editor and browser. The launch leads with concrete demos and a benchmark (13.86% on SWE-bench vs 1.96% prior) and frames the product as a collaborator rather than a replacement.

principles.text: Position AI as a teammate that builds alongside you or works independently, so engineers do more interesting work.
principles.quote: Devin is a tireless, skilled teammate, equally ready to build alongside you or independently complete tasks for you to review.

principles.text: Give the agent the same tools a human would need, in a sandbox, so it can do the whole job.
principles.quote: We've also equipped Devin with common developer tools including the shell, code editor, and browser within a sandboxed compute environment—everything a human would need to do their work.

principles.text: Build in real-time collaboration: report progress, accept feedback, and work through design choices with the user.
principles.quote: Devin reports on its progress in real time, accepts feedback, and works together with you through design choices as needed.

principles.text: Launch by showing concrete, varied end-to-end demos (build, deploy, debug, fine-tune, real Upwork jobs) rather than abstract claims.
principles.quote: We even tried giving Devin real jobs on Upwork and it could do those too!

principles.text: Back the launch with a credible public benchmark and be transparent about the eval setup.
principles.quote: Devin correctly resolves 13.86%* of the issues end-to-end, far exceeding the previous state-of-the-art of 1.96%.

principles.text: Ramp capacity deliberately: launch in early access with a waitlist while scaling up.
principles.quote: Devin is currently in early access as we ramp up capacity.

sources.title: How Cognition grew Devin from $1M to $73M ARR on under $20M net burn, then acquired Windsurf
sources.originalTitle: Funding, growth, and the next frontier of AI coding agents
sources.summary: Scott Wu announces Cognition's $400M+ raise at a $10.2B valuation and shares the growth numbers behind it. He explains the logic of owning both IDE and agent products and how the Windsurf acquisition accelerated enterprise growth.

principles.text: Grow efficiently: Cognition went from $1M to $73M ARR with under $20M total net burn.
principles.quote: Cognition’s Devin ARR grew from $1M ARR in September 2024 to $73M ARR in June 2025, as usage increased exponentially. Our growth remained efficient throughout, with total net burn under $20M across the company's entire history.

principles.text: Offer both product forms users want: an IDE for hands-on control and agents for delegated async work.
principles.quote: Engineers naturally want both: the IDE for when you want to make each decision yourself, with a speedup from AI assistance, and agents to delegate complete tasks asynchronously.

principles.text: Acquire a complementary product with low customer overlap to compound growth and complete your suite.
principles.quote: We had < 5% overlap in enterprise customers pre-acquisition, and combining the rapid adoption of Devin with Windsurf’s IDE product and scaled GTM machine has been a massive unlock.

principles.text: Buying a scaled go-to-market machine plus a product can quickly lift ARR; the Windsurf deal more than doubled it and combined enterprise ARR rose 30%+ in seven weeks.
principles.quote: Our acquisition of Windsurf more than doubled our ARR. More importantly, it gave us the complete product suite for AI coding.

principles.text: Land category-defining enterprise customers as proof and as a growth engine.
principles.quote: Devin and Windsurf now power category-defining customers including Goldman Sachs, Citi, Dell, Cisco, Ramp, Palantir, Nubank, and Mercado Libre.

principles.text: Build the product you always wanted for yourself, with a small team of long-time friends, and invest in the team above all.
principles.quote: We hunkered down in a New York apartment and built the product we always wanted for ourselves.

sources.title: How Cognition acquired Windsurf: deal structure, team treatment, and the strategic logic
sources.originalTitle: Cognition's acquisition of Windsurf
sources.summary: Scott Wu announces Cognition's acquisition of Windsurf and shares the internal note to his team. It shows how to structure an acquisition around people (full vesting acceleration, equal treatment), and why combining an autonomous agent with an IDE and a scaled GTM engine is a strategic unlock.

principles.text: In an acquisition, treat every acquired employee well; make honoring their talent a top deal priority.
principles.quote: One of my top priorities in structuring this deal was to honor their talent, hard work, and accomplishments in making Windsurf the great business it is today.

principles.text: Make the deal terms concrete for people: everyone participates financially, cliffs waived, vesting accelerated.
principles.quote: 100% of Windsurf employees will participate financially in this deal

principles.text: Treat new hires exactly like existing ones, with transparency, fairness and respect, then operate as one team.
principles.quote: Every new employee of Cognition will be treated the same way as existing employees: with transparency, fairness, and deep respect for their abilities and value.

principles.text: Buy distribution and talent, not just product: pairing a leading agent with an IDE and a scaled GTM machine is a big unlock.
principles.quote: combining the rapid adoption of Devin as the leading fully autonomous agent with Windsurf’s IDE product and scaled GTM machine will be a massive unlock.

principles.text: Handle sensitive announcements with respect: let the acquired team hear it first from the leaders, in the right way.
principles.quote: The Windsurf team deserves to hear this from Jeff and me in the right way, so please keep everything quiet in the interim out of respect for our new colleagues.

principles.text: After the deal, keep the acquired team running as-is short term while investing heavily in integration over time.
principles.quote: In the immediate term, the Windsurf team will continue to operate as they have been

sources.title: Cognition's AI Productivity Guarantee: pricing AI on measured outcomes, not usage
sources.originalTitle: AI should earn its keep: Introducing the AI Productivity Guarantee
sources.summary: Scott Wu argues AI vendors should prove value, not just report usage metrics like tokens or lines of code. Cognition built an estimator that scores each Devin session in human-engineer hours, validated it against customer estimates, and backs it with up to $10M in credits if value falls short of spend.

principles.text: Measure outcomes, not activity. Usage metrics like tokens and lines of code don't tell buyers what value they get.
principles.quote: The industry needs to move from maximizing usage metrics to maximizing outcomes — and right now, there’s no good standard for measuring that. AI vendors should be the ones to provide it.

principles.text: Put money behind your claim: a financial guarantee tied to delivered value is a strong trust and sales signal.
principles.quote: if Devin delivers less engineering value than you’re paying for, Cognition will fund your usage up to $10M until it does.

principles.text: Pick a metric that tracks effort and value, not volume. Hours of useful output beats lines of code.
principles.quote: We measure in hours of productive output because lines of code don’t correspond to effort: a critical bug that takes hours to investigate might be a two-line fix.

principles.text: Validate your measurement against real user judgment; averaging across many tasks smooths out individual error.
principles.quote: No single estimate is perfect, but across many tasks with varying complexity, the highs and lows average out.

principles.text: Be honest about what the metric is: productive output is a baseline, and true ROI needs business context that hands-on customer teams provide.
principles.quote: It does not replace measuring ROI, which requires deeper context on the business value of each task.

principles.text: A guarantee is only safe if delivery is embedded: pair it with embedded teams, enablement and spend controls.
principles.quote: Our teams embed directly into customer accounts: identifying high-value projects, pair-programming with engineers on their backlog, running enablement workshops on productively managing fleets of agents, and measuring outcomes.

sources.title: How Cognition and Windsurf merged in 72 hours and shipped relentlessly for a year
sources.originalTitle: One Year of Building Together
sources.summary: Scott Wu and Jeff Wang reflect on the Cognition-Windsurf deal and the year after. The merge worked because the two companies' strengths (engineering vs GTM) were complementary and products didn't overlap. A "Just Keep Shipping" cadence took run rate from $73M to $500M+ and headcount from 44 to 350.

principles.text: Acquire for complementary strengths: pair a strong engineering org with a strong GTM org, with non-overlapping products.
principles.quote: Cognition had built one of the best engineering orgs in Silicon Valley and was looking for a GTM org; Windsurf had built one of the best GTM orgs and was looking for engineering. Our products didn't even overlap

principles.text: When a rare opportunity appears, move fast and show up ready to sign on the spot.
principles.quote: On the Cognition side, we knew we had to act fast. ... We prepared to head to Windsurf's offices on Saturday with a printed LOI, ready to sign on the spot.

principles.text: After a merger, set the tone with immediate shipping; make 'just keep shipping' the cultural motto.
principles.quote: Three days after the deal closed, we shipped Wave 11. We called it "Just Keep Shipping" and it set the tone for the year.

principles.text: Unite the team with shared-fate framing: one boat, everyone in it together.
principles.quote: "there's only one boat and we're all in it together."

principles.text: Consolidate brands and surfaces over time so the product is available everywhere with any model.
principles.quote: Then, we finally unified into one brand with the launch of Devin Desktop, your home for software engineering. Now Devin is available on every surface with any agent and any model.

principles.text: Back your product claims with risk-bearing offers and open evaluation to build trust.
principles.quote: We like to call ourselves the Switzerland of AI, so we put model evaluation in the open with Arena Mode and a public leaderboard. We put our money where our mouth is with the AI Productivity Guarantee.

sources.title: Why Cognition acquired The Interaction Company (Poke): betting on always-on, proactive cloud agents
sources.originalTitle: Welcoming The Interaction Company to Cognition
sources.summary: Scott Wu announces Cognition's acquisition of The Interaction Company, maker of Poke. It shows how he picks acquisition targets: a team with a shared thesis (always-on cloud agents), fast execution, and a product people love for being proactive and personal.

principles.text: Agents should feel like a friend: proactive, personalized and fun, not like software.
principles.quote: The Interaction team has built an agent that people love: it’s proactive, it knows you, and it’s fun to talk to. That’s exactly how working with Devin should feel

principles.text: Shared long-term bets and fast, ambitious teams make the best partners.
principles.quote: They are exceptional people who move extremely fast and aim for only the most ambitious products. And from the beginning, our teams have been making the same bet: always-on cloud agents.

principles.text: Distribution through a native channel people already use (texts) drives engagement.
principles.quote: Poke is a personal agent that lives in your texts. It messages you first, follows up with you, and feels less like software and more like a friend.

principles.text: After an acquisition, keep the product stable for users and improve it with your own infrastructure.
principles.quote: Today, Poke users can continue using the product just as before. Soon, Cognition’s models and infrastructure will make Poke even faster and more reliable.

sources.title: The Wu Tapes: how Scott Wu built Cognition and Devin with focus, neutrality and hunger
sources.originalTitle: The Wu Tapes: Q&A with Cognition's Scott Wu
sources.summary: A long Q&A with Cognition founder Scott Wu on his path from math olympiads to building Devin, an AI coworker. He covers company focus, staying model-neutral, founder traits, using forcing functions to commit, and why the AI agent should behave like a coworker rather than a tool.

principles.text: A company can have many functions but only one goal; that single goal defines everything it builds.
principles.quote: I think focus is really important for a company. You can have different functions, different verticals. But I think you can only have one goal.

principles.text: A company's DNA is rigid: customers, products and business model all root in one mission, so choose it carefully.
principles.quote: I think the DNA of a company is in some ways kind of rigid, more so than people usually expect.

principles.text: Stay model-neutral: nobody knows which model wins, so being a trusted partner that uses each model where it fits is a strength.
principles.quote: Nobody even knows who's going to have the best model in 12 months. And so I think that by getting to work with all the different models, using each whenever they're best for specific use cases, we can quickly adapt

principles.text: Founders succeed on intelligence plus hunger; the rest flows from analyzing mistakes and relentlessly improving.
principles.quote: I guess my take on this is that the two qualities that really matter in our fields are intelligence and hunger.

principles.text: Use a forcing function to commit fully and move fast when you've been planning to start.
principles.quote: But it was a good impetus, a nice forcing function for us to try to go fast and to actually take it seriously. Which is sometimes what you need in a startup.

principles.text: Design the product as a coworker, not a tool: its own machine, working in your existing systems, even from naming.
principles.quote: We've always thought about it in the coworker form.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu explains how Cognition struck the Windsurf deal between Friday night and Monday morning, why a "husk" left behind can hold real value, and why he thinks AI coding is only starting. He also covers usage-based pricing, agents vs IDEs, RL and curated data, and takes feedback on Cognition's marketing.

chunks.heading: Why Scott went after Windsurf in a weekend: speed over diligence
chunks.text:
- Cognition learned about the Google/Windsurf split on Friday, "the same time everyone else did," and reached out cold that evening.
- Scott's framing: ask "what is the correct way that things should happen here." With customers, staff and recruiters all scrambling, a month-long (or even week-long) diligence process was not an option.
- His analogy: "the bank goes into receivership Friday night, you got to have an answer by Sunday and by Monday morning."
- The timeline he describes:
  - Friday night: first call.
  - Saturday: verbal agreement.
  - Sunday: terms and legal hashed out.
  - Monday morning: signed and announced.
- Cognition accepted it would not go as deep on diligence as it would like. It judged it could still understand the business well enough at a high level.
- Priority was giving customers and employees a clear answer fast: Cognition would support the product and keep things running smoothly.
- He credits the Windsurf leadership team (Jeff, Graham, Kevin) for working around the clock for their team.
- He declined to give the cash/stock split ("a mixture of both"). He also declined to say what share of Cognition's revenue goes to Anthropic.

chunks.heading: Why the "husk" was actually valuable: complementary assets
chunks.text:
- Online, people argued all the best researchers left and nothing was left behind. Scott disagreed.
- What remained, in his words: an amazing product many people use, the entire customer book, all the code, a lot of the data and proprietary IP, and "a really incredible team."
- It was somewhat incomplete as a piece, but fit what Cognition needed.
- Team fit:
  - Cognition is focused on the core engineering and product team.
  - Windsurf built a strong go-to-market, marketing, finance and operations team.
- Product fit: the two were "very naturally complementary."
- His general point: "often there are actually a lot of really valuable pieces that get left behind" in these deals.
- On the new deal-structure norm (acqui-hire style splits), he said there's "an unspoken covenant that as a founder you go down with the ship," and that it has changed over the last year. He called that "a bit disappointing."

chunks.heading: Combining IDE and agent into one product
chunks.text:
- Biggest question since the deal: what is the combined IDE-plus-agent experience.
- His view: years from now these systems will look different and may not share today's terms. In the near term, both IDEs and agents matter in a developer's workflow.
- Workflow he imagines:
  - Plan a task in the IDE, using retrieval, search and the wiki to see what code it touches.
  - Hand it to an agent to do the bulk of the work.
  - Review and touch up the code locally in the IDE.
- The goal is moving "from synchronous to asynchronous to synchronous," being present only where needed and parallelizing the rest.
- Near term, Cognition plans to keep the philosophy of both Devon and Windsurf and run both products, then work on the intersection for users of both.
- Longer term he sees this as the next human-computer interface: expressing intent instead of writing code. "Tony Stark does not pull up his laptop. He goes and talks to Jarvis." He estimates 10 to 20 product levels to get there, each taking roughly 2 to 3 months, so "a few years."
- He thinks none of the players are close to the future of software engineering yet and that there will be more than one winner in code.

chunks.heading: Devon's positioning, pricing and growth
chunks.text:
- Pricing: usage-based, essentially by the hour. The aim is to be about 10x cheaper than the value of an engineer's time.
- Usage growth: between January and October, Devon usage grew roughly 5 to 10x in both self-serve and enterprise, excluding Windsurf. He claims this is comparable to the growth of consumer-leaning rivals over the last 6 to 8 months.
- Who uses it: real engineering teams, from startups to some of the biggest companies. Sessions start in Slack or Linear, Devon opens pull requests in GitHub, and it learns to onboard to a repo.
- Why Devon gets less buzz: IDEs took off about a year before agents (IDEs sometime last year, agents in the last 6 months), so people know them better. He expects agents to be as familiar in 6 to 12 months.
- He contrasts this with Replit and Lovable, which he sees as more consumer-leaning products solving a different problem, such as getting non-coders to a working product.
- Marketing feedback he took on board: Cognition should tell its story better. He noted the Windsurf marketing team is now an asset.
- Suggestion he received and endorsed: Cognition had been quiet about its traction (it was "almost better if people don't hear that agents are working"), but now that everyone is building agents it makes sense to be more public.

chunks.heading: Where value accrues in AI and where code is headed
chunks.text:
- On value capture: it occurs "wherever you are able to establish real differentiation in your space."
- On the foundation labs: he expects them to do extremely well. Cognition's piece is optimizing for specific software-engineering capabilities and shipping a great product experience around them. He says "you really need both."
- On competing with labs: Cognition focuses on how humans and AI work together to produce code, and on teaching a model to use real tools (pull Datadog logs, debug a front end live, learn a codebase representation).
- Market size: there are about 30 million software engineers. Whether the value captured is 5%, 10%, 20% or 30%, the bigger point is getting the technology and products to where everyone moves much faster.
- Productivity today: he estimates 1.5x to 2x faster for engineers who use the best AI tools well, in aggregate. In three years he sees no reason it shouldn't be 10x.
- Why more code: he expects more than 10x more code, citing Jevons paradox. Most software people use (banks, healthcare, insurance, customer tools) is far worse than top products like YouTube, TikTok and Instagram.
- Percent of code written by AI is a flawed metric: lines vary in importance (protobufs vs. core logic) and "written with the help of AI" varies in degree. He prefers measuring how much faster an engineer is per hour.
- His forward view of the engineer's role: more "technical architect, technical product manager," deciding what problem to solve and how to architect the solution.

chunks.heading: What is next for coding agents: deep context and RL
chunks.text:
- Biggest unsolved problem: deep context, the difference between code and software engineering. That means:
  - Working in a large, complex codebase.
  - Building an intuition and representation of how pieces interact.
  - Learning to use tools to diagnose and debug.
  - Reusing knowledge from similar past tasks.
  - Testing a front end and knowing what it should look like.
- He says this is a practical problem that can't be solved in a sandbox, so it needs real software-engineering practice.
- His case for continued progress: RL is "the biggest breakthrough of the last year and a half." With a clean set of target behaviors, environments and a definition of success or failure, "you roughly can solve any benchmark."
- The open question in every vertical is defining the benchmark. His example: for an accountant, a failed audit is a fail signal, but you'd want shorter feedback loops.
- Change in belief: two years ago the story was more data. Now it's a small, highly curated dataset for the exact use case, with environments and feedback loops set up correctly. "A lot of compute, not a lot of data."
- Example: Cognition's Kevin 32B model, trained with RL on agent trajectories for writing CUDA kernels (KernelBench), beat state-of-the-art models on that task.
- Even with zero further progress in AI code, he says "the world would still be entirely different," and engineers who don't use AI are simply slower.

chunks.heading: Talent and market outlook
chunks.text:
- On AI talent pay: he thinks it is "quite reasonable." He argues AI is the biggest technology shift in our lives and that fewer than 10,000, and probably closer to 100 to 1,000, people truly set its trajectory.
- He says competition for talent is as fierce at the application layer as at the foundation labs.
- Foundation lab consolidation: he said something like two to six players, "three to five seems pretty reasonable."
- Valuation view (framed loosely): he expects both the foundation labs (around $500B combined for the private ones) and the application-layer leaders (he guessed $50B to $100B for companies like Perplexity, Sierra, Decagon, Harvey, Cognition and Cursor) to go up a lot in aggregate.
- He cited Sam Altman's old "bubble theory" post as the model for betting against bubble talk.
- Advice on studying CS: yes. The degree is "more a degree in how to think," covering first-principles problem solving and how computers and databases work, which stay valuable.
- Personal trait he's proudest of: emotional calm under stress. He describes himself as competitive and easily frustrated, but able to stay composed.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu explains how Cognition pivoted around eight times before landing on Devin, and how its roughly 15 engineers each run up to five Devins in parallel. He covers stickiness over moats, fighting for top hires, and executing the basic startup advice relentlessly.

chunks.heading: How Scott frames Devin and the shift from text completion to autonomous agents
chunks.text:
- Devin is "a fully autonomous software engineer" that works on tasks end to end and asynchronously. You tag it in Slack or Linear, and it opens pull requests in GitHub.
- Cognition's founding bets, made in late 2023:
  - High-compute reinforcement learning was the next paradigm shift. Models do work on a task, get evaluated on whether it was correct, and learn from that. Code suits this well because it has "an automated feedback loop": you can run it.
  - The product experience would move from text completion (GitHub Copilot-style, also marketing, support, education) to agents. An agent makes decisions, interacts with the real world, takes feedback, and iterates over multiple steps.
- Timeline:
  - Hackathon mode in November 2023, starting from an Airbnb booked around Thanksgiving. The first work was agentic loops for contest programming problems.
  - Incorporated around the start of 2024, prototypes to early users in February, launch in March 2024, first customers in April.
  - Self-serve in December 2024, and Devin 2.0 a few weeks before this episode.
- Scott says the team pivoted "like eight times" within coding agents. The core question behind every product decision is: "what is the future of software engineering?"
- Many features did not exist at launch: Slack, the GitHub integration, Linear, an interactive planning phase, and touching up Devin's code. Even talking to Devin mid-task had to be invented. Originally you handed off a task and got finished code back.
- He puts the work at "a 50-50" split between model capability improvements and product interface and tools, because users already know chatbots but need to learn how to use agents.
- Seniority analogy: a high school CS student at launch, then a college intern, now a junior engineer. He prefers the phrase "jagged intelligence". Devin is far better than a human at some things (such as retrieval and processing lots of code) and worse at others.

chunks.heading: How Cognition uses Devin to build Devin
chunks.text:
- The engineering team is about 15 people, and the whole company is 26-27.
- Devin merges "several hundred pull requests" into production in the Devin codebases every month.
- Share of PRs written by Devin: "in the neighborhood of a quarter" at recording time. He said it had grown exponentially internally and that "we expect it to be more than half" by the end of 2026.
- Most engineers work with up to five Devins at once. The flow is to decide the five things to get done today, then give one to each Devin.
- The human's role is the 10-20% that needs judgment:
  - Defining exactly what is being solved.
  - Steering architecture and class design.
  - Testing the front end and giving one or two lines of feedback.
- Teammates can chime in on a Devin session in Slack with context (for example "the reason we did it initially was X and Y"), and Devin adjusts. Others review Devin's GitHub PRs and Devin responds to the comments.
- Devin can start other Devins through the API, so it splits big tasks into parallel sessions. This needs credentials and is not on by default.
- On agents versus humans: a human has one context tied to one thread. An agent can run several lines of exploration at once while sharing all the context.

chunks.heading: What to hand Devin: tasks, not problems
chunks.text:
- "You want to be giving Devin tasks, not problems." Devin is best on well-defined work that is easy to verify and test.
- Good fits:
  - Quick front-end features, such as the live demo where it added a link to Lenny's newsletter in the Devin web app sidebar.
  - Bug fixes.
  - Adding tests and documentation.
  - Scoping tickets and answering codebase questions.
- Bigger asks work too, but expect to steer Devin more.
- Devin asks clarifying questions mid-run (for example whether a link should open in a new tab), and you can answer at any point. If you don't, it decides itself.
- It tests its own work. On Devin's own codebase it will log into Devin and start a session to check its changes.
- Advice for new users, his "one-liner": "treat Devin like your new junior engineer." Specifically:
  - Pick the tickets for the day or week and start with the easier ones.
  - Get the repo set up first and give it one-pointer tasks so it learns the codebase.
  - Make sure it has a virtual machine that can run tests, the linter and CI.
  - Scale up over time.
- Early on, many users saw a blank screen and asked for a huge re-architecture. That is the failure pattern the onboarding now steers away from.
- Typical team adoption pattern:
  - A few enthusiasts do the setup (repos, lint, CI) and give Devin initial tasks to "build a foothold".
  - Others see the stream of PRs and join, and Devin already knows the repos by then.
  - The early adopters pave the way for the rest of the team.

chunks.heading: Product surface: Wiki, Search, Linear automation, and the codebase representation
chunks.text:
- Devin indexes a codebase into a high-level architecture it can zoom into. Scott compares this to how engineers work: they never load every line, they hold an abstraction and zoom in. This lets it scale to very large codebases.
- Devin Wiki is generated documentation with architecture diagrams and component detail (shown on a DeepSeek repo fork). Cognition built it for the agent, and then found "humans really are interested to understand this codebase representation as well."
- Devin Search is a Q&A mode over a repo.
  - Scott says users want an explicit "just ask, don't start the task" control, to see relevant snippets or the wiki without kicking off work.
  - Improving capability for Q&A specifically also justified a separate feature.
  - Over time he sees the product as a suite of tools around a core agent, not one monolith, because real engineering is messy.
- Linear automation (rolled out the week before recording):
  - Add the Devin label to a ticket and Devin posts its scoping thoughts, relevant files and snippets, and a confidence level.
  - If you agree, you start a session that does the work.
  - Product managers use it to understand the codebase. Scott cites Claire Vo, who uses Devin to scope tasks, ask data questions, and check things like whether a feature is merged or behind a flag.
- Onboarding: teams use Devin to onboard new engineers, who can ask codebase questions without feeling awkward about asking a mentor.

chunks.heading: Positioning, stickiness instead of moats, and focus
chunks.text:
- Scott frames the competitors (labs, IDE companies, other agents) as strong teams. He argues the whole space will move "an order of magnitude" faster and there is a lot to do.
- Cognition's stance is that it has been "laser focused on agentic coding" since the start. That focus shows up in:
  - The usage-based revenue model with ACUs.
  - The interfaces (Slack, issue trackers).
  - The capabilities.
- He says there are "20 generations" of agent coding products ahead. A far-future one may not show you code at all: you describe changes to the running product ("make this button rounder", "start a table and index it on x, y, z") and the agent builds them.
- On defensibility, he prefers "stickiness" to "moats", and says nothing prevents others from entering at any layer. Sources of stickiness for coding agents:
  - Accumulated learning. Devin builds a representation of your codebase, stack and process over time, like an engineer who has been at the company for five years.
  - A multiplayer effect. Knowledge from every teammate's sessions flows into new sessions, and Devin is shared across Slack, GitHub PRs and Linear.
  - A clear tie to value. Software quality always matters, and developers are willing to learn new tools if the result is better.
- On base intelligence, his "hot take" is that it is "basically already there". Cognition does not pre-train models. It works with the labs' research teams. No single base-model release was a step change for Devin, although each release improves it.
- Cognition's effort goes into "teaching it all of the idiosyncrasies of real world engineering": how to use Datadog, diagnose a given error, and make a GitHub PR. In his words, this is teaching "the model to mirror the complexity of the real world".

chunks.heading: Trade-offs Cognition debated: opinionated versus general, and the startup niche advice
chunks.text:
- Scott says the common advice is to "focus on a really niche cohort" and do things that don't scale. He calls it great advice across the board, but notes it is complicated by generative AI, where a single product can serve many uses.
- Users have ordered DoorDash with Devin and built websites from scratch. Most product features are built for PRs and engineering teams, but Cognition is fine with people using Devin for other things, as long as they know the limitations.
- Cognition still goes back and forth on how much to support those other uses.
- The other debate was whether Devin should be one comprehensive experience or a suite of tools. He says it has trended toward a suite, with the core agent as "the core piece".
- The name "Devin" came early from the founders' "Dev Walden" and "Dev Steven" prototypes, built when everyone worked independently and then consolidated.
- Branding has both hexagons and an otter with a laptop, because the team never settled the debate.

chunks.heading: The startup basics, executed extremely: speed, hiring, closeness to customers
chunks.text:
- Scott says 18 of the roughly 26-27 people on the team have started companies before. His counterintuitive lesson is that the "three to five things" of startup advice are repeated for a reason, and that building well "sometimes just comes down to doing those three to five things just even more than you could possibly expect."
- His list:
  - Move fast.
  - Hire great people.
  - Build something people want.
  - Stay as close as possible to customers.
  - Always think about where things are going, not where they are today. In AI that means next week as well as 10 years out.
- On speed, he gives the timeline: hackathons in November and December 2023, officially a company in January, prototypes to users in February, launch in March, first customers in April.
- On hiring, he says to "fight to all ends" for the people you want. His examples:
  - An MIT junior who aced the interview, and who wanted to join but whose parents wanted him to graduate.
