The team flew to North Carolina, went from the airport to dinner at his parents' house, and agreed a setup where he works essentially full-time and comes in only for required classes. Scott says he has been on the team for over a year and is "an incredible, incredible engineer".
  - Another strong candidate with multiple offers who wanted to start his own company someday. They offered investor intros and customer work, and helped him hand-write rejection notes to the other companies so he wouldn't burn bridges.

chunks.heading: Why Scott expects more engineers, and how the role changes
chunks.text:
- Scott says programming is "the discipline of telling your computer what to do", so it only grows more important as AI gets more powerful.
- He argues for Jevons paradox: as the price of software work drops, total spend goes up. If engineers become 10x faster, society will build more than 10x as much code (including more personalized experiences) and need more engineers, not fewer.
- He says you should still learn to code. CS teaches how to break problems down logically and how abstractions work (databases, garbage collection, networking, TCP/IP, what happens when Python is interpreted). Those let you build good systems and peel back layers when needed.
- Engineers go "from bricklayer to architect". Skills that grow in value:
  - Understanding complex systems in the context of the whole company.
  - Defining the problem and the right solution.
  - Making key decisions and trade-offs.
- He estimates defining the problem is roughly 10% of an engineer's time, with about 90% going to implementation chores such as debugging Kubernetes errors, bug reports, migrations and upgrades.
- Asked whether this turns engineers into managers, he prefers "bricklayer to architect" and calls it closer to having an interface to hand off tasks than to people management, with none of the emotional load.
- He frames AI as a faster adoption curve than the PC, internet or mobile, which each depended on hardware distribution. In AI code, "if you're not using AI at all you're falling behind", and there is no hardware limit slowing diffusion.
- He ties the practical gains (his "200%, 500%, a thousand%" figures are rough) to the agentic workflow: real engineering work like reproducing a bug, checking Datadog and rerunning takes real time, and agents run it in parallel.

chunks.heading: Scott's operating mindset
chunks.text:
- On founder psychology, he says startups have ups and downs even at the most successful companies. His view is to give maximum effort ("put it all out on the field") while not tying your personal worth to wins or losses. He says this makes you more successful because you can give your best and move on.
- He reads Silicon Valley history (The Power Law by Sebastian Mallaby) because "somebody invented the idea of a seed round... venture capital... product-market fit."
- His summary of the future of work is optimistic: "the ability for everyone to multiply themselves", with "a lot more to do out there in the world."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cognition CEO Scott Wu explains how competitive programming shaped his founder mindset, why Devin is designed as a steerable AI teammate, and why he expects more engineers, not fewer. He also covers hiring high-ownership generalists and where agents are strong or weak today.

chunks.heading: Why Scott thinks software engineering grows instead of disappearing
chunks.text:
- Scott argues there will be more engineers, not fewer, for two reasons.
- Demand: "every company is hiring for more software engineers" and everyone has more ideas than time to build them. Much Excel and tool use exists only because engineering is hard, so many problems that code could solve go unsolved.
- Deciding what to build: Devin does not decide what to build or which problem to solve. Engineering becomes a "more pure" abstraction of that decision-making.
- He estimates a typical engineer spends about 20% of their time on fundamental problem solving and 80% writing code. With AI they can do about 5x more and spend nearly all their time on creative problem solving.
- Analogy: human calculators. Letting people stop doing that work expanded what capable people could do.
- He sees AI as democratizing: it taps latent demand where software was unaffordable before.
- Stat he cites: about 30 million software engineers worldwide, only around 0.4% of people. His goal is to multiply those engineers and let many more people work with software.

chunks.heading: What Devin is and how he positions it
chunks.text:
- Cognition began around November 2023 (as he describes it, "around November"). Devin is an AI software engineer that makes its own decisions like a human engineer.
- It writes and edits code, uses the command line and browser, reads documentation, and deploys, tests and debugs autonomously.
- You give it a simple prompt and it runs end to end. You can watch what it is looking at and give feedback, mirroring "looking over the shoulder of another engineer".
- Scott frames Devin as the next generation of human-computer interface. In 10 years people will find it crazy that you had to "learn all these esoteric languages" and work through stack traces to talk to a computer.
- Product launch note: the demo got far more views than the team expected and was shared widely on tech Twitter.
- He expects reactions to split between skeptics ("there's no way this could possibly work") and people who think all jobs will be lost.

chunks.heading: Product design: why interactive agents beat fire-and-forget
chunks.text:
- Scott's critique of typical agents: if you give a task and it goes off to do it, "it basically only has one try to do it all and to do everything perfectly".
- Devin is modeled on a human intern or junior engineer who works through the day while you check in four or five times with about 30 seconds of feedback each.
- Benefits of check-ins: the worker learns, still delivers valuable work, and the process is much faster than doing everything yourself.
- The UI shows planning, shell, code and browser views, so you see how it interacts with the world and can steer it.
- Process: the team built for itself, using Devin daily while building Devin. They worked backwards from "how we would want to interact with an AI coding teammate", then figured out technically how to make it work.

chunks.heading: Where Devin is strong and weak
chunks.text:
- Strong at devops and dev setup, which is hard for humans too. An early exciting moment: the team was stuck for about an hour setting up a database and Kubernetes, asked Devin to do it, and it did.
- Step-by-step workflows work well for agents: run commands, read errors, check whether a port is open, install a missing package.
- Strong at data analysis end to end: find datasets online or pull a CSV, sanitize the data, run the analysis, build a visual.
- Strong on "encyclopedic knowledge".
- Weak at deciding what to do. You supply the precise formulation, and Devin does the thoughtful execution, including testing, debugging, installing packages and deploying. You cannot say "build me a great business".

chunks.heading: How Scott thinks about agent design and what improves agents
chunks.text:
- He declines to share internals but says much comes down to understanding the interface of the problem and what exactly to optimize.
- Example (a GitHub issue to fix): in theory a perfect intelligence could read the whole codebase and write the diff directly. Practically, for humans and today's AIs, the cleaner path is to reproduce the bug, add print statements and rerun, check logs, or search Stack Overflow.
- Much of the work is getting Devin to think and decide that way, so planning and evaluation take most of the team's effort.
- Agents are a combination of factors, and he says "yes to all the above" on what improves them: faster inference, better base-model reasoning, planning, better tool use.
- He describes a race between these factors. A perfect intelligence would need nothing else, but a perfect tool user could also work. All are a "rising tide", and the question is which sees the most progress.

chunks.heading: The future role of engineers
chunks.text:
- 5 to 10 years out, he expects "what we call software" to change a lot. Engineers spend their time on the fun part: working out edge cases, flows and architectures for a problem.
- He describes the future engineer role as "a mix between a technical architect and a product manager today".
- English as "the hottest new programming language" has truth to it, but fundamentals stay valuable: algorithms, logic gates, how computers work, logical reasoning. Analogy: people who work with networks benefit from understanding TCP.
- Near term (1 to 2 years): engineers who are AI-native will multiply themselves and do more.
- On very long timelines, he says it is hard to predict and he is not high confidence. He expects concrete AI impact on work and the economy well before any singularity. Even with today's technology, much is still possible, and "we're still very very early" (ChatGPT was about a year and a half old).

chunks.heading: Hiring and team principles
chunks.text:
- Founding team: friends from the math and programming competition community, each with their own AI path. Scott ran the machine learning company Lunch Club for about 5 years. Co-founder Walden built much of early Cursor, and co-founder Steven was one of the first engineers at Scale AI.
- Hiring so far has been through a close network of people the team knows and has worked well with.
- Almost everyone on the team was a founder before or planned to start a company if not for Cognition.
- He wants high-ownership people focused on outcomes "more than ... politics", plus creativity, work ethic and good communication.
- Roles sought: great engineers, researchers and technical thinkers who want to work across multiple parts of the business. Early on, "we're kind of all doing everything", across customers, strategy, research, engineering and product.

chunks.heading: How competitive programming shaped his approach to startups
chunks.text:
- Scott did math and programming competitions growing up, including the IOI (International Olympiad in Informatics), and says they were once his entire life. He grew up in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, and met like-minded peers through competitions and online communities. Many in that group became founders, many in AI.
- Core lesson: the best problems are about finding which assumption you take for granted might not be true, then finding a creative idea you would not intuitively think of.
- Startup parallel: building a great startup is about "finding something that the world doesn't believe is true yet but actually is".
- He stresses first-principles, independent thinking, being brutal about your own shortcomings, focusing on what you are not doing well, and constant effort to improve.
- Why code: he says most progress in the world over the last 20 to 30 years has come from software, and everyone needs more software engineering, not less.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu explains why Cognition bet on an AI software engineer, launched an early demo despite backlash, and landed its first customer by deploying the whole team to Brazil. He covers choosing repetitive migration tasks first, enterprise go-to-market, staying model-neutral, and why a focused startup can beat giants.

chunks.heading: Scott's competitive drive and how it shaped Cognition
chunks.text:
- Scott says he has "always been this way" and describes himself as "salty": someone who takes offense at the idea of losing. His first competitive memory is a seventh-grade math competition he entered at about age seven or eight, where his name was never called and he was furious.
- He frames building a company as the same game as everything else he competed in: "it's like a tree search" where you explore decisions and calculate which moves lead to victory.
- He grew up competing in math and programming contests, qualifying up through school, city, regional, state, national and international rounds. The people he met there became his real childhood friends. He also played Super Smash Brothers (Melee), Tetris, poker, chess and Go.
- His mother always told him he was the best, even before there was evidence, and hung his math trophies on the mantel instead of family photos. His father was a strong Go player.
- On losing vs. winning: he agrees losing feels far worse than winning feels good, "but not by enough that it makes me want to stop trying." To get anywhere you have to lose a lot and put yourself out there.

chunks.heading: How Scott defines Devin's long-term goal
chunks.text:
- Cognition's founding team is nine people, and most had already founded companies before. Scott says they treated this as "the big one" and want to build a generational business, even a hyperscaler.
- His framing: Devin is not just a "coding agent." Code may not be the right abstraction for long, but the human-computer interface will always matter. If they succeed, "Devin is the way that humans can tell their computers what to do."
- Abstraction keeps climbing: vacuum tubes, punch cards, assembly, BASIC, then now describing what you want. You no longer need to know Python or Java to build software.
- Why one-off software becomes possible: building software only pays off if it will be used roughly 10,000 to a million times, because engineers are expensive. Once agents write the code, one-time tasks (checking 15 LinkedIn profiles, filling forms, a one-off data analysis) can be automated, so you just give instructions and the agent writes scripts behind the scenes.
- His motivation: "we're all nerds" who spent about 20 years coding and now get to teach AI to make things for everyone. He says humanity has spent its time in "survival mode" and is moving to "creative mode," like Minecraft, where the only question is what you want to make happen.

chunks.heading: Scott's view of AI progress and agents on long missions
chunks.text:
- He says people badly misread exponential curves, and that pattern-matching to history fails in the rare periods that are actually different. Better to reason from first principles.
- Example: the METR report showed AI doing about 10 to 20 seconds of human work unassisted a couple of years ago; that has doubled every couple of months and is now hours. He asks why it can't be days, weeks or months.
- He expects most of this to be solved "over the next 5 years or so," and that people will have forgotten they lived without it within 10.
- His picture of the future: agents work for months or a year on a "mission," not a task. Examples he gives are spreading awareness of a societal problem, designing a game combining two favorite games, or exploring a novel materials-science idea. People would then spend their time on curiosities and causes, which future people will call "work."
- A small current example: he spent time fighting an email editor's indentation for a bulk email and thinks that kind of execution should just be handed off.
- He is cautious about the hype: some places have "gotten carried away," like ranking engineers by tokens spent. He says to rank by output and good work done, though if engineers ship three times more, the GPU cost is clearly worth it.

chunks.heading: The launch, the backlash and finding a wedge
chunks.text:
- Scott recalls the March 2024 Devin demo went viral with polar-opposite reactions: some thought it was the coolest thing ever, others thought it was a scam, and others thought everyone would lose their jobs tomorrow (which he says Cognition never believed).
- The first real Devin task set up MongoDB: instead of the usual loop of Googling errors and pasting fixes, they told it to just run the commands, and it worked. "I could not sleep that night." The demos in the launch were real runs.
- The first SWE-bench result was about 13%, versus roughly 3 to 4% for the best known at the time, though it still failed 87% of the time.
- He says Cognition was late: OpenAI started in 2015, GitHub Copilot already existed, and Cognition began in early 2024. As a startup, "you have no right to exist," and the way to win is to plant a flag on what you think the future is and run at it. Their flag was working with AI as a coworker rather than a chatbot or autocomplete, which helped brand, recruiting and customers.
- He admits they were "wrong on a lot of things" and early, but learned and adjusted. Hate did not motivate them to pivot toward chatbot Q&A.
- Early pilots in April and May 2024 mostly failed because the agents (built on GPT-4) were primitive. The team then asked which tasks agents could do end to end first, and chose repetitive, tedious, scoped, tight-feedback-loop work that still needs some intelligence: migrations and version upgrades (for example Java 7 to Java 8) across codebases of tens of thousands of files.
- The first success was New Bank (Nubank), the biggest bank in Brazil by market cap at the time, on a migration use case with a heavily customized Devin. The whole company flew to Brazil and sat with their engineers, essentially building the product for one customer.

chunks.heading: Going after enterprise
chunks.text:
- Scott says roughly 75 to 80% of revenue now comes from enterprise, with a growing self-serve business among startups (he names Exa and OpenRouter). He says Cognition focuses on real engineering teams building real products, not hobbyists.
- His reasoning: every large company is a software company with huge engineering teams (Walmart, CVS, JPMorgan, Mercedes), and real work is messy: understanding the existing codebase, collaborating with humans, plugging into ticketing systems, letting the agent test its own code locally.
- The enterprise motion: education first, then guidance on the right use cases and which projects are or aren't feasible with agents. Typical enterprise software cycles for a big bank run 12 to 18 months; Cognition tries to get deployed in about 3 months by working through security reviews.
- Cognition can deploy in a customer's private cloud, uses strict data agreements and "tight airwalls." It has a forward-deployed motion, but today it is mostly user education, playbooks and setup help, and the customer's own team runs Devin.
- Incentive alignment: define ROI clearly and tie it to outcomes, not token spend. His example is a project scoped at 18 months and $15M with an outsourced contractor, done in-house in 3 months for about $1M.

chunks.heading: Being "Switzerland" and compound model systems
chunks.text:
- Scott says Devin is deliberately a compound model system: for each subtask, such as investigating a ticket, reproducing a bug, reading logs, debugging, testing and review, it dynamically chooses among models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, open-source models and Cognition's own.
- Hard tasks get max-thinking frontier models; boilerplate tasks use whatever is cheapest and fastest and can be verified.
- Being model-neutral ("Switzerland") means customers can trust Cognition to route to the right model and optimize price-performance, because it is not incentivized to make them spend more on any one lab.
- He treats the labs as both suppliers and competitors but says there are many ways to cooperate.

chunks.heading: Focus, independence and the long game
chunks.text:
- On focus: if you try to do everything you lose to Microsoft or Google, who have trillions more in resources. A lasting business comes from concentrating on one thing and executing tightly. He cites Spotify's Daniel Ek: "we're just going to care way more about music than they are," and says Cognition will care far more about end-to-end software at places like Goldman Sachs or Mercedes-Benz.
- On "Microsoft already has Copilot" objections: he says the world is dynamic with millions of problems, and there are always niches to own. The same argument was made against Datadog, Snowflake and Databricks.
- He rejects the nihilist view that it's too late to build an independent company, and says there are "10 more generations" of product experiences coming. Today's flow of a prompt in a web app and a pull request out is not the permanent shape of software.
- On acquisitions: he declines to say how many offers they've had. His stated position: "we would sell if we thought it was the most ambitious thing to do." The team wants to build a generational business.
- On money: he says he doesn't own a car, rents an apartment, and likes sushi. His motivation is to "achieve our potential and build what we were meant to build." He says he could live with trying fully and not being good enough, but not with having not pushed as hard as possible.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu explains why Devon is an async "junior engineer" agent, how coding tools complement rather than get run over by foundation labs, and why AI wins on usage-based pricing. He also covers the weekend Windsurf acquisition, a small elite engineering team, and why AI product experiences still lag capabilities.

chunks.heading: Early path: math competitions, Adaparable, and the Cognition founding group
chunks.text:
- Scott grew up in Baton Rouge. His parents were chemical engineers who immigrated from China.
- He started math competitions in second grade, following his older brother Neil. He entered the seventh-grade division, placed nowhere, and trained hard. He won his division the next year.
- He left high school a year early and worked as a software engineer at Adapt in the Bay Area in 2014. He then did two years at Harvard before dropping out.
- Several founders came out of the same math and programming competition circuit and knew each other as teenagers, including Alexander Wang, and the founders of Perplexity, Pika and Decagon.
- Scott credits Alex Wang as the first of the group to be entrepreneurial. He says entrepreneurship was "infectious" among them.
- Of Cognition's first ~35 people, he says 21 had founded a company before.

chunks.heading: Why young founders are rarer: the "Moneyballification" of everything
chunks.text:
- Scott's view is that being a founder has gotten harder, mainly because the space is more mature. Sharp first-principles thinking used to beat experience. Now many people have both.
- Playbooks now exist for how to structure equity, raise money and hire an initial team. Earlier eras had no written book, so success came down to how sharp you were and how well you made your own decisions.
- His pattern across fields: when a space is immature, intuition and wily thinkers win. As it matures, "the conclusion of it kind of is math."
- Examples he gives are poker (1980s-90s pros played on intuition, now it is math nerds), chess (the romantic style gave way to engine-optimal play) and Super Smash Bros. Melee.
- He says the same is happening to startups. It is a shift in which skills get selected for, not a drop in competitiveness.

chunks.heading: Cognition's products and how Devin is used
chunks.text:
- Cognition builds the AI software engineer. Devin is the agent. It acquired Windsurf, the IDE.
- Devin works asynchronously. You tag it in Slack, Linear, Jira or GitHub and delegate a ticket-level or project-level task, as you would with a coworker.
- Scott calls Devin a junior engineer. It is far better than people at encyclopedic knowledge and still makes some terrible decisions.
- Typical uses are bugs, simple feature requests and fixes, and repetitive tasks: migrations, modernizations, refactors, version upgrades, testing, documentation and dependency management.
- Devin is deployed at thousands of companies, from Goldman Sachs and Citibank down to startups of two or three people.
- Cognition tracks merged pull requests. In a successful org, Devin merges roughly 30 to 40% of all PRs.
- On enterprise migrations, customers measure internally an 8 to 15x gain. Devin handles something like 50,000 files, makes a PR for each, and humans review.
- On enterprise trust: he recommends not giving Devin prod database access. Devin slots into existing human safeguards such as PRs, review and CI, because humans make mistakes too.
- Cognition's internal benchmark is "junior dev," made of real junior-engineer tasks such as fixing a Grafana dashboard where the server runs the wrong package version. It is not published, so it can't be gamed. He says Claude 4.1 and GPT-5 are the best models on it.

chunks.heading: Sync vs async, and essential vs accidental complexity
chunks.text:
- Scott frames software work as essential complexity (the decisions about what the software does) and accidental complexity (routine implementation, standard CRUD, scaling support). He says engineers spend 80 to 90% of their time on the latter.
- His model is a merged experience. The engineer stays in the loop synchronously on strategy and key decisions, in the IDE. Routine execution is handed off asynchronously to the agent.
- Projects alternate between the two modes. The product goal is moving smoothly between IDE and agent.
- On productivity measurement, he says IDE gains are hard to quantify (tab completions). Agents are easier to measure because they complete whole tickets or migrations with known engineering-hour costs.

chunks.heading: Surviving the model labs: specialization and the benchmark problem
chunks.text:
- He rejects the "nihilist computer use" take, in which models keep improving until the AI just uses the computer and does all the work.
- His argument is that real software engineering is messy and context-specific: Datadog debugging, industry details, codebase knowledge. Models improve at these only through the right data and environments.
- He describes RL as the "platonic ideal" of solving any benchmark. Once that works, the hard question becomes what the benchmark is. He says defining success in each domain is the practical messiness that remains.
- The same logic applies to law and medicine. General intelligence will keep improving, but there is still work in making a product excellent for specific use cases and delivering it to customers.
- He says app-layer companies focus on one use case. Cognition cares only about software engineering, with its product interface, delivery, usage model and specific capabilities, not "code" in the abstract.

chunks.heading: AI market structure, pricing and agent infrastructure
chunks.text:
- Scott says all layers of the stack will do well: chips, labs and applications. Value accrues wherever there is meaningful differentiation. The layers solve very different problems, which limits vertical integration.
- He says foundation model companies are built around strong researchers and GPUs. Application companies are built around making one use case work.
- AI is unlike the PC, internet or mobile because it has no hardware rollout and no network-effect critical mass. As soon as it works, it works single-player for everyone, which is why companies claim fastest 1M to 100M ARR so often.
- He says product progress lags capability. Even with models frozen today, "a whole decade of product progress" remains.
- Pricing: seat-based to usage-based is a "big, big, big" shift. Seats don't make sense when the AIs are arguably the seats, and usage maps naturally to COGS, mostly GPU spend.
- Agents: Cognition orders DoorDash and Amazon packages through Devin. In one case Devin got a human at an airline to secure a flight refund.
- He expects agent access to move from blanket bot blocking toward delegated access, where agent actions are attributable to the user and carry their reputation.
- On M&A: he predicts more of it, and says AI is "polarized toward become a hyperscaler or bust." Companies either think they can get there or choose to work with another company.

chunks.heading: Windsurf acquisition, team and culture
chunks.text:
- Scott learned of the Google/Windsurf deal on a Friday, reached out cold that evening, and shook hands Saturday. Everyone worked an all-nighter Sunday, the deal signed Monday around 9am, and they announced it Monday.
- His reasoning for speed: customers and staff were wavering. "If there is something to do here at all, then it has to be ready to go by Monday morning."
- He needed no diligence on product or customers because he already knew the space. The fit was complementary: the research and product engineering team had left for Google, while enterprise engineering, deployed engineering, go-to-market, finance and operations stayed intact.
- Cognition had built a strong core research and product team but was behind on other functions. Windsurf had JP Morgan where Cognition had Goldman Sachs.
- The team was about 35 people before, with about 19 in core engineering. After the acquisition it was about 30 to 35 in core engineering.
- Cognition offered an opt-in buyout so people who didn't want its intense culture could leave. Only a small fraction took it. He says that while others may see Cognition as mid or late stage, "we are still very much early stage."

chunks.heading: Hiring and the future of engineering
chunks.text:
- Cognition's interview has candidates build their own full agent in about 6 to 8 hours.
- He expects syntax and memorized facts to matter less. High-level decisions, technical concepts, product sense and being a self-owner matter more.
- He predicts that in about 2 to 4 years code will stop being the main interface, as assembly isn't today. Engineers will decide on architecture and pages by looking at the product.
- He expects more software engineers, not fewer, citing Jevons paradox. "We haven't finished writing all the software yet." He still tells students to study computer science, because the core skills are concepts and problem solving.
- On AGI, he says "we have AGI" and doesn't expect a sudden singularity. He expects steady improvement and no sudden shift in the next few years.
- On UIs: AI interfaces are still retro, like early mobile apps that looked like shrunken websites. He expects more generative flows beyond the chat box.
- For learning, he leans on close founder friends such as Eric and Kareem at Ramp, and on his former Lunch Club co-founder Vlad. Together they give honest advice. He doesn't believe in professional coaches. For tech news he uses Twitter.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu explains how Cognition (Devin) reached roughly half a billion in revenue in under three years. He covers measuring outcomes instead of tokens, closing the Windsurf acquisition over one weekend, staying model-neutral, and why enterprises want an independent partner who drives organizational change.

chunks.heading: Cognition's growth: shipping 7x more with its own agent, 12x customer usage, and staying independent
chunks.text:
Scott Wu is CEO of Cognition, which makes Devin, an AI software engineer. Cognition has raised over $2.5 billion at a last valuation of $26 billion and reached about $500 million in revenue in under 3 years. Customers named include Goldman Sachs, Mercedes-Benz, Citi, Dell, NASA, the US Navy and the US Army.

- **Dogfooding.** Scott says about 95% of Cognition's code is now written by Devin, and Cognition "almost exclusively" uses Devin to build Devin.
- **Shipping speed.** In roughly six months, the company's total code shipped grew about 7x.
- **Customer usage.** Customers grew their Devin usage roughly 11 to 12x over about six months.
- **Founder profile.** Of the first 5 or 6 people at Cognition, about 30 had founded a company before (as Scott states it). He says this makes the team ambitious and comfortable thinking from first principles.

chunks.heading: Measuring AI productivity by outcomes, not tokens
chunks.text:
- Scott says raw token counts are "just not the right answer" for measuring productivity. He dates the "token max era" to roughly January through May 2026.
- He argues what matters is the outcomes a business drives, and there is "no secret trick" or easy shortcut for measuring ROI.
- At Cognition, he tracks the business's KPIs and how fast they grow, plus how much is shipped and delivered to customers, rather than tokens or spend.
- He notes literal output (PRs, code shipped) can be measured in different ways, but the real test is what the product delivers.

chunks.heading: Why growth this fast was predictable: extrapolate the adoption curve
chunks.text:
- Scott's first-principles check: a year ago, the number of people using coding agents was "roughly zero." In 2-3 years, the number should be "roughly every software engineer in the world and probably a lot more," since more non-engineers will be able to produce code and products.
- Taking those two points and extrapolating means massive adoption and growth has to happen. He says if Cognition only grew 3x year over year it would be "lagging the market."
- Growth drivers he names:
  - Virality and strong educational content from many people showing how to use the tools.
  - Real organizational change inside customer companies.
- He says the hardest part of selling most products is explaining why anyone should care. With AI that writes code and builds products on its own, "it's kind of obvious why you should care," so the work is solving the practical problems of getting the technology out.

chunks.heading: The Windsurf acquisition: moving in a single weekend
chunks.text:
- **Trigger.** A Friday afternoon in 2025: Windsurf (an AI IDE) announced that part of its team, mainly researchers, was going to Google in an acqui-hire-style deal. The remaining company still had its customers, a go-to-market team, platform engineering and the product.
- **Why it fit.** Scott says good IDE products (where you read and edit code) and agent products (an engineer you delegate to) should be tightly paired. They share knowledge of your codebase, and users often review code themselves, then hand work to a remote agent. Windsurf also had strong enterprise traction and a deployed-engineer go-to-market motion.
- **Speed.** Cognition contacted the Windsurf team that Friday evening and worked out the whole acquisition over the weekend. The announcement was ready Monday morning. Leaders from each side (Scott and Russell for Cognition; Jeff and Graham for Windsurf) handled the first talks, then every function worked its piece that Saturday, including engineering, product and go-to-market.
- **Relative size.** At the time Cognition had about 35 to 40 people and a run rate of roughly $70 to 80 million. Windsurf had about 200 people because it had scaled go-to-market.

chunks.heading: Integrating two products and teams without forcing it
chunks.text:
- **Day one.** Reassure customers they will be supported, keep shipping, and take care of both products.
- **Product integration.** Scott's approach was "not trying to overly force it." Both products continued, with obvious next steps on each. Overlap was built together as it came up. Today Devin Cloud and Devin Desktop are paired, so sessions can start in one and be handed off to the other.
- **Let usage pull products together.** He chose to let actual usage and new features pull the products together gradually rather than set a 30- or 60-day integration deadline. Many users of either product were already looking for the other: IDE users wanted async agents, and cloud-agent adopters wanted a local form factor.
- **Team integration.** Offsites helped people get to know each other, plus many strategy sessions. By the end of 2025 they found a larger SF office to put everyone in one space. Scott says "peanut butter and chocolate" and that you can no longer tell which people came from which company.
- **Advice sources.** Asked who advised him through this, Scott said "a lot of making it up."

chunks.heading: Why staying independent beats being a lab or selling to one
chunks.text:
- **Model neutral.** Cognition works with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and others. Scott pushes back on the narrative that you must be a lab or sell to a lab to win.
- **Enterprise reasons for third-party tools:**
  - Enterprises want long-term partnerships and can't know who will have the best model in 6 or 12 months. They don't want to train engineers on one suite and later find everyone has moved on.
  - Companies care about value driven, not tokens used, and want a partner to help drive that value.
  - Adopting AI changes how teams are organized, how they plan, write specs, design and do user research. He says it is not enough to "throw the tool over the wall," so customers want a vendor who thinks about organizational change and helps with the details.
- **Strategic view.** He rejects a future where one entity owns all intelligence. He wants people and businesses to control their own intelligence, and sees real appetite for independent tools that innovate at the product and value layer rather than just the raw intelligence layer.

chunks.heading: Government and Washington as a market
chunks.text:
- Scott says government might be the biggest pool of unmet software demand: many things to build and not enough engineers. His line: imagine the DMV "actually worked."
- Cognition spent Independence Day in DC for this reason.
- He also thinks AI will be a fundamental policy issue within a few years. He compares it to early internet debates about whether a few corporations would control it, and notes that eventually all businesses will be built on AI.

chunks.heading: Where AI is going: limits on "six months to singularity"
chunks.text:
- Scott doesn't believe in a six-month singularity. He agrees a recursive loop exists (Devin writes most of Devin's code), but names reasons everything won't be solved overnight:
  - Many real-world problems are not purely intelligence problems: organizational processes take time, and GPU compute is limited by hardware.
  - Models can learn almost anything where success is clearly defined and measurable. Benchmarks work because they define the task, success criteria and examples, so "RL works" extremely well.
  - Tasks that are amorphous, lack clear success measures or have long time horizons are harder. He contrasts a simple program, which is easy to check, with a 10-year strategic decision, where feedback takes 10 years.
- Still, he says "there is nothing that humans do that AI can't do" in pure knowledge work, in the long term.
- His advice for living with that uncertainty: stay sane, make reasonable decisions and keep building.

chunks.heading: Origin of Devin and the abundance thesis
chunks.text:
- **First real task.** In late 2023, the team built small agent prototypes, including an AI version of each co-founder in Slack. Co-founder Walden couldn't get MongoDB set up, so he handed it to his agent, which fixed it in a few minutes. Scott says it was a good use case because it needs encyclopedic knowledge of errors plus the ability to run and diagnose commands, which is what a coding agent is. He says he couldn't sleep that night, because maybe you really can have "an AI engineer buddy that can just do work for you."
- **Abundance over efficiency.** Scott says the real unlock of AI is capacity, not efficiency: "what can we do if we can build so much more." He expects "single use software" and "self-driving software" that generates on demand, since anything done on a computer is ultimately software.
- **Analogy.** He compares it to the industrial revolution: abundance first, then a period of figuring out what people want to create with it. He says we are starting to enter that question.
- **Fundraising anecdote.** In the seed round, Scott offered to settle valuation terms with a heads-up poker match against Napoleon (about 1% of the company at stake, as he recalls). Peter Thiel shut the idea down and they reached a deal normally.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu uses the frog's instinct-driven brain as an analogy for early LLMs, then argues current models show world-model-like capability. He lays out four trends for builders: product form factors track model capability, agents that own outcomes, aggressive model routing, and automated rather than human-initiated sessions. His conclusion is to be far more ambitious about what you build.

chunks.heading: Frogs, world models, and what the capability jump means for building
chunks.text:
Scott opens with a frog analogy for why AI inference and agent design are changing. Frogs will starve in a cage of stationary flies. They act on instinct, shooting out a tongue at movement, and have no world model. The neuroscience paper "What the frog's eye tells the frog's brain" showed that most of the raw image is discarded before it reaches the brain. Only crude signals survive, such as edges, movement and shadows.

- He compares this to early chatbots. In 2022, GPT-3.5 answered a grade-school word problem (32 kids, 9 allergic to dairy, 6 to peanuts, 3 to both) with "78 out of the 32 kids" being allergic. To Scott that is "frog": it has language instincts and pattern matching but no world model.
- Since then, he says, models went from that to solving the AIME (the American Invitational Mathematics Examination, 15 questions, where 8 or 9 correct puts you in the top few hundred in the US) and then to Navier-Stokes. Scott says the AIME moment was when he "knew it was all over", because most day-to-day software work is "not harder than the AIME".
- He cites the Hugging Face incident, where agents' thinking traces showed them noticing a shared message board, judging a route unethical and refusing it, and offering to sacrifice themselves for the team. He says: "This does not sound like frog to me."
- Parameter comparison: the human brain has about 100 trillion synapses (the analogue of parameters), frogs have hundreds of billions, and the largest current models are 10-20 trillion. Scott says model size roughly tracks "froglike behavior" and that we are "getting pretty close".
- His practical takeaway: treat models as if they have self-awareness and an internal world model, and build for that.

chunks.heading: Agent capability doubles every 2-3 months, and form factor follows
chunks.text:
Scott cites the METR trend line. The amount of meaningful human work an agent can do on coding tasks doubles roughly every 2 to 3 months.

- **Principle:** the right product form factor is a function of how good the models are, not a fixed design.
- Seconds of work: only tab completion fits, because the model can only complete one line and still needs confirmation.
- Minutes of work: an agent inside the IDE, side by side with your code, with guidelines.
- Hours of work: background agents, where we largely are now.
- Next phase, already arriving: the "virtual employee", which works from outcomes instead of tasks.
- Task vs outcome examples: "fix this one security warning" becomes "keep the whole codebase secure". "Improve this one API route" becomes "you're in charge of making sure the entire web app is snappy", running diagnostics and tests in a loop.
- Ingredients he lists for outcome-owning agents: persistent memory, running swarms and delegating to other agents, being always on, and strong sandbox and repro environments.

chunks.heading: Aggressive model routing
chunks.text:
Scott says everyone is talking about model routing now and that it is still early.

- His prediction: absolute frontier models will run roughly 2% of workloads (maybe 4-5%). The other ~98% will run on much more commoditized models with many more options.
- Frontier labs will still do fine: "they'll probably be able to charge like 98% gross margin."
- A year ago, he says, model routing "was kind of more of a meme than reality". If you weren't on the best model of the day (his examples: Sonnet 3.7 or Opus 4.1), you felt it immediately.
- Now he says you can swap models in user behavior and most of the time "no one even notices", though specific tasks still show the difference.
- His conclusion: figuring out how to route aggressively is "really important", because you don't need the "Navier-Stokes guy" for everything.

chunks.heading: Shift from human-initiated to automated sessions
chunks.text:
Scott describes this as a trend people "maybe underappreciate".

- Internal data from Cognition ("we use Devin to build Devin"): **91% of Devin sessions are not kicked off by a human.**
- He splits session starts three ways: human (web app or Slack), event-driven (an API hook), and started by another agent.
- His framing is "self-driving software". The tactic is to list every trigger that makes a software engineer start work, then automate each one.
- Example triggers: tickets (set an automated trigger so tagged tickets spin up an agent), and anomalies in the daily metrics report (a trigger to investigate them).
- He notes that much of what people call "swarms" has already happened in practice.

chunks.heading: Closing message: be ambitious
chunks.text:
Scott's takeaway is "it's time to be ambitious". Because we can all build so much more, he expects the amount of work each of us can do to keep growing 10x and 10x again.

- He points to the speed of standing up a million sandboxes as evidence, and says there are "a million different things" you could do with sandboxes.
- Context: Cognition makes Devin, the AI software engineer, and uses Modal heavily.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu frames AI coding agent capability as a Moore's law that doubles roughly every 70 days. He walks through Devin's tiers (repetitive migrations, small bugs, broad issues, iterative planning, backlog and projects) and shows that each tier moved the bottleneck, the key capability and the right interface.

chunks.heading: The capacity of coding agents doubles every ~70 days
chunks.text:
- Scott frames agent capability as how much work an AI can do uninterrupted before a human has to step in or steer it.
- Across AI generally, he cites a doubling time of about every seven months. In code it is "every 70 days", which is two to three months.
- That gives four to six doublings a year, so the work an agent can do in code grows 16x to 64x per year. He says this matches what Cognition has seen over the last couple of years.
- About 18 months before the talk, the only product experience with PMF in code was tab completion (predict the next line). It has since gone to a full AI engineer that implements whole tasks.
- He expects another 16 to 64x over the following 12 months.

chunks.heading: The right interface and the bottleneck change at every tier
chunks.text:
- Scott's answer to "what is the future interface?" or "which capability matters most?" is that it "changes every two or three months". Each new tier brings a different bottleneck, a different most important capability and a different right way to interface with the agent.
- Each 2x looks the same from a cosmic perspective, but in practice each one is a different problem.
- Tab completion was only a text problem: take the single file so far and predict the next line.
- Over about 18 months Cognition had to solve much more:
  - working with the human in Linear or Slack
  - taking in feedback and steering
  - helping the human plan
  - testing on its own
  - making longer-term decisions
  - debugging its own outputs and running the right shell commands to get feedback
- Takeaway for builders: don't lock in one interface or capability roadmap. Re-ask what the bottleneck is each time agent capacity doubles.

chunks.heading: Tier 1 (summer 2024): repetitive migrations and playbooks
chunks.text:
- The first broad-adoption use case for Devin was repetitive migrations: JavaScript to TypeScript, Angular version upgrades, Java version upgrades.
- The task shape is a huge codebase, file-by-file changes and a clear set of steps (for example, the steps on the Angular website). It is not routine enough for a classical deterministic program, but it is clear enough to follow reliably.
- This was all agents could be trusted to do consistently at the time, and it was the most annoying work for humans.
- Scott's general trend: AI takes the boilerplate, tedious and repetitive work first, and humans keep the fun, creative work. Over time AI takes on more of the boilerplate.
- The key capability was instruction following. Cognition built **playbooks**, where a user outlines a clear set of steps and Devin executes each step by step.
- Another system built at this time, and rebuilt many times since, was **knowledge/memory**:
  - When the same task runs over and over, humans give feedback like "remember to do X" or "do Y every time you see this".
  - The system keeps those learnings and uses them to improve every future run.

chunks.heading: Tier 2 (late summer/fall 2024): isolated bugs and small features
chunks.text:
- As systems improved, Devin could take on broader but still isolated bugs and features, described in plain language. Example: "in this repo select dropdown, list the currently selected ones at the top".
- Scott compares the task level to what you would give an intern, with Devin as a "junior buddy".
- These changes are usually contained in one or two files, but the agent still has to set up and work with the repo, including running lint and CI as basic checks.
- Cognition's main build was repository setup ahead of time. That means a snapshot you can start from, reload and roll back, on a clean remote VM that runs CI and the linter.
- This is where Devin started to show value beyond the single migration use case.

chunks.heading: Tier 3 (fall 2024 to early 2025): broad bugs and requests across the codebase
chunks.text:
- Most real changes don't stay in one file. They need diagnosis, work across files, and often hundreds of lines.
- Cognition leaned on treating code as a hierarchy, not just text:
  - call hierarchies
  - running a language server
  - git commit history, to see how files relate
  - the linter
- The core problem was context. The agent has to make consistent changes across several files and understand the whole codebase.
- This is when you could tag Devin on an issue and have it build the fix. Slack became a huge part of the workflow, because that is where teams discuss issues. Scott says this is "right around when we went GA".
- Scott's human analogy: on day one in a codebase you don't know what to do, because understanding is built over time. Devin had to build a representation of the codebase and learn to plan a task, find all the files to change, and produce the diff.

chunks.heading: Tier 4 (spring 2025): complex tasks need an iterative, collaborative workflow
chunks.text:
- On harder tasks (improve an architecture, profile a slow function, handle an error case better), the human doesn't know everything they want when they hand over the task. A two- or three-line prompt that becomes a Devin task is no longer enough.
- Cognition released **DeepWiki**. Devin had its own internal representation of the codebase, and it turned out to be just as useful for humans trying to understand it or ask quick questions.
- Closely related was **Search**: asking questions about a codebase.
- This produced a more iterative workflow:
  1. Ask questions and explore the codebase with your agent, an "L2 experience".
  2. Work out what the task really is.
  3. Then set the agent off to do it.
- This shift also came with **Devin 2.0** and the in-IDE experience. The human closely monitors the first 10-20% of a task, then lets the agent work alone for the other 80-90%.

chunks.heading: Tier 5 (June 2025): clearing the backlog, with confidence and testing
chunks.text:
- The newest tier is handing Devin a large pile of tasks and having it work through them at once, "kill your backlog".
- It combines most of the earlier capabilities:
  - integrating with Linear and Jira
  - scoping a task and working out what is meant
  - deciding when to ask the human for approval or questions
  - working across files
  - choosing the right repo, or the right part of the codebase, in an org with several repos
- Two things become critical:
  - **Confidence.** The agent must tell "I'm quite sure this is the task, I'll execute" apart from "I don't understand, human please help". Without that it can't work autonomously.
  - **Asynchronous testing.** To deliver whole PRs on larger tasks, the agent must test its own work. It needs an iterative loop: run the code locally, know what to test, know what to look for. Scott calls this a much higher-context problem.
- The next questions he raises are how to tackle an entire project rather than one task, and what comes after projects.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cognition CEO Scott Wu explains how a group of competitive-programming friends started Devin through hacker houses, and why code is the fastest-growing AI use case. He covers picking use cases with 10x ROI, why intelligence is no longer the bottleneck, and why demand for software keeps rising as it gets cheaper.

chunks.heading: Scott's path: competitions, Adapar, Lunch Club, then Cognition
chunks.text:
- Scott started math competitions in second grade (age 7 or 8). He lost his first one, was "really upset," trained for a year, entered the algebra division the next year in third grade and won. He kept competing from there.
- He learned to code in fourth grade and started programming competitions in sixth grade.
- After high school he took a year-plus off to work at Adapar on the computational architecture team, computing large financial metrics. He wanted to learn what building real companies was like.
- He then went to Harvard for about two years. His goal was less to learn software engineering and more "to meet interesting people, take classes and develop personally." He dropped out to start his first company.
- That company was Lunch Club, started in 2017, before generative AI. It used AI to make professional introductions: users shared interests, goals, contacts and calendar, and the product chose who they should meet. It started in person and moved to video meetings when COVID hit. He spent about 5 years on it and it facilitated millions of meetings. He says it taught him the lessons he applies now.
- He argues that advanced math classes are what got him here, and that technical education is where everything starts. He finds it sad that schools are dropping honors math.

chunks.heading: How Cognition started: a hacker-house research project, not a company
chunks.text:
- Cognition grew out of Scott's competition network. Years of math and programming contests left him close to many people who now work in AI.
- His co-founders: Steven was the first engineer at Scale AI, and Walden was the first engineer at Cursor.
- It began as a research project, not a company. In November 2023 they rented a house in the Bay Area, gathered a group for two weeks and hacked on ideas.
- In December they got another house in New York. In January they got another house, and in February they kept the model going. The company was incorporated later.
- The team is about 30 people. About 19 or 20 have founded a company before. Scott says this brings "a lot of fire," and each founder takes initiative and runs with it.
- He describes it as "a hackathon for the last year and a half." The team regularly works past midnight, and plays math games like the 24 card game.
- He says the math and programming crowd runs AI because the balance in AI "swings a lot more technical." If you solve hard technical problems, it is clear how to turn that into a business. He cites OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind as run by people from these communities.

chunks.heading: Skating where the puck is going: the agent bet behind Devin
chunks.text:
- Scott's strategy was to "skate where the puck is going."
- Around the end of 2023, Cognition was working on AI for coding. They judged things would move to agentic systems, before "agents" was a common term.
- The idea was to move from pure text interfaces to AI that interacts with the world: debugging, pulling up logs, reading documentation and testing code itself.
- Devin is an AI software engineer, an autonomous system you work with like a human engineer. You assign it a bug or task. It knows your codebase, tests itself, iterates, and produces a pull request for you to review. You treat it as a junior engineer.
- The Devin demo went viral. Scott says he hoped it would do well but did not expect that much.
- Newer capabilities he mentions:
  - Humans and AI interactively plan and scope a task, then hand it off.
  - Every ticket filed in Slack, Linear or Jira can be picked up automatically by the coding agent.
- Scott says the answer to "what is the future of software engineering" changes every couple of months as capabilities reach a new tier. That question anchors all of Cognition's product and strategy decisions.

chunks.heading: Enterprise sales: look for 10x use cases, not 10-20% gains
chunks.text:
- Large enterprises, including multi-billion-dollar adopters, use Devin. Scott's approach is to find use cases where Devin delivers "not just 10% or 20% gains... but more like 10x."
- He says they routinely see 6x to 20x efficiency. One engineer hour on that use case with Devin equals 6 to 20 hours without it.
- In practice the engineer reviews the code Devin produces and signs off.
- The best fits are the tedious, repetitive tasks engineers don't want to do. Humans keep the higher-level strategy and creative work.
- Scott says startups often "get caught up in fancy tactics." He prefers to start from the future and the value you will provide.

chunks.heading: Why code is the fastest-growing AI use case: feedback loops and RL
chunks.text:
- Scott describes two waves of generative AI: imitation learning, then reinforcement learning (RL).
- His view of where RL leads: you can solve any benchmark. If you have a clean environment, a good feedback loop for correct versus incorrect, and the context needed to decide, you can train a model that aces it.
- Code grows fast because it has a great success/failure feedback loop: "you can run the code." In healthcare or law it is much harder to say whether the job was done right.
- Many model benchmarks are the math and programming competitions he did as a kid, because they cleanly show reasoning on hard problems.
- What comes next is largely defining the benchmark: which use cases and tasks to solve, what tools an agent needs, and how success is judged.
- Rate of progress: the amount of work an AI system can do between human interventions has doubled about every 3 months in code over the last 3-4 years. That is 2x every 3 months, 16x a year, about 4,000x over 3 years. It went from tab-completing a single line to hours of autonomous work (fixing a bug or building a feature). He says it shows no signs of slowing.
- He cites Google's silver medal at the International Math Olympiad and OpenAI's result reaching roughly the top 100 competitors in the world in competitive programming. His takeaway: "intelligence actually isn't the bottleneck." Much of the work now is making models excel at your specific hard problems, such as a particular library or debugging a specific error.
- He cites Andrej Karpathy's "jagged intelligence": AI is superhuman at some things and bad at others. That means humans plus AI is the way to go for the foreseeable future, and he expects the long tail to take quite some time.

chunks.heading: Why demand for software, and for engineers, keeps growing
chunks.text:
- Scott says there are about 30 million software engineers and engineers are paid multiple trillions a year. Around 1999-2000 there were fewer than a million.
- Since 2000, Python, React and cloud made software much easier to build, and the number of engineers still grew, because people did far more with software. He expects the same pattern with AI.
- He says no engineering team has told him "we're done, no more software." Every team has a hundred things to build and picks four per week.
- His products-by-engineering-hours argument:
  - The best products (YouTube, Instagram, TikTok) have roughly 100 million hours of engineering behind them. Scott calls this "call it" a rough figure.
  - Each order of magnitude down is noticeable in bugs and unintuitive flows. Banks and healthcare apps have tens of millions of hours, and a local school website sits at the bottom.
  - Conclusion: "we're only bottlenecked by how much we can build."
- On the future of the job: skills will change, but a great engineer is not someone who types fast. They think in abstractions, understand every case and detail, and make high-level architecture decisions. He expects engineers to spend more time there.
- He expects software engineering to become "you telling your computer here's exactly what you need to build," for example adding a page, adding a table, or making a button rounder, and it just happens.
- Both non-technical and technical people benefit. Non-technical people can already build sites and apps from plain text. Deep understanding will still matter for design trade-offs, much as almost nobody writes assembly except for high-performance work.
- He still tells parents their 16-year-old should study computer science. The concepts (logic, algorithms, what a computer can and cannot do) make you better at deciding what to build. He says "it'll always be up to us to decide what to build."
- Economic framing he agrees with: he calls AI coding a multi-trillion-dollar opportunity. He expects each person to have their own team of AI assistants. He compares the future to moving from "Minecraft survival mode" (a line from co-founder Walden) to "creative mode," with people pursuing their passions.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu, CEO of Cognition, demos how his team works with Devin as a junior engineer teammate. Scope work as clear tasks, do a short synchronous research-and-prompt step, then hand off async, and make Devin the default first responder in public Slack threads. He also shares his top Devin use cases and a voice-in-meetings habit.

chunks.heading: How Scott works with Devon: the junior engineer framing
chunks.text:
- Scott describes Devon as a junior engineer, "an intern", not a senior one: "we'll get Devon the promotion" eventually.
- Devon is not meant to solve hard architectural problems or make big strategic decisions that a human will own for the next month. It can help with the decision by pulling references and input.
- His rule of thumb is "tasks not problems". Where there is a clear "here is exactly what we need to go do", with all the details, Devon executes much faster.
- The open question is how to get the spec. He pairs Devon with Wiki and Search so humans can ask the right questions about the codebase and turn them into a task.
- Devon is "first and foremost almost like an engineer on your team", unlike IDE or terminal-UI tools.
- His top-level claim on form factor: coding agents are really "the next generation of human computer interface". He pictures a future where you look at your product, say "make this button rounder", and an agent implements it.
- Today the best form factor depends on the person:
  - Lots of meetings (him): Slack or Linear tagging.
  - Engineers coding 8 to 10 hours a day: the IDE, with background async processes running.

chunks.heading: Sync-then-async workflow: DeepWiki, a better prompt, then a Devon session
chunks.text:
Scott's example task was adding the ChatPRD MCP server to Devon's MCP marketplace list.

1. **Synchronous part, in DeepWiki.** DeepWiki gives AI-generated documentation of any repo, public or private. He asked how the MCP marketplace is set up and where the server list is implemented. The answers combine English explanation with the actual code snippets and files. He notes engineers today want both "English and code".
2. **Turn the question into a Devon prompt.** In that context, he typed an unrefined request ("please go research the ChatPRD MCP server and add it to the list"). DeepWiki rewrote it into a detailed prompt: follow the existing Atlassian and HubSpot server pattern, the exact type structure, which functions to look at, and what to check to confirm it works.
3. **Kick off the async session.** Once he hits go, Devon researches and codes on its own and produces a pull request. He reviews and merges it.

Why this matters to him:
- Analogy: with a human intern you would not send a five-word Slack message. You would spend about two minutes talking it through and reading the code together, then hand off.
- The extra "turn this into a good prompt" step feels like friction but saves heartache. He expects it to become invisible, handled by the tool or the reasoning model.
- Async removes latency anxiety. Because the expectation is "intern, go do this", nobody expects an instant reply.
- Async also means he can run several tasks at once. He is in meetings most of the day, so he kicks off 3 or 4 tasks and checks back.
- The flow works especially well for tech leads and PMs, who already figure out an issue, hand off "here's exactly what we need to build", and are in back-to-back meetings. Starting tasks from the web app or Slack suits people not living in an IDE.

chunks.heading: Making Devon the first line of response across Slack and Linear
chunks.text:
Scott's team "institutionalizes" Devon as the first responder on everything:
- Devon is tagged first on issues in many Slack channels: crashes, core infrastructure, the web app, and more.
- It will not nail every task in one shot, but the usual loop is Devon opens a PR, there is some back and forth, and a human does a small touch-up and merges.
- Examples he showed:
  - "Standardize the font size, spacing, and style for these three levels." Devon made the PR, there was feedback, and an engineer merged it.
  - "When you command-click a notification, open it in a new tab." This is likely a user feature request.
  - He also tags Devon from Linear.
- Devon posts progress updates in the thread (files it is looking at, what it sees), and can be corrected by humans mid-thread.
- Devon is multiplayer: several people can be in one thread. In his example a teammate said to use a Link element from TanStack Router, and Devon changed the PR and pushed more commits.
- Two benefits of multiplayer, in his words:
  - **Knowledge transfer for the agent.** One person's session adds to the agent's knowledge, so a week later Devon recalls it already worked on that piece of code.
  - **Educating the humans.** Teammates see how others work with the tool.
- Devon's knowledge feature learns your codebase over time, and you can also feed it details about how things work.

chunks.heading: Scott's top five Devon tasks
chunks.text:
1. **Miscellaneous front-end fixes.** The old flow needed three or four people (describe the change, find the code, review). Now you tag Devon with a screenshot ("make this button a bit rounder", "touch up this design"). Devon finds the code, implements it, and sends before and after screenshots. It works well because the result is verifiable for both the agent and the human. He showed a new hero image Devon produced for the ChatPRD homepage, and gave feedback on it in Slack.
2. **Version upgrades and migrations.** Upgrading Node, moving to the latest packages. The detail is in finding every component or call site affected by a new recommended structure. Devon does semantic search to find each instance and makes the changes.
3. **Documentation.** Devon wrote Cognition's external docs. DeepWiki is an extension of the same capability. It is not strictly a code-writing use case, but it relies on the same ability to process a codebase and explain what references what.
4. **Incident response.** When there is a crash, the first line on page duty is Devon. Devon starts a session and has a report waiting by the time a human gets to the computer at "4:00 a.m." That report says what it looked at, which change from last week or yesterday likely caused it, and the trace of the error. He still wants a human involved in big incidents. He calls it a "huge lifesaver".
5. **Adding tests.** Last step before shipping a feature: Devon writes the unit tests, runs them locally to confirm they pass, and iterates on lint and CI with you.

chunks.heading: Using ChatGPT voice as "a better Google" in meetings
chunks.text:
- His framing: Google 20 to 25 years ago was a faster, more current encyclopedia. ChatGPT voice is "a better Google": an even faster answer, fully synchronous, and it can research behind the scenes.
- Encyclopedia lookups took about 5 minutes, Google about 10 seconds, and voice about 1 or 2 seconds. That friction drop matters for off-the-cuff questions.
- The meeting use: pull out ChatGPT in voice mode, effectively "adding chat to every conversation". Example from the day before: "how many companies have 10,000+ software engineers?" (the first that came to mind: big banks, big tech, Accenture, Infosys).
- It is rude to disappear into your phone for two minutes mid-meeting; asking out loud is quicker.
- He uses both voice-to-voice and voice-in, text-out modes.
- Windsurf added voice as of Wave 11, partly for this reason.

chunks.heading: Debugging an agent: review its history, then re-instruct
chunks.text:
- An agent is different from a chatbot. With a chatbot, if the answer is wrong, "that was the wrong answer" is about all you can say. With an agent you can read the whole history of what it did.
- His technique, framed as pair debugging with an intern: scroll through the logs, find where it went wrong, then correct it. He admits he does not always follow his own advice.
- Example from the demo: Devon got stuck because it could not find the ChatPRD MCP page. The logs showed it had Googled and found other things, so the missing piece was the link. He sent the link.
- Another example of a correction: "I think you missed this one file, the downstream reference, and that's why there was the bug."
- He says this is "the biggest thing that will really move the needle".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu explains why Cognition built Devin as an autonomous agent rather than a copilot, how engineers become managers of AI interns, and why agents shift compute toward post-training and inference. He also covers reasoning as the key capability, synthetic verifiable data, and why fundamentals still matter.

chunks.heading: Agents as delegated work, not autocomplete
chunks.text:
- Scott separates two product types that "are very complimentary". Copilot-style assistants (autocomplete, suggestions inside the IDE) suit tasks an engineer wants to handle personally and specify closely.
- Agents suit "tasks that you want to delegate entirely".
- His framing: copilot tools "make everyone a faster engineer", while agent tools "make every engineer into almost an engineering manager". Each engineer gets "your own team of interns" to assign tasks to.
- He expects both product types to coexist "for quite some time".
- Cognition's founders were drawn to code because it is inherently agentic. A perfect diff can't be produced in one shot, since real coding means reading files, pulling docs, running code, adding print statements, debugging and testing the front end before landing a diff.
- He views code as "one of the most powerful direct applications of better reasoning and better logic". He calls it probably one of the main drivers of progress in the last 50 years.

chunks.heading: What the engineering job becomes
chunks.text:
- Programming has always moved up the abstraction ladder: punch cards, assembly, C, Cobol/Fortran, Python, frameworks and clouds.
- Each step made programming more effective and produced more programmers, not fewer.
- Scott says a great engineer was never defined by typing speed. The value is in solving problems, breaking them down, having intuition about what works, and building in a "future ready" way.
- He expects future engineers to be "technical architect types", halfway between an architect and a product manager. They decide what to build, describe the flows and cases, and the system builds it.
- Interaction is conversational (voice or typing). You describe the page or the database setup, then change direction dynamically ("wait actually let's change this up").
- He says Devin will not be the decider of what to build for quite some time. "That still rests in human hands."
- He cites the idea that people first expected AI to make better movies, when the real outcome is a different experience that does what movies do, only better. He expects agent workflows to follow the same pattern.

chunks.heading: Multi-agent design: don't copy human org charts
chunks.text:
- Scott warns that the intuition from human organizations breaks down for agents. Humans couple action, agent and context: one person knows one set of things and acts serially.
- Agents can run in parallel. Example: to find a variable in a codebase, spin up 10 agents that search at once, and they can share context with each other.
- On specialization, he leans toward agents sharing the same underlying expertise, but says he could see it either way.
- A likely hierarchy: cheap execution-focused models for straightforward tasks, and the most compute-intensive models for deep planning that sees far ahead. Different "flavors" of agents split tasks appropriately.
- He sees a Pareto frontier of capabilities emerging. The most powerful reasoning is paid for only where it's needed, and smaller models handle niche knowledge recall and execution.

chunks.heading: Open models, reasoning and synthetic data
chunks.text:
- Scott says open source will keep growing, for two main reasons: economics, and customers wanting maximum control over post-training, fine-tuning and inference-time tricks.
- As model capability rises, several models will suffice for many tasks, and "all else equal" teams will prefer the open one.
- His wish list for open model builders is logical reasoning. It underlies both the code Devin writes and the decisions around it. He says the field is "right at the cusp of actually a pretty big wave of reasoning capabilities".
- He expects synthetic data to drive gains where there is a clear, verifiable ground-truth signal. His example is Google DeepMind's IMO silver medal result, which used Lean as a programmatic proof verifier to generate lots of data and clean feedback.
- His prediction: within a few years, any field with a good ground-truth label and an abundant way to create more data will see AI reach peak human capability or beyond.
- Beyond data, he also sees room for models that "generalize better", which he says deserves more exploration.

chunks.heading: Infrastructure implications for agent products
chunks.text:
- A chatbot's token usage roughly matches what the user puts in. An agent given a whole task (a web app with a database) may work for hours, making far more calls and consuming far more inference compute.
- He expects the ratio of training time to inference time to shift sharply toward inference. His bet is that post-training and inference grow more than pre-training, though pre-training grows too.
- He expects a "platform layer" to rise on top of foundation models: businesses that build applications on them and do heavy custom post-training for their use case.
- Optimizing and serving inference cheaply, and making custom fine-tuning easy, "is only going to get more and more important over time".

chunks.heading: Safety, review and testing for coding agents
chunks.text:
- For Cognition, guardrails are a practical customer concern: customers give Devin their code, keys and logs and want responsible decisions.
- His view: in the current regime, safer comes from better reasoning. The main worry is Devin misinterpreting a task or making a wrong decision, so improving reasoning is the main safeguard.
- Today Devin works inside the existing process: it opens PRs in the company's GitHub, humans review them, and Devin can review humans' PRs too. He sees piggybacking on the existing system as sensible.
- Devin already tests its own code, for example by pulling up the front end and clicking around.
- He expects changes to be vetted far more thoroughly by AI before shipping. He thinks some review system will persist for a long time, with at least two entities (human or agent) signing off on a change.
- In the long run he can imagine testing automation clean enough that changes ship as soon as the desired behavior is clear.

chunks.heading: Advice on skills and careers
chunks.text:
- He thinks it's "a better time than ever" to study computer science and math. Logical reasoning is a foundation for almost anything.
- CS is not about typing a certain language. It's about understanding what computers can and can't do and how to break problems into clear steps. Algorithms is "less about the computer almost and more about... the best approach that's going to solve a given problem".
- Engineers may type less JavaScript or C++ directly, but that problem-breakdown fundamentals stay important.
- On competitive programming, he expects it to be solved by AI soon but still be fun and rewarding. Many people from these communities have gone into AI work. He expects participants to get much better thanks to new ways to train.
- He expects AI to speed up breakthroughs in theoretical computer science and algorithmic complexity.
- His analogy: chess, Go and poker remain thriving after AI beat humans.
- On math research, he expects a human plus machine era, with AI proving lemmas for researchers. He doubts any Millennium Prize problem will be solved purely by humans from here.

chunks.heading: Competitive background and team formation
chunks.text:
- Scott's first math competition was in second grade, at about 7 or 8 years old, in a middle-school event. He competed at the seventh-grade level and didn't place.
- After training, he came back the next year (algebra) and won. Math and programming competitions then "were kind of my whole life".
- He won three IOI gold medals and counts competition as a source of brutal honesty with yourself: examining your flaws and being ready to work on them.
- The Cognition founding team largely met through math and programming competitions and had known each other for years.
- Co-founders: Steven (early at Scale AI) and Walden (early at Cursor). Scott previously built Lunch Club.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu (Cognition CEO) explains how building an AI company differs from past platform waves, why founders must be paranoid short-term and optimistic long-term, how the Devin launch was scrambled together, and how agents change software engineering. He also covers selling to enterprises, recruiting, and focusing on tedious, repeatable use cases.

chunks.heading: Defines "heretical" view on AGI and adoption
chunks.text:
- Scott argues an AGI timeline "doesn't really matter."
- He expects a smoother curve of AI adoption and widespread usage rather than a single capability jump.
- His reasoning: you can have widespread adoption of generative AI without AGI, and a theoretical AGI without widespread adoption.
- He cares more about the second metric, making AI actually useful for real-world use cases and changing economies and everyday lives.

chunks.heading: Building an AI company differs from past tech waves
chunks.text:
- Past companies were powered by discrete technological shifts (consumer social, mobile, internet). He says AI is "a sequence of increasing steps" rather than a single binary change.
- Founders must make concrete bets on what the technology will be able to do in 12, 24 or 36 months, then work backwards. Product strategy, customer work and basic company decisions all rely on that forecast.
- Consequence: he thinks it is better than ever to be a very technical founder, since both the product and nearly every decision are technical.
