- Core company-building principles are unchanged: a Rockstar team, building something people want, distribution, growth, first-principles thinking.
- On the foundation-model market he compares it to the clouds. Heavy capex, big economies of scale, and room for differentiation lead to an equilibrium of roughly two to five big platform players with huge margins. Many applications get built on top, so he dislikes the word "commodity."

chunks.heading: Founder mindset: long-term optimist, short-term paranoid
chunks.text:
- Founders should be honest with themselves about what is working and what is not.
- He rejects the trope of "unbridled optimism" in the short term. Be optimistic about the long term but "really paranoid in the short term."
- In AI the ground moves fast (models, hardware, robotics all progress at once), so expect big surprises and challenge your own assumptions.
- Startups' main advantage is the ability to adapt and move quickly, so use it.
- On when to quit, he cites Paul Graham's "determined but not stubborn." At each point write the story of how this becomes a massive success and list what must happen for that to be true. Then ask whether the original thesis still holds and whether this is still the best thing to work on.
- His warning: people are told to "drink their own Kool-Aid," but "a lot of doing startups is really just being honest with yourself."
- His core advice for founders: build something people want. It is easy to proxy that with team size or number of people who tried the product.
- He also advises not being afraid to look dumb: do things that are very different and very new.

chunks.heading: Math/EV mindset ("Moneyballisation") for startup decisions
chunks.text:
- His background is math and programming competitions (including the IOI). He says sales, product strategy and similar decisions "map to just doing math questions."
- He describes a trend he calls the "Moneyballisation of everything": startups are becoming more analytical, like sports and poker, with founders breaking down each situation to find the optimal strategy rather than relying on raw intuition.
- His self-described superpower: breaking each situation into logical reasoning and applying principles of logic. Since you are doing something nobody has done, you learn playbooks but must decide from first principles.
- Example of EV thinking on effort: he and a co-founder flew to North Carolina to have dinner with a recruit's parents, bring gifts, and explain the mission. It was about eight hours total (a 2-3 hour dinner plus travel, back the same night). He says the ROI was "unimaginably high" for landing an MIT student whose parents were hesitant, even though it felt dumb and might have made no difference.
- His framing: ask what the chance is that it does something meaningful and what you get out of it, and "the math at some point is all there."

chunks.heading: Product strategy: agents as decision-makers, not chatbots
chunks.text:
- For two to three years, products were chatbot-style: feed the model a prefix and take the suffix (ChatGPT, Q&A, marketing copy, customer support, GitHub Copilot).
- His thesis: the bigger value is in "an actual decision maker." His analogy: a legal assistant to talk to is cool, "but what about if you just had a lawyer."
- That is why Cognition built agents from the start. Devin browses the web, runs commands, stores secrets, plans, and optimizes multi-step processes.
- Planning and reasoning generalize: improving Devin's browser use also improved its ability to make decisions in testing and other tasks.
- He sees UX for agents as "super underdeveloped." Cognition invests in how you interact with Devin: its browser, shell, conversing with it, talking to it asynchronously while it works, giving feedback, and running multiple Devins in parallel (the engineer acts like a manager of a team of Devin interns).
- He does not share how Devin works internally, but says investment that transfers across models (such as datasets capturing desired behavior for RL or fine-tuning) generalizes better than model-specific work, which is how to prepare for the ground moving.

chunks.heading: Go-to-market and finding product-market fit for Devin
chunks.text:
- The first real signal: while setting up MongoDB, which was a tedious whack-a-mole of googling errors, the team handed it to a prototype Devin. It worked, which was "one of the really exciting moments." Iterating with customers and being customers themselves is among the most important things.
- Customer use cases today are "the more tedious or repetitive" ones: code migrations and re-platforming (for example thousands of files, or a migration to Flutter), front-end issues, triaging logs and debugging sessions, and tasks with tight feedback loops (Devin can change code and test it on a local front end).
- He notes AI is better at repetitive tasks, and engineers do not want to do them anyway, so Cognition has largely avoided engineer defensiveness. Such migrations often lag because they are painful.
- Real customer work is messy. Examples: connecting to Datadog to read logs, learning the code base over time, running the dev environment locally, and rules that must be applied thousands of times. He calls these "brain dead" but high value.
- Sales motion: go into orgs and look for both top-down support (executives who want AI) and bottom-up support (developers who want to try it). Budget source varies (innovation, general tech, or dev tools). What matters is real excitement plus clear use cases that work. He contrasts fighting for every little thing with the customer saying "let's try it today, let's buy it today."
- Limits: Devin would not build a whole complex system from scratch on the first try. Cognition focuses on cases that are repeatable and clear enough for real ROI.
- On the high valuation (a figure around $2 billion was raised by an audience member), he says they are very early but going after a very big goal, and asks "how much is software worth as a category."

chunks.heading: Launch lessons from the Devin release
chunks.text:
- He says the launch was not very intentional. A Bloomberg article was planned, and over the weekend before they scrapped their whole video and started over.
- The article was due Tuesday at 6am and they were still filming at 1am, so they asked for a delay and got 9am, the three hours they needed. They stayed up all night writing the blog post, making the video and showing example runs of Devin.
- His lesson: figure out what makes your company and product unique. They disliked the first video because any company could have made something similar. The final version simply showed what the product looks like and how it works in action, and talked it through. It was less formatted but better.

chunks.heading: Future of software engineering and code
chunks.text:
- At Cognition, Devin already built much of their front end, API integrations, and internal dashboards and tracking.
- He argues demand for code is "more than 10x the supply" (and likely more). Every company has about 30 projects and has to pick four. There is also large unmet demand for single-use software that does not make economic sense today (for example clicking through LinkedIn profiles or placing an order could be code but is not worth paying someone to write).
- He expects more software engineers, not fewer, as when moving from assembly to C to Python.
- The role shifts toward something between a PM and a technical architect: break the problem down, define details, edge cases and flows precisely, then hand it to an agent. The net result is building far more.
- He thinks code is treated as precious only because it has been expensive to write. He expects tiers of code, where most code is written once and thrown away or is dirtier, and says "a lot of our emotional attachment to how we think about code is actually the second order effect of how hard it is to write code."
- On code quality in an AI world: keep one human on git blame for each commit (an ownership mentality). Devin opens PRs in their own repo and a human reviews and merges them. He expects code in an idiomatic style, to the point that you reason about logic and edit that rather than reading code.
- On memory: context windows will keep growing, but he does not expect a world where you shove an entire code base and history into the context. Humans have very short context but excellent retrieval, and problem solving does not require millions of tokens.
- On roles: great designers, engineers and PMs share the same core skill of breaking a problem down and choosing the right solution. Getting good at using Devin takes time. People must learn how granular to make tasks, how to prompt it, and how to parallelize it, since working with an agent differs from working with humans or chatbots.

chunks.heading: Team building
chunks.text:
- Most of the founding team has known each other for around 10 years. He has known co-founders Steven since high school, and Walden for a long time. They share a competition background and spent years building different things in AI.
- His advice: for the initial team, work as much as possible with people you know directly or have a very strong mutual connection with. At some point you have to branch out.
- When recruiting, go to unusual lengths (see the dinner with a recruit's parents above).
- Interviewing, he says, is also where non-obvious effort pays off since a good candidate's hesitation can be a family concern rather than a lack of interest.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cognition's CEO explains the sync-to-async spectrum of AI coding tools, why form factor follows model capability, and why post-training with custom RL environments is Cognition's bet. He also covers why computer science fundamentals matter more as engineers become architects, and how he thinks about founding.

chunks.heading: How Scott defines AGI and why he calls it "here"
chunks.text:
- Scott says "AGI is here," with a self-aware "facetious" caveat. His test: what would people have called AGI ten years ago? Passing the Turing test, solving hard technical problems, and acting in the real world. He argues these are largely done: Turing test passed, gold-medal IMO and IOI results, agents that reason and interact.
- He thinks there is no single hard cutoff, because humans always do the part that is not yet automated. Definitions like "AGI does 80% of knowledge work" are slippery: that share of work was automated long ago (tractors and the like) if you compare to what people did a thousand years ago.
- Humans are "humancentric" in how they judge this. Even if a few thoughts could produce whole products, people would still say AI cannot do the important work.
- He notes the exponential in how long agents can operate has kept holding, despite the saying that you can't keep predicting points on an exponential curve.
- On Dan's "AGI is when it is economically profitable to never turn your AI off" definition, he agrees an always-on agent doing meaningful work is the right idea. He pushes back on "economic value" as the yardstick, because value depends on how substitutable the output is (if everyone has AGI, they compete with each other).

chunks.heading: Why Scott started Cognition: "I just have to try"
chunks.text:
- Cognition is his second company. He ran Lunch Club for about 5 years before this.
- He describes walking into the company rather than planning it. He and long-time friends were exploring AI ideas and found AI coding the coolest thing, as "nerds." The commitment came once it was clear AI coding would take off and RL would work, unlocking new product experiences.
- His decision frame: try and give it everything, and find out it did not work out, or don't try and wonder. He wanted to give it a go.
- Principles he states: work with people you really like, since you spend most of your time working. And "leave it all on the field": control the inputs, not the outcome, and be able to live with the result.
- He would do it even if it failed, and calls even a collapse (AI winter, hardware problems) "an amazing two years."
- Devon's unofficial otter logo reflects how the team thinks of the product: "our little buddy" with his own computer, typing away on tasks. He says if they believed this was the end of programming, they would be far less excited.

chunks.heading: What software engineering becomes: abstraction, architects and skipping the hazing
chunks.text:
- Long term, he expects engineers to operate at higher and higher levels of abstraction, like the jump from assembly to Python or JavaScript. Eventually you express ideas in English, look at your product rather than your code, and the "Jarvis, Iron Man style future" is correct. Keyboard and mouse may not stay the right input.
- Calculator analogy: teachers once picketed against calculators. Some skills fade (multiplication tables), but humans with tools can do much more.
- The skills that matter more: logical fundamentals, breaking down problems, articulating answers, strategic trade-offs and architecture. The skills that matter less: debugging Kubernetes, knowing obscure libraries, esoteric syntax.
- He thinks computer science becomes more valuable, not less, because you are at the helm making decisions, and those decisions come from fundamentals.
- "Turning brick layers into architects." A "sick" software engineer is not someone who types fast; they break down problems, have good feel, think logically and cover the cases.
- Many professions have a "hazing" period of boring work in the first years. AI lets people skip rungs and become managers or architects directly, like an "officer's school." Devon takes the boring work that juniors used to absorb.

chunks.heading: Sync versus async coding tools: the spectrum and how to hand off
chunks.text:
- He sees two form factors. The IDE category (tab complete, chat with codebase) makes you faster with hands on the keyboard. The agent category runs asynchronously in the background on full tasks.
- Until agents can handle everything, you want both. He guesses this phase lasts about three years, after which you mostly dictate to some agent form factor.
- It is a spectrum, not a binary. Tab complete is the most synchronous ("speculative coding," in his words). Cascade in Windsurf and CLI agents like Claude Code sit in the middle: multi-step, but you check in more, and they do not usually open pull requests, work with all your systems or test everything. Devon is fully autonomous.
- The open question he highlights: how to use the tools in tandem and hand off between them. His example of the lifecycle:
  - Fleshing out the idea and decisions (which user buckets get the feature, what replaces what in the UI): synchronous, live conversation with the agent, which surfaces code paths and edge cases while you decide.
  - Writing the PRD or spec: still collaborative.
  - Implementation, testing, making it work: async, you don't need to be involved once details are settled.
  - PR review and reading diffs: synchronous again.
- His view: flows naturally go sync, async, sync, async, and tools should support the whole cycle.

chunks.heading: Why Claude Code took off, and the form-factor hyperspace
chunks.text:
- He credits Anthropic with an incredible product experience and says two things happened: capabilities improved enough to handle day-to-day work more autonomously, and Anthropic "put a lot of love" into the experience.
- His slightly contrarian take: the CLI itself is not the most important part. The right form factor depends on capabilities, and internally Cognition debates whether it should live in the IDE, Slack or a web app. Their answer: "the form factor just is a software engineer." What matters is what the tools do and how you expect to work with them. Engineers spend time in the terminal, IDE and Slack, and tools will integrate with more of them.
- How he distinguishes the three paradigms:
  - Windsurf tab completion augments you.
  - Devon is the software engineer sitting next to you with their own virtual machine and a repo they spun up themselves.
  - Claude Code is "handing the reins over to your AI buddy to take the wheel of your computer."
- He describes a hyperspace of design choices: sync vs async, local vs remote environment, in the IDE vs elsewhere, single-player vs multiplayer. Different single points are valuable, Devon is one, Windsurf another, Claude Code a new one Anthropic unlocked. He expects many to coexist for a while, since the best depends on use case and flow.

chunks.heading: Why Cognition bought Windsurf and how it fits with Devon
chunks.text:
- Devon's bet is an agent with its own persistent cloud computer, like onboarding a software engineer. Because it has its own environment, it can learn to run tests and handle tasks that nothing else does.
- Even before the Windsurf acquisition, they were asking how to make an experience more accessible and more synchronous. Windsurf was "a great opportunity."
- His adoption path: Windsurf is a fast time-to-value option you can download and use immediately. Over time you learn to work with the Cascade agent and with DeepWiki indexing, which naturally pulls you toward the agentic flow. Humans have to learn to work with async agents, so the transition has to run sync to async.

chunks.heading: Post-training, RL environments and where Cognition focuses
chunks.text:
- Cognition does post-training (fine-tuning and RL) but does not pre-train base models. His reasoning: as a startup, your edge is speed and focus, and Cognition's core DNA is understanding real-world software engineering nuance and teaching it to models to build a great product.
- Examples where post-training fits: having Devon predict its own confidence in a task, and training on workflows like pulling up Datadog, finding the logs, debugging and making the right edits. These need custom data models do not learn on their own. He also mentions COBOL, which models are not adapted to though it is real work.
- Code has a cleaner feedback loop (you can run it, and version control gives full history).
- His RL view: the "platonic ideal" is that you can solve any benchmark, so the real question is what the benchmark is: the tasks, environments, tools, decisions and the success criteria. If you describe these exactly and collect enough data, you can train a model to do it. Defining "good" is the hard part.
- Three ways to get capability: (1) the data exists on the internet (pre-training, which he thinks is converging), (2) experts handcraft RL environments, (3) agents learn continually on their own. He expects to eventually get to (3), but building real agents and environments is the primitive needed for both (2) and (3).
- Tight rewards example: a Grafana eval where the agent must get a broken dashboard running (fix package version locks, follow successive errors) and then answer what the dashboard says. If it didn't get it running it can't answer, and if it did it always can, so the signal is clean. In open-ended live learning the reward is harder: you could get the dashboard running and still have a wrong number.
- On brittleness: it depends on task design. If the task requires recalling exact package versions from memory, it won't generalize. If the agent must search, read the docs, read the logs and open the relevant file, it learns to interact with the real world to gain information, and that skill generalizes.

chunks.heading: The personal agent Scott wants someone to build
chunks.text:
- Outside Cognition, he is most excited about a mass-consumer agent on your phone that handles things for you. He thinks capabilities are already there, and that flight booking is the over-used example.
- Examples he wants: calling and booking reservations, dealing with messages, tracking package deliveries, reordering Amazon items.
- Cognition has experimented with Devon for this: they order their Amazon packages with Devon. Devon has memory, stored secrets and a browser. A Slack message or Linear ticket is the wrong form factor for it, so "somebody else should build the right" interface.
- He predicts this will exist in about 12 months.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu explains how Cognition grew shipped software 10x in six months with only ~40% more engineers, by having AI agents own tasks end to end and start work on their own. He argues companies should measure real business outcomes (not tokens or lines of code) and treat AI capacity as a way to build 10x more software, not cut engineers.

chunks.heading: What an "infinite army of software engineers" changes: agents that close the loop
chunks.text:
Scott frames the core question for any company as: "What would you do with an infinite army of software engineers?" His premise is that every company is now a software company. Goldman Sachs, Mercedes-Benz, Lowe's and Elevance each have tens of thousands of engineers and huge backlogs (car software and process management, transaction processing, internal tools). Cognition (makers of Devin, the AI software engineer, started about 2.5 years ago) sells to these enterprises across the US, Europe, Latin America, Asia Pacific and the Middle East.

- He compares it to the internet: "we don't say that companies are internet companies anymore."
- His point is that the question is practical, not theoretical, because AI coding capacity is already here.

chunks.heading: Cognition's own proof: 10x software shipped in six months
chunks.text:
Scott's favorite internal stat is that Cognition uses Devin to build Devin, and its shipped software volume exploded.

- From November 2025 to end of April 2026, Cognition shipped 10x the software.
- Headcount grew only about 40% (roughly 45 to 60 engineers).
- AI coding was already a big thing in November 2025, so this is not a story about early adopters catching up.
- The share of code committed by Devin rose to 90%+. Cognition uses Devin for "pretty much everything."
- Scott's framing of the scale: at 13% AI-written code (December 2025), a 1,000-engineer team gets about 130 extra engineers of bandwidth. At roughly 90%, it is "like you are doing 10 times as much," or about 9,000 AI engineers alongside 1,000 humans.
- At 13%, AI handles one-off features and repetitive tasks. At around 90%, it covers pretty much everything.

chunks.heading: Why it works: longer autonomous tasks and closing the loop
chunks.text:
Scott credits two things for the jump: model capability and agents doing every step.

- **Model capability:** He points to the METR chart of task length an AI can complete without interruption. GPT-3.5 managed about 30 seconds of work (the "ChatGPT moment," an assistant or chatbot). The latest models have nearly broken the scale; the longest tasks in the dataset top out around 16 hours, and multi-day work is next. Every lab's flagship model improved, so he says models are now "good enough" to do these tasks.
- **Assistant vs. engineer:** 30-second tasks make a chatbot. 16 hours or more makes a full AI software engineer you can give a whole project to and ask to own end to end.
- **Closing the loop:** The first big AI coding breakthrough was GitHub Copilot's tab complete, which only wrote code. Now the agent does every step autonomously: understands the codebase, plans the change, writes the code, uses a computer to test its own work, and reviews it. You tag Devin on a ticket or a customer issue and it solves it. Scott says this is "how you get the real gains."

chunks.heading: Event-driven, parallel agents: most Devin sessions start without a human
chunks.text:
Scott argues you should run agents as parallel and event-driven as possible, giving Devin the same hooks that would prompt a human engineer to act.

- At Cognition, the majority of Devin sessions are now started asynchronously by automated triggers, not by a human saying "Devin, please do this." He shows weekly data of interactive vs. async starts.
- Devin also starts sub-agents and plans specific tasks.
- Example triggers:
  - Monitor API route performance, compare against one week ago, and spin up a Devin if it is noticeably slower.
  - An error appears in Datadog, so a Devin spins up to investigate.
  - Bulk CVE remediation: scanners flag vulnerabilities and warnings, and Devin fixes them automatically.
  - Big version upgrades and large code base refactors, with Devin tackling every file in parallel.
  - Bug triage: a customer report goes straight to a Devin, skipping the human who would have started it, and a pull request is ready for review.
  - Everyday development: PRs, testing and building features end to end.
- He says agents can use the computer, work with every integration, test code and use a browser, so you can treat them as full software engineers. (Anecdote: in Japan a user asked which honorific to use for Devin: "-san, -kun, -sama?")

chunks.heading: Measure business outcomes, not tokens or lines of code
chunks.text:
Scott says the "token maxing" era "lasted for approximately 6 months" (roughly January to May 2026) and that you should move past it.

- Counting tokens is "almost exactly the same" as counting lines of code written.
- He tells the story of an engineer whose weekly report said -200 lines of code: they re-implemented a system with a better, faster, cheaper architecture, deleting 800 lines and writing 600. The lesson is that lines of code is the wrong metric.
- He cites Uber as the famous example of burning its entire annual token budget in 3 months. His view is that the answer is not to maximize token use.
- What to measure instead: the outcomes you want to drive, productivity, what you do with the added capacity, and "actual project outcomes" delivered end to end. Hold agents to the same standards as human engineers.

chunks.heading: Why human engineers still matter: there is 10x more to build
chunks.text:
Asked what happens to human software engineers, Scott's answer is that every engineer becomes about 10x more productive, "but guess what? We have 10 times more things to go build."

- Enterprises employ thousands or tens of thousands of engineers because there is so much software to build, and he says there is actually 10x more of it to do.
- Examples of software that should be better: a Department of Motor Vehicles "except it works," medical records with a genuinely good product experience, and banking apps that let you do everything you want.
- He calls this "the golden age of software engineering": abundance is arriving now, and a team doing this correctly can do 10x more.
- His closing question for every company: "What do you want to build?"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cognition CEO Scott Wu explains how the Devin team went from demo to real enterprise deployments, why they had to speed-run design and marketing, and why humans should stay in charge of what gets built. He also covers Brazil as an organic early-adopter market and his balanced approach to investing amid AI uncertainty.

chunks.heading: Scott's view on what AI changes: humans decide, agents execute
chunks.text:
- Scott is "very bullish on the AI capabilities." He expects AI to get to logical, decision-making work, including math problems, but says that is different from AI ruling the world.
- His model: humans decide what to build, what to do and what to create. AI helps with execution. Otherwise "the humans aren't in control anymore."
- Humans stay accountable, which adds a layer of trust software can't carry. He agrees with the point that the human is responsible in a way no system can be.
- He argues there should always be a human-AI communication layer. The products that matter sit in between: what information the agent shows the human, how the human gives thoughts back, and how they iterate together.
- Capability alone doesn't deliver value. You still need thoughtful product experiences, education and onboarding for people to use agents.
- His framing: AI moves life from "survival mode" to "creative mode" (a Minecraft analogy). In survival mode you mine every block and build every shelter yourself. In creative mode you have all the tools and can build whatever you want. He expects AI to remove barriers so people can pursue their passions.

chunks.heading: Building Cognition: what changed between demo and real deployment
chunks.text:
- Cognition builds Devin, the AI software engineer. It works with big companies, startups and everything in between on shipping software faster.
- Scott's founding bet was that the technology would get much better. He says it was still surprising how stark the improvement was over two years.
- He saw the background agent take off in 2026. Consumer agents with the same form factor now exist for many use cases.
- Early on it was "much more of a demo or a prototype." It did fun hobby tasks, but working on a real code base is "very different work."
- The company had to learn what deploying at a real company involves: big code bases, real use cases and integrations.
- Enterprise deployment demanded sophistication fast. Scott says Silicon Valley fixates on raw intelligence, but getting it into the real world and into everyone's daily work takes much more.

chunks.heading: Speed-running company functions
chunks.text:
- Scott says Cognition had to "speed run building all these functions" in two to three years.
- Example: no designers in-house until about 8 or 9 months before this interview. He says they should have hired one much earlier. The product had cool things but "definitely did not look good" until recently.
- Marketing was the same: Cognition only started ramping it up much more recently.
- Takeaway he implies: don't wait on design and marketing because the core tech is the star.

chunks.heading: Brazil as an international market
chunks.text:
- Cognition is opening offices in Brazil and growing internationally in a few places. Brazil has been a meaningful hub.
- Early partners included Nubank and Itaú. The first international trip after founding was to Brazil, and Cognition held a developer conference there the following year.
- His demand logic: Brazil has huge demand for software and not enough software engineers. The fix is making each engineer much more effective with AI.
- He calls Brazil an early adopter across the board.
- Brazilians online call the product "Divino." That started organically, with folks talking about it online and natural demand.
- Cognition's response: "We should do more," and build out its own local presence on top of the organic community.

chunks.heading: Handling AI hype and uncertainty
chunks.text:
- Scott says he goes through "AI psychosis" himself every few months.
- Part of the hype is true: the world will be very different and many things humans do manually will go away. Part is overblown, like the idea that there is no worth in living and we become slaves.
- His stance on predictions: "anybody who claims that they know everything about what's going to happen in AI has been wrong basically every time."

chunks.heading: Investing: stay balanced and hedged
chunks.text:
- Scott says he has no idea how AI plays out in markets. He thinks AI as a whole still has a long way to go.
- Rule one: bet on AI broadly, not on one individual company.
- Rule two: be prepared for uncertainty. He says it's not wise, especially now, to go all in on one or two things, since a new model capability could reshape an industry.
- Keep a balanced portfolio and be ready to adapt to change.
- He believes the total market will go up because "we'll all be building much more in AI," but picking a single stock or pick would be "guessing."
- Method: decide which directional trends you believe in for the long term, then hold a mix of exposures that is still reasonably hedged.

chunks.heading: How Scott manages his own money
chunks.text:
- The large majority of his wealth is illiquid.
- Outside that, he applies the same logic. On where AI value accrues (chips, frontier labs, application layer, inference technology), he doesn't claim to know which wins. He sees a decent chance all of them accrue value and favors balance across those layers.
- His investments in friends' companies and others in the Valley follow that same spread view.
- His liquid money is largely a mix of tech ETFs, total market ETFs and some amount of Treasuries.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu explains how Cognition launched Devin, why code is the best domain for agents (clean feedback loops), and why they build everything in-house with a tiny, founder-heavy team. He also argues software engineering becomes more valuable as abstraction layers rise.

chunks.heading: Scott's product: Devon as a fully autonomous AI software engineer
chunks.text:
- Cognition's product is Devon, which Scott describes as "a fully autonomous AI software engineer" and a full asynchronous coding agent that takes on whole tasks.
- Devon works across the end-to-end stack. It writes and edits code, runs the linter and tests, executes commands, installs packages, reads tickets, and talks to the user in Slack. In short, it uses the same tools a human engineer would.
- The company was founded in November 2023. When Scott said "AI software engineer" in 2023, "everyone thought we were kind of crazy."
- Scott frames the product as "turning the brick layers into architects." Every engineer becomes an eng lead with their own team of Devons, assigning tasks and answering questions.
- His self-driving analogy: autonomy comes in phases (automatic shift, then cruise control, then no driver's license needed). Devon today is aimed at technical users with existing codebases, doing new features, bug fixes and upgrades.
- Honest capability assessment: Devon is "a junior engineer today." Six months earlier it was "like a college intern," and twelve months earlier "like a high school CS student." It can't yet handle really tough architectural questions or massive projects alone.

chunks.heading: Launch playbook: the viral demo, then general availability
chunks.text:
- The launch article (Bloomberg) was supposed to go out at 6 a.m. on a Tuesday. Scott asked them to hold it, and it went out at 9 a.m. because the team needed more time. The demo video still wasn't filmed by 1 a.m. the night before.
- The launch checklist, run by a very small team:
  - Get investors and friends to help promote it.
  - Write a blog post that articulates "what we think the future is going to look like."
  - Put out the demo runs.
  - Get it to initial early users so they could give firsthand feedback.
- The team did not expect the level of attention: "we were honestly shocked."
- After launch, the criticism was that Devon was taking engineers' jobs. Scott's response: once you put something out, "you're not really in control of your own narrative anymore." The lever he does control is getting the product into people's hands.
- That meant general availability in December 2024: anyone could "put down a card," sign up, pay, and connect their GitHub repo. Before that, Devon was mainly sold to enterprises.
- Scott's stated rationale for GA: let people see "the good and the bad and everything" and try it themselves. He is upfront that Devon "is certainly not magic" and does some things well and some not.
- Afterwards, adoption became more organic. Companies posted GitHub graphs showing Devon as their number one contributor.

chunks.heading: Competitive positioning: the autonomous agent category
chunks.text:
- Scott sees three categories of AI coding product:
  - Code completion tools and AI IDEs.
  - Zero-to-one "build me a cool website" tools, mainly for non-engineers.
  - The AI software engineer, the direction Cognition has "always been building towards."
- He says Devon "is still rather unique" as a full autonomous agent, and that Cognition "kind of invented the category" and "believed in agents before anyone else did."
- On the competition, he stays generous: "there's a lot of really great teams," and the market is large enough that overlap isn't zero-sum. He argues that the idea of full autonomy "either resonates or it doesn't with folks," and that is what sets Cognition apart.
- Why code is a defensible space: its ceiling is unusually high. A trivia question has one best answer ("Thomas Jefferson"), but with code "there is always another level of understanding," more efficient or better ways to build, so there is real room for differentiation.
- The messy questions Cognition spends all its time on:
  - How does the agent learn over time?
  - How does it interact with humans and slot into the workflow?
  - How does it make the right decisions about the codebase?
  - How does it use tools like the browser, Datadog or CI?

chunks.heading: Product design for agents: beyond the chatbot
chunks.text:
- Scott says Cognition has not "cracked" agent UX. Chatbots are simple (ask a question, get an answer), but agents "actually do things and take actions in a real-world environment," so the interface differs for every product.
- Devon's specific surfaces:
  - GitHub: Devon makes PRs and responds to comments on them.
  - A clean way into Devon's VS Code.
  - Visibility into the shell commands it runs.
  - Visibility into Devon's browser.
  - Tagging Devon on Slack issues.
  - SSH into Devon's machine.
- His prediction: a "proliferation of vertical-specific agents." A legal agent wouldn't use VS Code and GitHub, so each vertical needs its own tools and workflow integration.
- Guardrails follow how human teams already work. Devon never pushes straight to master or production. It creates its own branch and opens a PR, and a human reviews and merges. Access is tightly scoped per task, and Devon slots into the same permission models large orgs already use.
- Build vs. buy: Cognition builds the agent infrastructure in-house because it wants "such tight control" over the action space, how Devon learns over time, and how the right files are pulled into context. Scott calls these "the meat of what makes Devon special."

chunks.heading: Technical approach: compound system, RL, and feedback loops
chunks.text:
- Devon is a compound AI system that relies on multiple models working together.
- Scott splits the Gen AI era in two:
  - 2022 to roughly early 2025: imitation learning (train on the internet, get something that talks like the internet).
  - Now: reinforcement learning, which works when you have a clearly defined set of tasks and a clean feedback loop for success versus failure.
- He expects specialization. For customer service, sales or legal AI, a clean loop means you can train a model toward near-perfect results on it. Differentiation then lies in what behaviors you define, what the model uses to make decisions, and what tools it has.
- Why code took off first: you can run it. In accounting, by contrast, the feedback might be "you get audited a year later." In code, the result is real output that "is not fakeable," which gives a tight loop for judging whether Devon succeeded on a task.
- The hardest problem he names: Devon learning over time. A great engineer on day one is still less useful than someone with 10 years at the company. The open question is how Devon distills, for example, 500 sessions with different engineers into the best action for the current task. It pulls in retrieval, context and search.
- Building an AI engineer has two parts: "the computer" (connectivity to tools and information, VMs, infra, rolling back state, parallelizing and forking) and "the brain" (knowing how to use tools to raise the probability of success). He compares it to a human debugging process: pull, run locally, reproduce the bug, read logs, edit, retest. A human who just "yolos" a diff rarely succeeds.
- Team time is split across 3 to 4 rotating pods. If forced to pick one focus, it is the brain side (capabilities and intelligence), with infra and core product interface close behind. Scott says he sees no single glaring bottleneck.

chunks.heading: Hiring and team: small, dense, high-drive
chunks.text:
- The team is about 25 people and has been kept "pretty small and pretty steady." Roughly 15 months in, it works late: "in the office after midnight most days," with a brainstorm that ran past 1 a.m. the night before.
- About 18 of the team have founded companies before (Scott included). Scott's logic: they are clearly capable of running a company alone but come together to build something bigger.
- Many early hires came from the international Olympiads. The team has 20 gold medals at the International Olympiad, along with those 18 former founders.
- Ambition is a hiring filter: "we're going after really the biggest thing. You don't end up with a medium-sized outcome." The mindset is "this is going to be the big one."
- December launch examples of range: one engineer (a top CTF team member) sized VMs and prepared infrastructure for load; another pulled an all-nighter perfecting product features; the president flew to Madrid for a 36-hour trip the week after a 36-hour Paris trip. The team has traveled to South America, Asia and the Middle East in one year.
- Pitch to candidates: for "a bunch of programming nerds like us," teaching an AI to code is "the coolest possible thing we could be working on." Contact is scott@cognition.ai.

chunks.heading: View on the future of software engineering
chunks.text:
- Scott calls this the start of "the golden era of software engineering."
- He says CS is still worth studying. At its core, software is about telling a computer what you want it to do, and the durable skill is problem solving: decomposing problems, designing solutions, understanding what architectures work.
- On programming languages: he expects Python to eventually feel like assembly does today, used only by people who need to peel back the layers.
- Data point he cites: until around the year 2000 there were fewer than a million software engineers, and today there are about 30 million. Making programming easier has grown the field, not shrunk it.
- On the line between idea and execution: it has always shifted. Hosting your own website once meant servers and DNS, before Cloudflare. If AI takes the 90% that is execution, humans do the 10% ideation "10 times more," and that boundary keeps moving toward 99.9%.
- Predictions:
  - The next 2 to 3 years bring about as much change as the last 40 in software, with entirely new frameworks and processes.
  - Single-use software, built for one purpose and used once, will appear.
  - Jevons paradox applies most in software: cheaper software means more uses for it. He ranks products by tier (billions of users, 100 million, 10 million, down to a community school website) and sees large gaps in quality that are not built today simply because they would take months of engineering time.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu explains why Cognition raised over $1B at $26B, how revenue grew from ~$37M to near $500M run rate in a year, and why staying independent and model-neutral is a strategic advantage against the big labs. He also argues AI will increase, not reduce, the number of software engineers.

chunks.heading: Why Cognition raised $1B at a $26B valuation
chunks.text:
- Scott raised over $1B, led by Lux Capital, General Catalyst and 8VC, at a $26B valuation.
- He gives two reasons for the round:
  - Scale aggressively: "scale our compute" and grow the team.
  - Stay independent: remaining an independent business is "really really important for us."
- His framing for demand: "every company in 2026 is a software company." AI is "doing real work at real companies everywhere."
- Enterprise proof points he cites:
  - Cognition works with all of the top five US health insurers, which are building far more tooling for their care providers, cutting costs and covering more people.
  - Banks use it to deliver software to their customers.
  - Other customers include the Treasury and NASA.

chunks.heading: Revenue growth trajectory and the 2026 target
chunks.text:
- Run-rate progression Scott has shared over time:
  - Early 2025: a few million dollars.
  - June 2025: about $37M.
  - June 2026: "close to 500 million," in about two years of business.
- His 2026 goal for the team is one metric: "we firmly intend to cross a billion in revenue run rate." He wants to keep going beyond that and grow "at as many of the companies in the world that we can."
- He reads the growth as evidence of demand rather than of a crowded-market win: there is far more demand for software than supply of engineers.

chunks.heading: Market sizing logic: 10x the engineers, more than 10x the software
chunks.text:
- Scott's sizing argument:
  - There are about 30 to 35 million software engineers in the world today.
  - Cognition wants to make all of them 10 times more efficient.
  - He thinks there is "a lot more than 10 times more software to build."
- His supporting stat: there were under 1 million software engineers 20 to 25 years ago (the start of the century), and that rise came with a massive increase in the software produced.
- His conclusion: making engineers more efficient produces more software, not less.

chunks.heading: Independence and neutrality as a positioning strategy against the labs
chunks.text:
- Asked about the threat from big labs, Scott says it works "the other way around": being fully independent and neutral is "the best way for us to be aligned with our customers."
- How the position works:
  - Cognition works closely with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI and others, including on research.
  - Devin is a "compound system" that works with all of these models.
  - Customers get "the best model for every different use case."
  - He calls Cognition "the Switzerland in the equation."
- The incentive point: Cognition is incentivized to serve whatever model is best for each case, rather than a single series of models.
- On Cursor possibly being acquired by SpaceX, he argues the ecosystem is "broad enough and vibrant enough" for different players in different positions. First-party lab products will keep existing, but model neutrality is "an important position in the space."
- On further M&A (he references last year's Windsurf deal), he says there will "sure" be more, but his own focus is growing the business and serving customers.

chunks.heading: Devin adoption and the effect on engineering teams
chunks.text:
- Scott describes Devin as the first AI software engineer, and says teams adopting coding agents at scale "are able to do much more and execute much more aggressively on roadmaps."
- Work mix: the large majority is on existing code bases, continuing to build and add features, with new code as well.
- Dogfooding: more than 90% of the code written at Cognition is written by Devin, and the team uses it all day to build Devin itself.

chunks.heading: Hiring and the future of the software engineering job
chunks.text:
- Even with that productivity, Cognition keeps scaling headcount.
- Scott expects the job to evolve and some skill sets to change, but says "we will have far more people doing this and building software and building products, not less."
- His reasoning is the same demand logic: more efficiency means more software gets built.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu explains why Cognition moved within days to acquire Windsurf after its Google licensing deal. He covers the complementary IDE-plus-agent product fit, a shared enterprise focus, building conviction by using the product firsthand, and why speed mattered for the team and customers.

chunks.heading: Cognition's acquisition of Windsurf: how Scott found and closed the deal
chunks.text:
Scott Wu is the CEO of Cognition, which builds Devin, the first AI software engineer agent. In July 2025, Google struck a licensing and acqui-hire deal with Windsurf, and Cognition bought what remained of the company within days. Scott first heard the news on Friday afternoon, and the deal was done by the start of the following week.

- Scott saw "such a clean fit": Windsurf is one of the leading IDEs, Cognition builds the agent, so together they offer IDE plus agent.
- Both companies have a clear enterprise focus, in how they do business, in their customers and in their teams.
- Scott describes the Windsurf team as a group he had been "huge fans of" from the beginning.
- He calls the announcement a "real acquisition", as opposed to an acqui-hire.

chunks.heading: How Cognition got to conviction quickly
chunks.text:
- Cognition had tried Windsurf's product itself and used it a lot, so it did not need a long diligence process to form a view.
- Scott frames Windsurf as complementary rather than competing: a "very different" offering in the AI code space.
- After one conversation with interim CEO Jeff Wang, both sides saw it as a perfect fit.
- Scott's reasoning for speed: "the sooner that we could get to an outcome, the better for the team and for the customers."
- Terms disclosed: every Windsurf employee received "immediate consideration" as part of the deal, and Windsurf employees became part of Cognition as one team. Scott did not give a cash/stock split or a price.

chunks.heading: Why the Google deal left a usable company behind
chunks.text:
- Scott's account of the structure: the Google deal was meant to be a "clean cut", leaving the product, the IP, the go-to-market team, the marketing team and the enterprise engineering team intact.
- Those left-behind components were exactly what Cognition was looking for.
- Scott says it is "a bit disappointing" that acqui-hires are becoming more common, because "a lot of great teams … get left behind."
- He treats the Windsurf deal as an alternative: instead of leaving the remainder of a company stranded, buy it and keep the team, product and customers together.

chunks.heading: Product thesis: the foreground and background agent combination
chunks.text:
- Windsurf is an IDE that lets a developer at the keyboard "go faster and produce code faster."
- Devin is an AI software engineering agent that developers delegate tasks to.
- Scott's workflow examples:
  - Kick off the agent to do a first pass on a project, then use Windsurf to add the finishing touches yourself.
  - Plan in the IDE, then hand the sorted-out task to the agent.
- Jeff Wang (Windsurf's interim CEO) put the combination as "the foreground agent and the background agent" under one roof.
- Scott says both companies were always focused on "making software engineering work in the real world", rather than demos.

chunks.heading: Enterprise distribution as the shared advantage
chunks.text:
Scott points to enterprise traction as part of why the pairing works:
- In the days around the deal, Cognition announced that Goldman Sachs and Citi (referred to as "City Bank" in the transcript) were rolling out Devin to their teams.
- Windsurf was already working with JP Morgan.
- Scott says that going down the customer list and the sectors, "we found a lot of natural partnership."

chunks.heading: Why the deal prioritized the team and the customers
chunks.text:
- Scott's stated priority was an outcome that was good for Windsurf's team and its customers, which pushed toward moving fast.
- He and Jeff Wang say the structure meant all Windsurf employees came with immediate consideration, and Wang notes that investor and founder shares were wiped from the cap table, making the remaining company employee-owned. Wang's view is that this left many people happy.
- Scott closes by endorsing the idea that the approach could be repeated: after an acqui-hire, a lot of valuable pieces remain, and a buyer can keep them whole.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu demos Devin and explains why Cognition built a coding agent: code gives agents iterative feedback loops, and agent UX is a new product problem. He argues agents turn engineers into managers and that software demand will grow, not shrink.

chunks.heading: Scott's pitch for autonomous coding agents: what Devin is and why code is the first domain
chunks.text:
Scott Wu co-founded Cognition AI, which builds Devin, which he describes as a "fully autonomous software engineer". It has access to the same tools a human engineer would use: a shell, a code editor, and a browser. His thesis is that language models have moved from text completion to agents that make their own decisions.

- **Timeline:** Cognition started in November 2023 (about seven months before this talk) in a Bay Area hacker house, then moved between the Bay and New York in progressively larger Airbnbs as the team grew.
- **First wave of generative AI:** He calls these "text completion products": ChatGPT, Q&A bots, marketing copy, customer support, GitHub Copilot and Cursor. The model gets a prefix and completes the suffix.
- **Second wave (agents):** These add "some amount of autonomous decision-making". That demands a much higher bar of consistency, and it creates a new product design problem because "the UX of agents is something that's extremely new".
- **Why Devin exists:** The team are "coding nerds", and teaching AI to code was one of the coolest things they could think of.

chunks.heading: The name game demo: plain-English iteration as the interface
chunks.text:
Scott demoed Devin building a mobile-friendly "name game" site (he struggles to memorize names and faces) in one morning.

- **The prompt:** He gave Devin a TSV file of the roughly 170 World's Fair speakers with their faces and asked it to show two random faces, show one name, and have him guess which face matches.
- **What Devin did on its own:** It made a plan, created a directory, started a React app, read the TSV, built the code, and deployed a first version in a few minutes.
- **The first version was close but not right.** It still showed both names, and he says he probably hadn't specified that well.
- **Feedback loop:** He fixed it with plain-English feedback only: hide the names until the user clicks an answer, restyle the "play again" button, add a streak counter that resets to zero on a wrong answer.
- **Takeaway:** "If software engineering is just this easy, if you can just explain exactly what you want in plain English", the world looks very different. He says he actually used the game and learned the names.
- **Plans change:** He notes Devin's plan changes a lot over time as it gets new information or feedback, as a human's would.

chunks.heading: Dogfooding: Devin building Devin inside a production codebase
chunks.text:
The Cognition team uses Devin on their own product daily.

- **Example:** An engineer (Bryce) asked Devin to add a search bar component to the Devin sessions list. That PR was merged and is the session search bar in the product.
- **Setup that makes production work possible:**
  - Devin starts from a **machine snapshot** with the repo already cloned.
  - It uses a **Playbook** that holds details about the team's repositories.
  - It works inside the team's git environment and opens PRs.
- **Conversation style:** Feedback is like talking to another engineer. Bryce asked for a magnifying glass icon, told it to be idiomatic and use the Phosphor icon library, and said "no need to test, I trust you". Devin mentioned a login issue it ran into.
- **Scope of internal use:** Many of Devin's API integrations, internal dashboards and metrics tracking were built by Devin. He calls it "Devin building the company with the company".

chunks.heading: Why code is a good domain for agents
chunks.text:
Scott gives three reasons, beyond the team being engineers.

1. **Software engineering is more than typing code.** Real work is investigating a bug, reading across files, running commands, pulling up docs, running the front end to reproduce an issue, editing, and trying again. That maps naturally to an agentic workflow.
2. **Code gives feedback to iterate on.** Fixing one bug in a codebase of thousands of files and hundreds of thousands of lines is hard for humans and AIs alike. Humans do it by adding print statements, pulling logs, checking monitoring and jumping between files. Each step is a decision followed by running real code to see what happened. That gives agents a cleaner path to a solution.
3. **Agentic capabilities are improving fast.** Even a demo this simple "would have been almost unthinkable" two years earlier, and training data and methods are improving rapidly.

chunks.heading: Agent UX is its own deep product problem
chunks.text:
Scott argues agent products shouldn't just copy existing software or human collaboration. His point is that an agent differs from both.

- Early mappings are "how we use software today" and "how we talk with other humans". Devin's features partly resemble "looking over your own intern's shoulder": you can see its computer and the commands it runs.
- The real differences involve parallel work, information gathering and managing context.
- **Features listed as part of the product iteration:** shell, code editing and web browsing, plus forking and rolling back sessions, Slack and GitHub integrations, Playbooks, machine snapshots, secrets management, and tools for verification.
- **Recently shipped:** VS Code Live Share into Devin's machine, so a user can make an edit alongside Devin and tell it "I went ahead and did that edit for you". He notes there is no close parallel in today's software.
- He expects "a lot more iteration" here over time.

chunks.heading: How Cognition's own workflow changed: async, parallel, "every engineer becomes a manager"
chunks.text:
- **Parallel Devins:** An engineer with four tasks can give each to its own Devin and run four in parallel. He describes this as "turning every engineer into an engineering manager".
- **How he describes Devin:** "Very enthusiastic interns". They try hard, don't know everything, get small things wrong and ask lots of questions, so you iterate with each.
- **Slack-first workflow:** Tag @Devin in a conversation ("change this color"), Devin makes the PR, you hit merge. The team has done this from the gym or the car.
- **Mobile angle:** You can "write code" without your computer because you can describe the task to Devin and review the code afterward.

chunks.heading: What's next: engineers spend more time on problem solving, and demand for software keeps growing
chunks.text:
Scott frames software engineers as doing two jobs.

1. **Problem solving with code:** deciding the solution, the architecture, the flows and the edge cases.
2. **Implementation:** debugging, writing functions, writing unit tests.

- **Today's split:** He estimates the average engineer spends about 10 to 20% of time on the first and 80 to 90% on the second.
- **His claim:** Devin frees engineers to do more of the first. Setting up Kubernetes, debugging broken APIs, and handling version changes and migrations are the things he expects to hand off. The role becomes "a mix between a technical architect and a product manager".
- **Devin doesn't decide what to build:** "Devin is not the one that decides what to do or what to build."
- **Headcount argument:** The job will change, but "there's actually going to be way more software engineers than ever". His precedent is punch cards, then assembly, then C: programming tools changed and the number of programmers grew.
- **Demand argument:** Software has been "the number one driver of progress in the world in the last 40 or 50 years", and demand for it is probably far more than 10x what is being built now. Each engineer becomes 5 to 10x more effective, and far more software gets built.

chunks.heading: Q&A positions: access, junior engineers, and remaining challenges
chunks.text:
- **Access:** Cognition was letting in more people every week and scaling up with enterprise customers, with a large waitlist.
- **Debugging in context:** In Cognition's own codebase, Devin has a machine with the dev environment, server and front end, so it can reproduce a bug, debug it and retry.
- **Junior engineers and interns:** He expects demand to keep rising with supply and training to change. What makes a great engineer is not typing speed but understanding problems, knowing architectures and never missing an edge case. Juniors will use those fundamentals "earlier and earlier".
- **Biggest challenges for the vision:** "Basically everything": speed, consistency, access, integrations and the right product UX. He sees a "rising tide" from new hardware, foundation models and agentic research, and expects optimizations at many layers of the stack rather than one fix.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cognition CEO Scott Wu explains how Devin started, why an applied AI lab differs from a foundation lab, and why RL needs the right evals and environments. He predicts agents will expand across the whole software lifecycle (testing, codebase understanding, PR review) and shares founder advice on honesty.

chunks.heading: Applied AI lab vs foundation lab: research in service of the product
chunks.text:
Scott describes Cognition as an "applied AI lab", as distinct from a foundation lab. Both kinds of company do research and build products. The difference is which one serves the other.
- A foundation lab advances basic research, and products come out of that research.
- At Cognition it runs the other way. The goal is to build something people will use and deliver value to customers, and all research comes from that.
- Cognition does not spend time on new attention mechanisms. It works on "hairier" practical problems: how to process and understand a large codebase, what information to pull, how to build a fast agent that explores a codebase and finds the right things quickly, and how to teach Devin to use Datadog well so it can debug.
- Cognition partners closely with all the foundation labs.
- Scott's framing is that many labs focus on code, while Cognition focuses on software engineering. Example: "my Kubernetes is down, let me go through the logs, figure out what happened, restart the service and see if that works." That is more than analyzing logical code problems in a vacuum.

chunks.heading: RL's real constraint is choosing the benchmark
chunks.text:
Scott calls Karpathy's line on RL ("horrible but the best thing we have") a good description.
- In theory, with a good eval set, a defined tool set and a way to judge success or failure, you can give it to a model over and over and wake up to a model that aces that benchmark. In practice it is far more finicky.
- Solving any benchmark does not mean you are done, because RL does not generalize well. Debugging a particular Kubernetes deploy is something you have to have done before. Broad software engineering or math practice only goes so far.
- So the question for everyone in AI becomes which benchmark you want to ace.
- The work has converged on defining the exact environments, tasks and evals, and how success or failure is determined, then building models around that.
- Code was one of the first domains where RL works, because the feedback loop is clean. You can run the code instead of needing a human judge.
- The same logic explains why the best human competitive programmer may still beat AI. At the very hardest problems there is far less data on totally new problem types. He says the bottleneck is "the data and the evals that we create", not a fundamental intelligence gap.

chunks.heading: How Cognition started: the November 2023 window
chunks.text:
- Scott and a group of long-time friends were exploring AI ideas and chose code. They were coding nerds themselves and saw clear breakthroughs coming.
- The thesis, in late 2023: RL was starting to work in the labs, and full multi-step, iterative processes (now called agents, though the category had no name then) were about to work.
- They talked about starting something over a lunch in New York. Right after, on Friday November 17, news broke that Sam Altman had been fired from OpenAI. Scott's reaction: if there was ever a time to start a company, it was now.
- He sent an email at 11:59 that night to get the pieces together and build critical mass. Altman was reinstated about two days later, but by then the team was already moving.
- They rented a hacker house in Burlingame, California for about a week and a half and iterated on many ideas. At first these were theoretical, researchy ideas such as improving problem solving in code. A second and third hacker house followed, and eventually it became Devin.

chunks.heading: Product evolution and the doubling time of agents
chunks.text:
- 18 months earlier, single-line tab completion was the only thing that worked in code. Since then Scott counts about 10 generations of products: multi-line tab, chat with codebase, synchronous multi-turn agents, asynchronous agents, automated testing, wikis, CLI and more.
- He cites the chart of how long an agent can work without human guidance. In code it has doubled every two to three months.
- The problem form factor changes at each doubling, not just the duration:
  - Seconds is tab complete.
  - Minutes means navigating between files, finding the right things and running CI.
  - Hours means planning out an actual task.
- Model capabilities are coupled to form factor, so what works moves from the IDE to the CLI to async agents as capabilities grow.

chunks.heading: Betting on the whole software lifecycle
chunks.text:
Cognition's bet is on everything in the software lifecycle, not just writing code. Scott notes engineers spend a minority of their time literally writing code. The rest goes to reading and understanding the codebase, planning, reviewing and testing.

His predictions for roughly the next 12 months:
- **Automated testing:** still early, but computer-use agents will be very capable. An agent makes a front-end change, clicks through the whole thing and sends back a screen-cap video of what it tried and how it looks now.
- **Codebase understanding:** much better tools for a human working with AI to understand an unfamiliar codebase. Today nothing helps until you know exactly what code to write. He expects a tool where you say "I want to rearchitect the build system" and it feeds back how things are now, the trade-offs that were made and what you could do differently.
- **AI PR review and automated bug catching:** will get much better.

chunks.heading: Product strategy: stay focused on the long-term picture
chunks.text:
- The controversial decision Scott names first is Devin itself. When Cognition started, "everyone thought we were crazy" to build a fully autonomous engineer that iterates multi-turn. Features like wikis were similarly early, when no one was thinking about them.
- The motivating question is always: what is the future of software engineering?
- In a hot market where "everything is going crazy at once", it is important to stay laser focused on how code will actually be written in 5 or 10 years and to keep getting closer to that.
- The specifics depend on which capabilities come online, but the direction is the anchor.

chunks.heading: Founder lesson: be honest with yourself
chunks.text:
Asked what he learned between his first company, Lunch Club, and Cognition, Scott's advice for founders:
- The most important part of founding a company is being honest with yourself.
- Founders often feel they must always be optimistic and the one who pushes things forward. Long-term belief that it is possible is needed, but it does not mean blindly pursuing things when you already have evidence of what is and is not working.
- At Cognition they say things like "Devin was so bad at this thing" and openly call out what they could do better, asking whether a strategy is right.
- In a fast-changing world, the bet is not that you had the right view at the start but that over all your iterations and work you will get there.

chunks.heading: AGI and what matters in practice
chunks.text:
- Scott's "we have AGI already" comment is partly facetious. He finds AGI hard to define. If AGI means automating 80% of human labor, then the tractor would count, since at some point more than 80% of work was farming.
- Humans do the things automation cannot, so any "post" definition keeps moving. Under a "pre" definition, 80% has been automated many times.
- He likes the line that in 2017 the answer to "do we have AGI" was no, and in 2025 it is "define AGI". There will be no smooth cutoff.
- The practical shift that matters is AI changing day-to-day lives, making people much more productive and widening what they can do. He says that is already happening.
- On the IMO gold and similar results: most day-to-day work is not harder than that. It does not mean a model will do everyone's jobs, but it is proof that with the right feedback loops, curriculums and setup, models can learn incredibly hard things.
- On beating the world's best competitive programmer, a Cognition colleague, within 12 months: Scott puts it at about 75% likely, while the colleague is confident it will not happen.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu announces Devin, an autonomous AI teammate that plans, codes, tests and deploys using a shell, editor and browser. The launch leads with concrete demos and a benchmark (13.86% on SWE-bench vs 1.96% prior) and frames the product as a collaborator rather than a replacement.

chunks.heading: Devin's pitch: an AI teammate, not a tool
chunks.text:
Scott launched Devin (2024-03-12) as "a tireless, skilled teammate, equally ready to build alongside you or independently complete tasks for you to review."

- The framing is a teammate that works either alongside you or independently.
- The stated benefit: engineers focus on more interesting problems, and teams can "strive for more ambitious goals."
- Cognition describes itself as "an applied AI lab focused on reasoning." Scott says that solving reasoning unlocks new possibilities in many disciplines, and "code is just the beginning."
- The mission line: help people around the world turn their ideas into reality.

chunks.heading: What makes Devin work: reasoning, tools and collaboration
chunks.text:
Scott credits three capabilities.

- **Long-term reasoning and planning.** Devin can plan and execute complex engineering tasks requiring thousands of decisions. It recalls relevant context at every step, learns over time, and fixes mistakes.
- **Human-equivalent tools.** It has the shell, code editor and browser inside a sandboxed compute environment, "everything a human would need to do their work."
- **Active collaboration.** Devin reports progress in real time, accepts feedback, and works through design choices with the user as needed.

chunks.heading: Demonstrating capability with concrete, real-world tasks
chunks.text:
Scott's launch relies on specific demos rather than abstract claims:

- **Learning unfamiliar technology:** after reading a blog post, Devin runs ControlNet on Modal to produce images with concealed messages.
- **Building and deploying end to end:** an interactive Game of Life site, with features added incrementally, deployed to Netlify.
- **Finding and fixing bugs:** helping maintain and debug an open source competitive programming book.
- **Training and fine-tuning models:** sets up fine tuning for a large language model given only a link to a research repository on GitHub.
- **Open source issues:** given just a GitHub issue link, it does the setup and context gathering itself.
- **Mature production repos:** a SWE-bench task fixing a logarithm bug in the sympy Python algebra system. Devin sets up the environment, reproduces the bug, then codes and tests the fix on its own.
- **Paid work:** Scott says they "even tried giving Devin real jobs on Upwork and it could do those too." In the example, Devin writes and debugs code to run a computer vision model, samples the data and compiles a report.

chunks.heading: Benchmarking with SWE-bench
chunks.text:
Scott used SWE-bench, a hard benchmark of real-world GitHub issues from projects like Django and scikit-learn, as the proof point.

- Devin resolves **13.86%** of issues end to end, versus the previous state of the art of **1.96%**.
- Even when told the exact files to edit, the best previous models resolved only **4.80%**.
- Devin was evaluated on a random 25% subset of the dataset.
- Devin was unassisted; all other models were assisted (told which files to edit). The comparison is deliberately framed to favor the harder, unassisted setting.
- He promised a more detailed technical report later.

chunks.heading: Launch strategy: early access and waitlist
chunks.text:
- Devin launched in early access "as we ramp up capacity," not general availability.
- Call to action: join the waitlist at cognition.com/get-started or email the team, positioned as "Hire Devin" for engineering work.
- Demand and capacity are managed through the waitlist rather than open signups.

chunks.heading: Credibility signals: funding and backers
chunks.text:
Scott cites social proof from investors and operators:

- A **$21 million Series A led by Founders Fund**.
- Named supporters include Patrick and John Collison, Elad Gil, Sarah Guo, Chris Re, Eric Glyman, Karim Atiyeh, Erik Bernhardsson, Tony Xu and Fred Ehrsam.
- The company describes itself as "well funded" and grateful for industry-leader support, using the backer list to establish trust for an unproven new category.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu announces Cognition's $400M+ raise at a $10.2B valuation and shares the growth numbers behind it. He explains the logic of owning both IDE and agent products and how the Windsurf acquisition accelerated enterprise growth.

chunks.heading: Cognition's $400M raise and growth numbers (Sept 2025)
chunks.text:
Cognition raised over $400M at a $10.2B post-money valuation, led by Founders Fund. Existing investors Lux Capital, 8VC (who jointly led the previous round), Neo, Elad Gil, Definition Capital and Swish VC doubled down. New investors were Bain Capital Ventures, Hanabi Capital and D1 Capital.

- Scott frames the mission as "the future of software engineering": a world of software abundance where engineers become architects and task "an army of autonomous agents" with everything else.
- He says that when Devin launched in March 2024, it wasn't clear this future would become real. Devin "could knock some tasks out of the park" but was mostly "a very junior engineer."
- His view: the baseline has changed drastically, and agents already do real work alongside individual developers and inside large enterprise teams. What "first seemed a fringe theory quickly became an obvious reality."

chunks.heading: Devin's growth and capital efficiency
chunks.text:
- Devin ARR (before the Windsurf acquisition) grew from $1M in September 2024 to $73M in June 2025, as usage increased exponentially.
- Growth stayed efficient: total net burn was under $20M across the company's entire history.
- Scott presents this as the proof point behind the raise: fast ARR growth with low cumulative burn.

chunks.heading: Why buying Windsurf worked: IDE plus agent
chunks.text:
- The Windsurf acquisition more than doubled Cognition's ARR. Scott says the bigger value was getting "the complete product suite for AI coding."
- His framing of the market: the two main forms of AI coding tools are IDEs and agents.
  - The IDE is for when the engineer wants to make each decision personally, with an AI speedup.
  - Agents are for delegating complete tasks asynchronously.
- His conclusion: "Engineers naturally want both." Cognition will keep investing significantly in both Devin and Windsurf, and customers are already seeing the combination's power.

chunks.heading: Post-acquisition growth and enterprise distribution
chunks.text:
- Combined enterprise ARR was up over 30% in the seven weeks after buying Windsurf.
- Pre-acquisition enterprise customer overlap was under 5%, so the two customer bases were largely additive.
- Scott calls the combination of Devin's rapid adoption with Windsurf's IDE product and "scaled GTM machine" a "massive unlock." Buying an existing go-to-market engine was part of the value, not just the product.
- Named customers across Devin and Windsurf: Goldman Sachs, Citi, Dell, Cisco, Ramp, Palantir, Nubank and Mercado Libre. He calls them "category-defining customers."

chunks.heading: Team and hiring
chunks.text:
- Scott says the thing he's most proud of is the team.
- Windsurf's team joined. Two early Cognition investors, Christian Lawless (Conversion Capital) and Emily Cohen (Neo), made a high-conviction decision to join full-time.
- swyx joined the team; Scott is a longtime fan of his work, from Latent Space to AI Engineer.
- Founding story: a small group of engineers with a lifelong love of coding and over a decade of friendship, who "hunkered down in a New York apartment and built the product we always wanted for ourselves."
- The core mission stayed the same as the company scaled: build the future of software engineering.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu announces Cognition's acquisition of Windsurf and shares the internal note to his team. It shows how to structure an acquisition around people (full vesting acceleration, equal treatment), and why combining an autonomous agent with an IDE and a scaled GTM engine is a strategic unlock.

chunks.heading: Deal terms and what Scott acquired
chunks.text:
- Cognition signed a definitive agreement to acquire Windsurf, the agentic IDE (announced 2025.07.14).
- The acquisition covers:
  - The Windsurf IDE, "now with _full_ access to the latest Claude models".
  - Windsurf's IP, product, trademark and the brand it built.
  - $82M of ARR, with enterprise ARR doubling quarter-over-quarter.
  - 350+ enterprise customers and hundreds of thousands of daily active users.
  - World-class GTM, engineering and product teams, which Scott calls "above all" the most valuable part of the deal.
- Scott's stated rationale: combining Devin's rapid adoption as the leading fully autonomous agent with Windsurf's IDE product and "scaled GTM machine" will be "a massive unlock". At the time, Devin was already a top contributor for many enterprise engineering teams.

chunks.heading: Treating acquired employees well
chunks.text:
- Scott says one of his top priorities in structuring the deal was to "honor their talent, hard work, and accomplishments". He and Windsurf's Jeff worked together on the terms.
- Every Windsurf employee gets the same package:
  - 100% participate financially in the deal.
  - 100% have vesting cliffs waived for work to date.
  - 100% receive fully accelerated vesting for work to date.
- New employees are to be treated like existing ones: "with transparency, fairness, and deep respect for their abilities and value."
- His framing for a merged team: "There's only one boat and we're all in it together."

chunks.heading: Announcing an acquisition: sequencing and communication
chunks.text:
- Scott discussed the deal at an all-hands first, then sent the team a note the morning the agreement was signed.
- The information was highly confidential until 11am PT, after Windsurf's all-hands.
- He asked the team to stay quiet until then, "out of respect for our new colleagues". The Windsurf team "deserves to hear this from Jeff and me in the right way."
- He recapped the deal terms plainly (what is owned, ARR, customers, employee treatment) before the vision.
- The note closes by crediting his own team's work ("it's your hard work that has brought us here"), acknowledging "the work won't be easy", and asking everyone to give new colleagues "a warm welcome".

chunks.heading: Integration plan and operating approach
chunks.text:
- Near term: the Windsurf team keeps operating as it has been. Cognition stays focused on accelerating customers' engineering with Devin.
