- Over the coming months: Cognition will "invest heavily" in integrating Windsurf's capabilities and unique IP into Cognition's products.
- After the announcement, the aim is to work "as a united and aligned team".

chunks.heading: Mission and positive-sum framing
chunks.text:
- Cognition's mission: "building the future of software engineering." Scott says the deal lets the company "move even faster" on it.
- His view of where engineering is heading: "Within our lifetime, engineers will go from bricklayers to architects, focusing on the creativity of designing systems rather than the manual labor of putting them together."
- He calls the deal "a huge win for all of us in the positive-sum game we're playing", and says "there's never been a more exciting time to build."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu argues AI vendors should prove value, not just report usage metrics like tokens or lines of code. Cognition built an estimator that scores each Devin session in human-engineer hours, validated it against customer estimates, and backs it with up to $10M in credits if value falls short of spend.

chunks.heading: Pricing AI on outcomes: the case for a productivity guarantee
chunks.text:
Scott argues that companies are spending more on AI than ever without knowing what they get for it. Dashboards show activity metrics such as "tokens consumed and lines of code generated", but none answer "how much value is the business actually getting out?"

- He says the industry needs to move from maximizing usage metrics to maximizing outcomes.
- There is no good standard for measuring outcomes today, and he argues AI vendors should be the ones to provide it.
- His closing principle: "Every AI vendor should be able to tell their customers what they're getting for their money."
- He hopes other AI companies move in the same direction.

chunks.heading: The AI Productivity Guarantee (Cognition, June 2026)
chunks.text:
Cognition offers its enterprise customers a financial guarantee on Devin's output.

- If Devin delivers less engineering value than the customer is paying for, Cognition funds the customer's usage, via credits, up to $10M, until it does.
- Engineering hours are converted to dollar value using a standard global rate.
- That value is compared against each customer's actual consumption near the end of their annual contract.
- If the value falls short, Cognition issues the credits.
- The guarantee applies to enterprise deployments, and interested customers contact Cognition (existing customers go through their account team).

chunks.heading: Why Scott is confident enough to guarantee
chunks.text:
Scott lists the reasons Cognition could put money behind its product's productivity:

- The estimator's results, validated against engineers' own time estimates.
- A review of historical productivity data.
- Devin is model-independent: Cognition uses the right model for each task, which helps customers optimize price performance.
- Devin has fine-grained controls to manage spend and steer users toward more productive prompts.
- Cognition's engagement model: teams embed in customer accounts to identify high-value projects, pair-program with engineers on their backlog, run enablement workshops on managing fleets of agents, and measure outcomes.

The takeaway is that the guarantee rests on both the product and a hands-on adoption process that drives usage toward productive work.

chunks.heading: How the productivity estimator works
chunks.text:
Cognition built an AI estimator to measure the productive engineering output Devin provides.

- An agent reviews each completed Devin session and answers two questions: did the session produce useful output, and if so, how long would a human engineer have taken to produce the same work?
- The estimator sees the user's prompt, the PR if one exists, every action Devin took, and codebase context from DeepWiki.
- Sessions that ended in unmerged PRs, or were otherwise classified as unproductive, count as not useful.
- Output is measured in hours of productive output, not lines of code, because lines don't track effort: "a critical bug that takes hours to investigate might be a two-line fix."

chunks.heading: Validation and honest limits
chunks.text:
- Cognition asked users across its enterprise customers how long their Devin tasks would have taken by hand, then validated the estimator against those answers.
- Scott concedes "no single estimate is perfect", but argues that across many tasks of varying complexity the highs and lows average out.
- The estimator measures engineering productivity (hours of useful output). It does not replace ROI measurement, which needs deeper context on the business value of each task.
- Cognition's customer-facing teams work with enterprises on full ROI impact. The estimator provides a baseline of productive output.
- He says Cognition will keep iterating and publish what it learns.

chunks.heading: Takeaways for pricing and selling a product
chunks.text:
- Replace vanity usage metrics with a measure of delivered value, and have the vendor own that measurement.
- Back the claim with money: a capped guarantee signals confidence and shifts risk from buyer to seller.
- Tie the guarantee to a clear, auditable calculation (hours of useful output times a standard rate versus actual spend, checked near the end of the annual contract).
- Pair the guarantee with embedded customer success so customers actually reach the value being guaranteed.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu and Jeff Wang reflect on the Cognition-Windsurf deal and the year after. The merge worked because the two companies' strengths (engineering vs GTM) were complementary and products didn't overlap. A "Just Keep Shipping" cadence took run rate from $73M to $500M+ and headcount from 44 to 350.

chunks.heading: How Scott frames the Windsurf deal: speed, complementary strengths, and one boat
chunks.text:
- The deal came together in about 72 hours: a first call after 5 p.m. on a Friday, almost no sleep, a signed definitive agreement by Monday morning, and an announcement that afternoon.
- Cognition prepared to go to Windsurf's offices on Saturday with a printed LOI, "ready to sign on the spot."
- Scott describes the moment four people (Jeff and Graham from Windsurf, Scott and Russell from Cognition) got in a room as "time seemed to slow down. Everything clicked."
- His fit logic was complementary gaps:
  - Cognition had built one of the best engineering orgs in Silicon Valley and wanted a GTM org.
  - Windsurf had built one of the best GTM orgs and wanted engineering.
  - The products did not overlap: Cognition had a cloud agent (Devin), Windsurf had an IDE.
- Windsurf brought millions of users, a brand developers loved, and a strong team.
- The merger message to the Windsurf team: "there's only one boat and we're all in it together."
- Context he describes from the Windsurf side: many team members had just left for Google, recruiters were contacting those who remained, and customers were calling to ask what was happening.

chunks.heading: Post-merger cadence: "Just Keep Shipping"
chunks.text:
- Three days after the deal closed, the team shipped Wave 11, named "Just Keep Shipping." Scott says it "set the tone for the year."
- The shipping record over 12 months, month by month:
  - July 2025: Voice Mode, Named Checkpoints, @-mention past conversations, Planning Mode on by default, Devin's MCP Marketplace.
  - August 2025: DeepWiki in the IDE, Dev Containers support, 100+ bug fixes in a single wave.
  - October 2025: SWE-grep, IL6-ready.
  - December 2025: parallel agents, Git worktree support, Cascade Hooks, system-level Rules and Workflows for enterprise.
  - January 2026: Plan Mode, Megaplan, Agent Trace, Arena Mode.
  - March 2026: new token-based plans including Max, Devin can manage Devins, scheduled Devins.
  - April 2026: self-serve Devin plans, daily limits removed, per-message token counts.
  - May 2026: Android emulator support, Devin gets a Windows PC, Auto-Triage.
  - June-July 2026: Security in Devin Review, FrontierCode, Devin Fusion, Devin Security Swarm, Devin Security Vulnerability Remediation Program.
- The shipping pace included small quality items (bug-fix waves, limits removed) alongside headline features.

chunks.heading: Growth numbers since the merger
chunks.text:
- Revenue run rate grew from $73M to $500M+ since merging the brands.
- The team grew from 44 to 350 people.
- The team wrote 20M+ lines of code locally.
- Offices now span San Francisco, New York, London, Singapore, and Tokyo, with more international offices planned and teams on the ground in additional places.
- The company entered new industries and partnered with new teams such as automakers and systems integrators.

chunks.heading: Product strategy: own models, stay neutral, unify the brand
chunks.text:
- Cognition built its own models: SWE-1.5 (served at about 1000 tokens per second), then SWE-1.6, then SWE-1.7, launched the week before the post and described as "the most capable and efficient model we've trained to date."
- Positioning: Scott calls the company "the Switzerland of AI." Evidence for it: model evaluation is put in the open through Arena Mode and a public leaderboard.
- Surface strategy: Windsurf 2.0 brought every agent into a single command center. The company then unified into one brand with Devin Desktop, "your home for software engineering." Devin is now available "on every surface with any agent and any model."
- Other launches in the year: Devin Review, Devin CLI, Devin 2.2, and Cognition for Government.
- Commercial confidence move: the AI Productivity Guarantee, which Scott frames as putting "our money where our mouth is."

chunks.heading: How Scott describes the agent's progression
chunks.text:
- A year earlier, most AI code tools handled simple tasks like autocomplete or explaining a function. Devin was effective at isolated tasks such as script writing and bug fixes, with a gap to the long-term vision.
- Today he says Devin operates at a mid-to-senior level.
  - It launches, schedules, and manages other Devins.
  - Each new Devin learns from the history of the agents before it.
  - It tests its own work with computer use, self-verification, and autofixes.
- Where he thinks it goes next: a shift to "self-driving software development." Engineers become "super engineers," and people who never coded can leverage themselves in ways they never imagined.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scott Wu announces Cognition's acquisition of The Interaction Company, maker of Poke. It shows how he picks acquisition targets: a team with a shared thesis (always-on cloud agents), fast execution, and a product people love for being proactive and personal.

chunks.heading: Poke: a personal agent that lives in your texts
chunks.text:
- Scott describes Poke, made by The Interaction Company of California, as "a personal agent that lives in your texts."
- It messages the user first, follows up, and "feels less like software and more like a friend."
- Scale he cites: more than 100 million messages exchanged in the last three months. It is the only AI agent approved to text natively on Apple Messages.
- Reach: "hundreds of thousands of people" use it as "a partner in everyday life."
- The traits he credits for the product's appeal: it is proactive, it knows you, and it is fun to talk to.

chunks.heading: Why Scott applies the Poke model to Devin
chunks.text:
- Scott says the Poke traits (proactive, knows you, fun to talk to) are "exactly how working with Devin should feel."
- He frames the acquisition as combining two audiences. Devin is used by some of the world's top companies for software engineering. Poke is used by consumers in everyday life.
- The goal he states is to shape how humans and AI collaborate, and to build that experience together with the Interaction team.

chunks.heading: The shared bet: always-on cloud agents
chunks.text:
- Scott says the two teams have made the same bet from the beginning: always-on cloud agents.
- Cognition's role after the deal is infrastructure and models. Scott says "Cognition's models and infrastructure will make Poke even faster and more reliable."
- Poke users continue using the product as before, with no disruption at announcement.

chunks.heading: How Scott evaluates a team to acquire
chunks.text:
- Prior relationship: Scott knew and admired Marvin (the Interaction founder) and his team for years. Scott and Walden were early angel investors in Interaction.
- Traits he values: "exceptional people who move extremely fast and aim for only the most ambitious products."
- Product conviction comes first. He opens by saying that if you have used Poke, you know why they are excited, so a product people love is the core signal.
- Alignment on strategy matters: the teams were already placing the same long-term bet before the deal.

chunks.heading: Deal facts
chunks.text:
- Announced 2026-07-23: The Interaction Company of California joins Cognition.
- No price or terms are disclosed.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A long Q&A with Cognition founder Scott Wu on his path from math olympiads to building Devin, an AI coworker. He covers company focus, staying model-neutral, founder traits, using forcing functions to commit, and why the AI agent should behave like a coworker rather than a tool.

chunks.heading: Cognition's mission and why Scott stays "Switzerland"
chunks.text:
- Scott says Cognition's one goal is "to make it much easier for everyone around the world to build software." He frames the larger aim as moving people from "Minecraft survival mode" to "Minecraft creative mode" (a line he credits to co-founder Walden Yan).
- He argues a company can have different functions and verticals but only one goal. Cognition's goal differs from a foundation lab's, whose goal is advancing research itself.
- He believes company DNA is "kind of rigid, more so than people usually expect." The mission can change over time, "but not as much as you think." Customers, products and business model all root in that one thing.
- Why Cognition stays model-neutral ("Switzerland"):
  - It wants to be the trusted infrastructure partner that helps companies ship much more.
  - "Signing away our trust to a specific model would be a scary thing to do. Nobody even knows who's going to have the best model in 12 months."
  - Working with all models lets it use each where it is best and advise partners on which to use.
- He rejects Silicon Valley cynicism that new companies can't be built from scratch because incumbents "are going to go eat everything." He calls it "totally misguided" and says building something new is also "just more fun this way."

chunks.heading: Devin as an AI coworker, not a tool
chunks.text:
- Scott says Cognition always framed Devin as a coworker. It is a full agent with its own machine that does its own work, lives in the same systems (Slack, Jira, etc.) and works alongside you.
- The name was deliberate: "there's a reason we decided to call it Devin as opposed to naming it like a tool." He thinks of it as "its own being that can go and do stuff."
- Two years earlier this was an aspiration needing heavy handholding. Now, he says, "you really can just work with it as a coworker."
- A decent fraction of customers' Devin sessions are no longer started by humans. They are triggered automatically, or run in loops that look for problems in products and fix them. Devins now find the tasks as well as do them.

chunks.heading: How Cognition started: timing, forcing functions and RL
chunks.text:
- Scott's path: Addepar (performance engineering, some parts about 100x faster), two years at Harvard (dropped out), then LunchClub with Vlad Novakovski from 2017. He left LunchClub in June 2022.
- He treats the stretch after as a sabbatical: exploring crypto, security and zero-knowledge with Steven Hao and Andrew He, then getting deeper into AI after ChatGPT (November 2022).
- Why he started Cognition:
  - He followed research papers and saw reinforcement learning working on math and code, so "the logical next step was actually kind of obvious, but the next step wasn't published."
  - The thesis: reasoning is getting better, RL is working, so now is the time for a new lab.
- Forcing function: on November 17, 2023 (the day Sam Altman was fired) he was pitching the idea over lunch. He decided "if there's ever a time to do it, we should probably just do this right now."
- His view of founding: "The moment of just actually committing yourself... we've all started companies before... but this one is the big one. This is the one for life."
- Execution:
  - He organized a hacker house in Burlingame over Thanksgiving 2023, weeks after his mother died, and canceled family plans to do it.
  - He messaged AI people he knew and invited them to hack together.
  - A second house followed in December, and they kept the house going until January 2026.

chunks.heading: What actually drove AI progress, and how to read benchmarks
chunks.text:
- Scott sees models beating humans on the AMC (a hard high-school math competition) in early 2024 as a proof of concept. Hard problems require logical reasoning, creativity and long chains of reasoning that all line up. Models doing that with enough RL and the right data suggests practical tasks are achievable.
- He says the last two years had no huge breakthrough in attention or RL itself. Progress came from:
  - More compute and data.
  - Tackling real-world problems: training models against rubrics for what is good for a given task.
  - Deploying in the real world and building product experiences. He calls this "messy, practical work" and credits it, more than researcher techniques, for the explosion in AI usage.
- On "jagged" intelligence: he thinks models will always be jagged relative to humans, because they are trained on internet tokens and so excel at knowledge work first. He notes coding is literally "talking to a computer," so it is unsurprising it was the first great use case. It "almost says more about human intelligence than it does about computer intelligence."

chunks.heading: Where humans still have the edge, and what's coming
chunks.text:
- Scott's near-term view: AGI is "much more of an ascent" than a binary. Humans keep an edge in high-context, general-purpose work needing "soft context": decisions, principles and the history of why systems were built a certain way.
- He says retrieval is what humans do best, such as a memory triggered by one file of code ("four months ago I was working on this and we had this bug"), even though our context window is short (his joke: we could not handle 10-digit two-factor codes).
- Two AI problems he names for closing the gap: embedding search over all past conversations and code, and continual learning, where the AI updates its own weights as it goes. He expects both to be solved "maybe not so long from now."
- On the long run he does not think any single capability will stay uniquely human. Past "AI will never do X" claims (chess, Go, math, code, new theorems) were disproven.
- The METR result he cites: agents have moved from seconds to minutes to hours of human-equivalent work, doubling every few months. He asks what happens if that continues to days, weeks, then a year, and says "I think that is where we will get to."
- His framing of the shift: the last 200 years automated raw physical strength, and now AI is on the verge of automating raw mental strength. "The bottleneck to turning our dreams into reality will dramatically narrow." AI is "the lever that will ensure our dreams don't have to forever remain dreams."

chunks.heading: The 10% / 90% of building software, and automating drudgery
chunks.text:
- Scott's test for drudgery: ask how many ideas a person has in a day and how many they actually get to do. He guesses it is "probably like 5%."
- In software, he says no engineering team ever finishes everything they want: "you have 85 projects and you have to pick six because that's how much bandwidth you have."
- He splits the job into about 10% self-expression (trade-offs, architecture, what product to build) and 90% "code monkeying and execution." When people say they love building software, they usually mean the 10%.
- His prediction, which applies to every field: people will get to "do 10 times more of the 10% you actually love."

chunks.heading: Risks Scott worries about
chunks.text:
- His biggest worry is not AI itself but the friction from how fast it moves. He compares it to past revolutions (electricity, the internet, mobile, cloud), which are similar at a high level, but this one is faster. The Industrial Revolution played out over generations, and in earlier revolutions adopting two to five years late was still fine. "In this case, it has to happen faster."
- The bad outcome he names: a long period where only elites in SF have access and everyone else does not.
- A specific example: strong model cyber capabilities where much of the world isn't using them for defense while attackers use them for offense, which makes the balance "pretty tricky."
- His remedy is education and getting everyone on the technology at the same time.

chunks.heading: The founder profile: intelligence plus hunger, and the competition network
chunks.text:
- Scott says two qualities matter in his field: intelligence and hunger. The competition community selects for being "super smart" and "salty and want[ing] to beat everybody up." If you analyze what went wrong and adjust constantly, motivated enough to do it for years, you can usually get good at the downstream skills too.
- He says startup founding is going through a "Moneyball" arc like poker and chess, shifting from the Steve Jobs-type profile to a technical one. In AI especially, deep technical background is "extremely valuable" because the problems are deeply technical.
- He credits a network effect: Alexandr Wang was the first of their group to start a company, and "since we were all so tight... it was very much like, we should all go and do this." He and Alexandr kept a doc of startup ideas in middle school.
- Cognition itself was started with many friends from that competition network. He says "we were all very, very lucky to have each other" and notes many people do not realize entrepreneurship is an option.
- Habits he describes about himself: he thinks intuitively rather than memorizing theorem names, and he wanted to beat everyone regardless of age (third grader winning the ninth-grade division). His mother told him he had the potential to be the best, rather than comparing him to others.

chunks.heading: Personal drive and what he's choosing to do
chunks.text:
- Scott describes his mother's death on October 6, 2023 as one of the biggest events of his life. He spent over a year at home during COVID and moved back in 2023 as she got sicker. He says the period made him think about his values and his life's work. Cognition started the next month.
- On his purpose: "There's a chance AI is the most important event in human history, and coding is how it will learn to act and build things in the real world. If I was meant to do something... I think it's to be the guy who teaches AI how to code."
- His fear is not failure but not trying: "the world where I actually couldn't live with myself is the one where I took this thing that was a perfect match for everything I've always naturally loved... and just didn't give it my all."

People have asked about our culture and recent employee communications. Cognition has an extreme performance culture, and we’re upfront about this in hiring so there are no surprises later. We routinely are at the office through the weekend and do some of our best work late into the night. Many of us literally live where we work. We know that people who joined Windsurf didn’t expect to join Cognition and while we’re proud of how we work, we understand it’s not for everyone.

We gave our team the opportunity to decide. We offered for all employees who joined via acquisition to opt into our culture with full clarity on what entails. We know that we will lose some strong talent in doing this, but we truly believe the level of intensity this moment demands from us is unprecedented. While not everyone is looking for a culture like ours, everyone deserves respect and appreciation for their work.  Regardless of their decision, we accelerated and cashed out all four years of equity for everyone from Windsurf, even for the 85% of employees who hadn’t hit their one year cliff. And for those who opt out, we’re providing an additional nine months of pay on top of this.

As an engineer, you spend a lot more time reading and understanding code than you do writing code. But codebases aren't necessarily optimized for this; scrolling through a ton of CRUD functions tells you a lot less about what a file does than a clear explanation of why the code exists and how it fits into the system around it.

Think of Codemaps as an in-depth DeepWiki that you can create in real time on any section of your codebase. It identifies the key semantic pieces of your code and then organizes them in a way that is optimized for human readability.

Excited to hear what you all think!

I'm often asked what programming will look like in 10 years or if it's even worth studying CS anymore. The future of software engineering is the single biggest question we think about in building Devin: 🧵

At its essence, programming is about telling computers what to do. Someday these computers may do everything themselves, but until then instructing them properly will be more important than ever.

The practical question today is less about replacement and more about how every engineer can be maximally effective.

AI has already made coding significantly more efficient synchronously - adoption among top engineers is close to 100% - but synchronous improvement is inherently capped.

Token generation is fast but not instant, and moreover a lot of software engineering is dependent on real-time events like running CI, spinning up the local dev server, or processing logs.
This means the next big unlock will come from building the interface and capability to delegate to multiple agents in parallel.

But delegation is not a single-shot process, and you often don’t know every implementation detail of what you plan to build when you first sit down. The multi-agent flow needs to support the ability to hand off and back on easily - describe the change, have the agent build the first pass, and then have it run the product locally so you can easily look and decide what’s next.

I first learned to program when I was 9 years old and fell in love with the ability to turn my ideas into reality. Now, teaching AI to code at @cognition_labs has been a dream come true. We've still got a long way to go; if this sounds like something you'd like to work on, please DM!

GPT-4.5 has been awesome to work with. On our agentic coding benchmarks it already shows massive improvements over o1 and 4o. Excited to see the models' continued trajectory on code!

One interesting data point: though GPT-4.5 and Claude 3.7 Sonnet score similarly on our overall benchmark, we find that GPT-4.5 spikes more heavily on tasks involving architecture and cross-system interactions whereas Claude 3.7 Sonnet spikes more on raw coding and code editing.

As AI takes on increasingly complex tasks, we believe that multi-model agents that incorporate each model’s unique strengths will perform best.

Devin has saved companies millions of dollars and has shown as much as an 8x productivity boost in engineering time. Great to chat with Forbes about the work Devin has been doing with customers like Nubank, Ramp, and MongoDB! https://t.co/NIsOBH0Ox1
The new o3 price drop makes it 15x cheaper than gpt-4-32k, the SOTA model from two years ago. Meanwhile the number of use cases is probably up 1,000,000x. Kudos to the openai team!

When we started Cognition, we were a small group of engineers who shared a lifelong love of coding. We hunkered down in an apartment in NYC and built the product we always wanted for ourselves.

A lot has changed over the last 20 months but the core vision has not. We see a future where every engineer can become an architect - solving the most important parts of each problem and then working with a team of agents to do the rest.

AI has meaningfully enhanced the way we write code already but it seems clear that there are still bigger changes to come. If you're interested to work on building the future of software engineering with us, we'd love to talk to you!

Slack came out in 2014. At the time it wasn't obvious why you'd want to use it. We already had email for professional conversations; quick group messages felt too unrefined to use at work.

Coding agents are at a similar inflection point today. Most engineers are used to writing and reviewing every line of code themselves. The idea of working across multiple threads and delegating core parts of development to AI can sound scary at first.

But just as early Slack adopters learned a new way to work and became more productive, early users of coding agents have discovered the right usage patterns through trial & error and have learned how to do a lot more.

Over the last year and a half we’ve learned that coding agents are insanely powerful but come with a learning curve. So we sat down and wrote up everything we’ve learned from 250,000 merged PRs, from our own usage and our users’.

Today we’re sharing Agents 101, a platform-agnostic guide to using any coding agent. It’s a short doc on how to incorporate async agents into your flow and includes the actionable tips that we use to make Devin our top code contributor. We’ll be updating this regularly and would love to hear your thoughts.
https://t.co/eEtYi96lGR

Wow - it's been quite the month.

We announced Devin just a few weeks ago. It's been awesome to see all the support and feedback we've gotten since.

AI agents are just getting started. Two years ago it was unthinkable that an AI could write code, run commands, and browse the web. We're really excited for what the next two years will bring.

Our vision is for Devin to be the assistant that makes every software engineer 10x more productive. Software is such an important driver of progress in the world today - imagine what we could do with 10x more of it!

At the same time, we want to be clear that Devin is far from perfect today. Devin will often work but will often make mistakes, write bugs, or get stuck. We're excited to have more users try the product so that we can continue to build with your feedback.

There's a lot more work to do. If you're interested to build Devin with us, we'd love to hear from you!

Excited to try out OpenAI Codex! With each increase in capabilities, writing code with AI looks more like working with your own team of agents. Some of the open questions that remain for all of us:

-What data & tooling should the agent have access to? The codebase itself is the obvious one, but human engineers work with lots of other data sources on a day-to-day basis: CI, logs, documentation, issue-tracking, runtime info, and broad Internet access.

Think of software engineering as a pipeline. Historically, the hardest part was writing the code itself. Not the case anymore - honest question: how much of your code do you actually have to type at this point? For us it's probably <10%.

As agents get more capable, the bottleneck becomes less about writing code and more about two things: 1) making it easier for humans to understand, plan, and ask questions. 2) making it easier for agents to ingest all the real-world context surrounding your task.

Hence, DeepWiki & DeepWiki MCP. There's a "nihilist" view that as AI gets better, interfaces won't matter anymore. I think the opposite is true - AI will soon be so good that the way you interact & knowledge-transfer will be the only thing that matters.

Model routing is a hot topic but there are two challenges to doing routing for coding agents:
1) Even if different models can pass the task, there are subtle differences in behavior & style that mean they aren't perfectly interchangeable.
2) The initial agent prompt isn't enough to know the difficulty of the task. "Fix xyz bug" could be a one-line edge case or could require rearchitecting your entire product; you can't know until you've actually investigated the code.

How do you solve these problems? Well, you need evals that account for style and behavior, not just pass/fail. And you need the agent to be able to dynamically update and re-route. SWE-Bench style grading has been the standard for years now - you ask the agent to solve an issue and then run its code on a pre-constructed unit test.

The problem is that passing a unit test is only one part of writing production-ready code. You also want to evaluate agents on a number of other axes, including scope, coding style, and unintended side effects.

The result is our new benchmark FrontierCode - which has ~80% fewer false positives and for which the best model (Opus 4.8) only scores 13%!

Measuring someone's productivity by their token usage is a horrible idea. Giving everyone the same fixed token budget isn't much better. So what's the right way to roll out AI across your org?

We built a system to measure how many productive engineering hours every Devin task is worth, validated against a dataset of real engineers’ times estimates. The goal is to answer the fundamental question that companies are grappling with: how much real value are you getting from each of your agent sessions?

On top of that, we're giving an AI productivity guarantee! Now if Devin delivers less engineering value than you're paying for, we fund your usage until it does.

The whole industry needs to move from measuring activity to measuring output. We hope to see more AI companies taking this approach.

Most AI review tools today center around asking an arms-length agent to catch & report potential bugs. This is really valuable! But until we reach the point where you can confidently hit "Merge" on a 5000-line agent PR, you're still bottlenecked on reviewing the code yourself.

This will stay true for a while even as the tools get better. Would you rather have an arms-length AI that catches 80% of bugs or an AI-powered review UX that makes *you* 5x faster? Probably the latter since you'd still have to review the whole PR yourself to catch the last 20%.

Of course, the best review experience should have both! We built Devin Review with these thoughts in mind. Let us know what you think!
